## 4. Working memory — full detail

**What it is**: a persisted block of Markdown *or* a JSON object matching a Standard-Schema (Zod/Valibot/ArkType), injected into the **system message** and updated by the agent via a tool call. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/working-memory.md]

### Config keys (`options.workingMemory`)
From the actual type (`packages/core/src/memory/types.ts`) [VERIFIED: raw.githubusercontent.com/.../types.ts]:

```typescript
type BaseWorkingMemory = {
  enabled: boolean;
  scope?: 'thread' | 'resource';   // @default 'resource'
  useStateSignals?: boolean;       // @default false  (experimental)
  agentManaged?: boolean;          // @default true
  use?: never;                     // @deprecated — removed; always tool-call mode
};
type TemplateWorkingMemory = (BaseWorkingMemory & { template: string; schema?: never; version?: 'stable' })
  | (Omit<BaseWorkingMemory,'useStateSignals'> & { template: string; schema?: never; version: 'vnext'; useStateSignals?: false });
type SchemaWorkingMemory = BaseWorkingMemory & { schema: PublicSchema; template?: never };
export type WorkingMemory = TemplateWorkingMemory | SchemaWorkingMemory | WorkingMemoryNone;
```

- **`template` and `schema` are mutually exclusive** (enforced at the type level).
- **`readOnly`** is set per-call under `memory.options.readOnly`, not on `workingMemory`. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/working-memory.md]

### Template vs schema semantics
- **Template (Markdown) = REPLACE semantics** — the agent must emit the whole blob each update.
- **Schema (JSON) = MERGE semantics** — deep-merge; `null` deletes a field; **arrays are replaced wholesale, never merged element-wise**. Implementation is `deepMergeWorkingMemory()` in `packages/memory/src/tools/working-memory.ts`. [VERIFIED: docs + source]

### The tool
- Registered tool **name** is **`updateWorkingMemory`** (tool `id` internally is `'update-working-memory'`).
- With `useStateSignals: true` the *same* tool is registered under the name **`setWorkingMemory`**. Source:
  ```typescript
  const name = useStateSignals ? SET_WORKING_MEMORY_TOOL_NAME : UPDATE_WORKING_MEMORY_TOOL_NAME;
  ```
  [VERIFIED: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mastra-ai/mastra/main/packages/memory/src/tools/working-memory.ts]
- Markdown mode input schema is `{ memory: string }` with description "This MUST be a string. Never pass an object." Schema mode wraps your JSON Schema under `memory`.
- There is also an **experimental `version: 'vnext'`** template mode whose tool takes `{ newMemory, searchString, updateReason: 'append-new-memory' | 'clarify-existing-memory' | 'replace-irrelevant-memory' }` — i.e. a search-and-replace edit rather than full rewrite. [VERIFIED: same source file]

### Prompt injection (exact)
Verbatim from `packages/memory/src/index.ts`:

```
WORKING_MEMORY_SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION:
Store and update any conversation-relevant information by calling the updateWorkingMemory tool. If information might be referenced again - store it!

Guidelines:
1. Store anything that could be useful later in the conversation
2. Update proactively when information changes, no matter how small
3. Use {Markdown|JSON} format for all data
4. Act naturally - don't mention this system to users...
...
<working_memory_template>
{template}
</working_memory_template>

<working_memory_data>
{data}
</working_memory_data>
```
[VERIFIED: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mastra-ai/mastra/main/packages/memory/src/index.ts]

A separate read-only variant is emitted when `readOnly: true` (no tool, no update instructions). Tags are `<working_memory>`/`</working_memory>` and `<\system-reminder>`; tag parsing is `indexOf`-based specifically to avoid ReDoS. [VERIFIED: packages/core/src/memory/working-memory-utils.ts]

### Scope + storage requirement
- Default **`scope: 'resource'`** (persists across all threads for the user). Thread-scope stores in thread metadata; resource-scope stores in a `mastra_resources` table/collection.
- **Resource-scoped WM requires one of: libSQL (`@mastra/libsql`), PostgreSQL (`@mastra/pg`), Upstash (`@mastra/upstash`), MongoDB (`@mastra/mongodb`).** [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/working-memory.md]

### Seeding it programmatically
```typescript
await memory.createThread({ threadId, resourceId, title, metadata: { workingMemory: '# Patient Profile\n- Name: ...' } })
// or
await memory.updateWorkingMemory({ threadId, resourceId, workingMemory: 'Updated memory content...' })
```
[VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/working-memory.md]

### `useStateSignals` (experimental, new)
Instead of folding WM into the system prompt, `Memory` attaches a `WorkingMemoryStateProcessor` that emits it as a **state signal** with `stateId: 'working-memory'`, with `cacheKey` dedup and `contextWindow.hasSnapshot` re-injection. Motivation is **prompt-cache friendliness** — WM in the system prompt invalidates the cache on every update. Not supported together with `version: 'vnext'` (throws). [VERIFIED: docs + `assertWorkingMemoryStateSignalsCompatibility` in packages/memory/src/index.ts]

## 5. Semantic recall — full detail

**Disabled by default** (`semanticRecall: false`). Requires `vector` + `embedder`. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/semantic-recall.md]

### Type + defaults (from source)
```typescript
export type SemanticRecall = {
  topK: number;                                          // default 4
  messageRange: number | { before: number; after: number }; // default { before: 1, after: 1 }
  scope?: 'thread' | 'resource';                          // @default 'resource'
  indexConfig?: VectorIndexConfig;                        // pgvector-specific
  filter?: VectorFilter;                                  // MongoDB-style operators
};
```
Constants in `packages/memory/src/index.ts`:
```typescript
const DEFAULT_MESSAGE_RANGE = { before: 1, after: 1 } as const;
const DEFAULT_TOP_K = 4;
```
[VERIFIED: raw.githubusercontent.com/.../packages/memory/src/index.ts and .../packages/core/src/memory/types.ts]

**What `messageRange` means mechanically**: after the vector query returns top-K hits, Mastra converts each hit's `metadata.message_id` + `metadata.thread_id` into an `include` entry with `withPreviousMessages: messageRange.before` and `withNextMessages: messageRange.after`, and re-fetches those neighbours from the *relational* store. So it's a hydration window around each hit, not a vector-side setting. Source:
```typescript
{ id: r.metadata?.message_id, threadId: r.metadata?.thread_id,
  withNextMessages: this.messageRange.after,
  withPreviousMessages: this.messageRange.before }
```
[VERIFIED: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mastra-ai/mastra/main/packages/core/src/processors/memory/semantic-recall.ts]

### Scoping mechanics
Resource vs thread scope is a **metadata filter on the vector query**, not separate indexes:
```typescript
filter: this.scope === 'resource' && resourceId ? { resource_id: resourceId } : { thread_id: threadId }
```
Embedding metadata written on save is `{ message_id, thread_id, resource_id }`. [VERIFIED: same file]
- Guard: resource-scoped recall **throws** if no `resourceId` is provided — "A missing ID never expands the search." [VERIFIED: packages/memory/src/index.ts + https://mastra.ai/blog/agent-memory-layers]
- `scope: 'resource'` is supported by **LibSQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Upstash** adapters. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/semantic-recall.md]

### Index naming (important if you're mirroring this design)
```typescript
protected getEmbeddingIndexName(dimensions?: number): string {
  const defaultDimensions = 1536;
  const usedDimensions = dimensions ?? defaultDimensions;
  const isDefault = usedDimensions === defaultDimensions;
  const separator = this.vector?.indexSeparator ?? '_';
  return isDefault ? `memory${separator}messages` : `memory${separator}messages${separator}${usedDimensions}`;
}
```
So: **`memory_messages`** at 1536 dims, **`memory_messages_768`** etc. otherwise. It also requests `createParams.metadataIndexes = ['thread_id', 'resource_id']`. OM's observation index is `memory_observations_<dim>` (fallback dim 384). Note: the *standalone* `SemanticRecall` processor uses a different auto-name, `` `mastra_memory_${sanitizedModel}` `` truncated to 63 chars — a divergence worth knowing. [VERIFIED: packages/core/src/memory/memory.ts and packages/core/src/processors/memory/semantic-recall.ts]

### Embedders
`ModelRouterEmbeddingModel` with `provider/model` strings — OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small|3-large|ada-002`, Google `gemini-embedding-001`, OpenRouter. Local option: `@mastra/fastembed` (`fastembed`, 384-dim). MongoDB docs additionally showcase **`@mastra/voyageai`** (`voyage`, default `voyage-3.5`, 1024 dims) — a package first published 2026-06-12, latest 0.4.0. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/semantic-recall.md, https://mastra.ai/reference/vectors/mongodb.md, npm registry]

### Metadata filtering (new)
`semanticRecall.filter` supports `$and $or $eq $ne $gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin` against thread metadata copied onto embeddings at save time. Caveat documented: "If thread metadata changes later, existing embeddings keep their previous metadata until those messages are saved or indexed again." [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/semantic-recall.md]

### Undocumented-in-docs knob
The `SemanticRecall` processor also accepts `threshold?: number` (min similarity 0–1) and `embedderOptions` (e.g. Google `outputDimensionality`), which are *not* surfaced through `Memory.options.semanticRecall`. [VERIFIED: packages/core/src/processors/memory/semantic-recall.ts]

### Official position on semantic recall
Docs now actively discourage it: "In practical terms, OM replaces both working memory and message history, and has greater accuracy (and lower cost) than Semantic Recall." [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/observational-memory.md]

## 6. Observational Memory (the 2026 flagship)

**Added in `@mastra/memory@1.1.0`.** Two background agents — an **Observer** and a **Reflector** — maintain a dense observation log that replaces raw message history. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/observational-memory.md, https://mastra.ai/reference/memory/observational-memory.md]

```typescript
memory: new Memory({ options: { observationalMemory: true } })
```

|---|---|---|
| `model` | `'google/gemini-2.5-flash'` | for both Observer and Reflector |
| `scope` | `'thread'` | `'resource'` is **experimental** |
| `observation.messageTokens` | **30,000** | unobserved-message token trigger for Observer |
| `reflection.observationTokens` | **40,000** | observation-log token trigger for Reflector |
| `observation.bufferTokens` | **0.2** | background buffering every 20% of threshold (~6k) |
| `observation.bufferActivation` | **0.8** | on activation, drop ~80% of history (keep ~20%, ~6k) |
| `observation.blockAfter` | **1.2** | hard sync-observation ceiling at 36k |
| `reflection.bufferActivation` | **0.5** | start background reflection at 50% of 40k |
| `reflection.blockAfter` | **1.2** | 48k |
| `observation.previousObserverTokens` | **2000** | tail-truncated prior observations fed to Observer |
| `temporalMarkers` | `false` | inserts marker when ≥10 min gap |
| `activateOnProviderChange` | `false` | |
| `activateAfterIdle` | none | `number | '5m' | '1hr' | 'auto'` |

### Mechanics worth copying
- **Append-only, prompt-cacheable**: observations append rather than being retrieved per turn, so the prompt prefix stays stable. This is the core architectural bet vs. RAG-style memory.
- **Reflection rewrites the entire log** — it is not a third growing layer. "Each reflection rewrites the entire observation log... Memory stays bounded around the reflection threshold no matter how long the conversation runs."
- **Observation format**: two-level Markdown bullets with emoji priority + timestamps:
  ```md
  Date: 2026-01-15
  - 🔴 12:10 User is building a Next.js app with Supabase auth, due in 1 week (meaning January 22nd 2026)
    - 🟡 12:12 User asked about middleware configuration for protected routes
  ```
- **Three-date temporal model** (per the research post): *observation date*, *referenced date* ("my flight is January 31"), *relative date* ("2 days from today"). This is the only explicit temporal model in Mastra. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/research/observational-memory]
- **Token counting** uses `tokenx` locally, with provider-aware image heuristics, and caches per-part estimates in `part.providerMetadata.mastra`. Callers may supply authoritative estimates via `providerMetadata.mastra.tokenEstimate = { v: 0, source: 'client', key: 'client', tokens: 100_000 }`.
- **`ModelByInputTokens`** (added `@mastra/memory@1.10.0`) — tiered model selection by input size:
  ```typescript
  new ModelByInputTokens({ upTo: { 5_000: 'openrouter/mistralai/ministral-8b-2512', 40_000: 'openai/gpt-5-mini', 1_000_000: 'google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview' } })
  ```
- **Extractors** (`@mastra/memory@1.22.0+`) — typed structured extraction piggybacking on the Observer's already-primed context:
  ```typescript
  new Extractor({
    name: 'User profile',
    instructions: 'Extract stable user profile facts that should be remembered.',
    schema: z.object({ preferredName: z.string().optional(), timezone: z.string().optional() }),
    includePreviousExtraction: true,        // default
    metadataKeyPath: 'extracted.<slug>',    // default; false to skip persistence
    onExtracted: async ({ current, sendSignal }) => current.trim().toLowerCase(),
  })
  ```
  Built-ins `current-task`, `suggested-response`, `thread-title` use the same pipeline. Results stream as `data-om-observation-end` / `data-om-buffering-end` chunks. [VERIFIED: reference + https://mastra.ai/blog/introducing-memory-extractors]
- **`observation.manageWorkingMemory: true`** — OM's Observer owns working-memory updates instead of the main agent (adds `WorkingMemoryExtractor`, sets `workingMemory.agentManaged: false` and `workingMemory.useStateSignals: true`). This is Mastra's answer to "the agent forgets to call the tool."
- **Retrieval mode** — each observation group stores a `range` (`startId:endId`) pointing at the source messages, and a **`recall` tool** is registered with `mode: 'messages' | 'threads' | 'search'`, `cursor`, `anchor`, `page`, `limit` (default 20), `detail: 'low' | 'high'`, `partType`, `toolName`, `partIndex`, `before`/`after` ISO dates. `{ vector: true }` reuses the Memory instance's vector store/embedder for semantic search over observation groups.
- **Storage support for OM**: `@mastra/pg`, `@mastra/libsql`, `@mastra/mysql`, `@mastra/mongodb`, `@mastra/convex` only.
- **Async buffering is disabled automatically in `scope: 'resource'`.**
- Standalone use: `ObservationalMemory` + `ObservationalMemoryProcessor` from `@mastra/memory/processors`, wired into `inputProcessors`/`outputProcessors`.

### Client-integration gotcha (repeated across three doc pages)
"When you use OM with a client application, send **only the new message** from the client instead of the full conversation history" — otherwise client timestamps collide with stored ones and message ordering breaks. [VERIFIED: overview.md, message-history.md, observational-memory.md]

## 7. Memory processors

The docs page has been rewritten: **memory itself is now implemented as processors** in the agent pipeline. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/memory-processors.md]

**Auto-added when memory is enabled** (all from `@mastra/core/processors`):
- **`MessageHistory`** — hybrid. Input: fetch last-N + prepend (tagged `source: 'memory'`). Output: persist new messages, filter incomplete tool calls, bump thread `updatedAt`, skip if `readOnly`. Options: `{ storage: MemoryStorage, lastMessages?: number }`, `id = 'message-history'`.
- **`SemanticRecall`** — hybrid. Input: vector search + prepend. Output: embed & upsert new messages. `id = 'semantic-recall'`.
- **`WorkingMemory`** — input only. Injects WM as a system message. Options: `{ storage, template: { format: 'markdown'|'json', content: string }, scope, useVNext, readOnly, templateProvider, logger }`, `id = 'working-memory'`.

**Deduplication rule**: if you manually place one of these in `inputProcessors`/`outputProcessors`, Mastra will *not* auto-add its own — you get full ordering control.

**Execution order** (this is the load-bearing design detail):
```
Input:  [Memory Processors] → [Your inputProcessors]
Output: [Your outputProcessors] → [Memory Processors]
```
Rationale: an output guardrail that calls `abort()` runs *before* persistence, so **nothing is written to memory**. Same for aborting input guardrails (LLM never called, output processors skipped).

**`TokenLimiter` and `ToolCallFilter` are NOT memory processors** in current Mastra — they're generic processors you compose manually.
- `TokenLimiterProcessor` (`id = 'token-limiter'`), options `{ limit: number; strategy?: 'truncate' | 'abort' (default 'truncate'); countMode?: 'cumulative' | 'part' (default 'cumulative'); trimMode?: 'best-fit' | 'contiguous' (default 'best-fit') }`. Accepts a bare number. Uses `tokenx` (the old tiktoken `encoding` option is deprecated & ignored). Works as input processor (trim history) *or* output processor (cap generation). [VERIFIED: packages/core/src/processors/processors/token-limiter.ts]
- `ToolCallFilter` (`id = 'tool-call-filter'`), options `{ exclude?: string[]; filterAfterToolSteps?: number; preserveModelOutput?: boolean }`. No args = exclude **all** tool calls/results. [VERIFIED: .../tool-call-filter.ts]

**Custom processor interface** (`@mastra/core/processors`):
```typescript
export interface Processor<TId extends string = string, TTripwireMetadata = unknown> {
  readonly id: TId;
  readonly name?: string;
  processInput?(args: ProcessInputArgs): Promise<ProcessInputResult> | ProcessInputResult;
  processInputStep?(args: ...): ...;            // runs every step, incl. tool continuations
  processOutputStream?(args): Promise<ChunkType | null | undefined>;
  processOutputResult?(args): ProcessorMessageResult;
  processOutputStep?(...): ...;
  computeStateSignal?(...); processLLMRequest?(...); processLLMResponse?(...);
}
```
Docs' worked example is an `AttachmentUploader` that swaps base64 data URIs for URLs before persistence — motivated by a documented **record-size limits table**: DynamoDB 400 KB, Convex 1 MiB, Cloudflare D1 1 MiB; "PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and libSQL have higher limits and are usually unaffected." Docs also warn: "avoid mutating the input `messages` array or its objects directly." [VERIFIED: docs + packages/core/src/processors/index.ts]

Other shipped processors relevant to context management: `BatchParts`, `CostGuard`, `Moderation`, `PIIDetector`, `PromptInjectionDetector`, `RegexFilter`, `ResponseCache`, `SystemPromptScrubber`, `UnicodeNormalizer`, `LanguageDetector`, `SkillSearch`, `ToolSearch`, `StructuredOutput`, `ProviderHistoryCompat`, `PrefillErrorHandler`, `StreamErrorRetry`. [VERIFIED: gh contents packages/core/src/processors/processors + https://mastra.ai/llms.txt]

## 9. MongoDB support — the part that matters most for you

**Yes. `@mastra/mongodb` is a first-class, dual-purpose package: `MongoDBStore` (storage domains) + `MongoDBVector` (Atlas Vector Search).** It is one of only four adapters supporting resource-scoped working memory, one of four supporting resource-scoped semantic recall, and one of five supporting Observational Memory.

### `MongoDBStore` config
```typescript
import { MongoDBStore } from '@mastra/mongodb'
const storage = new MongoDBStore({
  id: 'mongodb-storage',
  uri: process.env.MONGODB_URI,        // `url` is deprecated
  dbName: process.env.MONGODB_DB_NAME,
  options: { retryWrites: true, maxPoolSize: 10, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000, socketTimeoutMS: 45000 },
  disableInit: false,                  // true => you must call storage.init() yourself
  skipDefaultIndexes: false,
  indexes: [{ collection: 'mastra_threads', keys: { 'metadata.type': 1 } }],
  // connectorHandler?: ConnectorHandler
})
```
Requires **MongoDB Atlas (cloud or Atlas Local via Docker) with Atlas Search enabled; MongoDB 7.0+ recommended**. `init()` is called automatically when passed to `new Mastra({ storage })`, but **must be called manually** if used standalone — otherwise "storage operations will fail silently or throw." [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/reference/storage/mongodb.md]

### Collections created
`mastra_workflow_snapshot`, `mastra_evals`, `mastra_threads`, `mastra_messages`, `mastra_traces`, `mastra_scorers`, `mastra_resources`, `mastra_notifications`. The memory domain source also manages **`mastra_observational_memory`**:
```typescript
const OM_TABLE = 'mastra_observational_memory' as const;
static readonly MANAGED_COLLECTIONS = [TABLE_THREADS, TABLE_MESSAGES, TABLE_RESOURCES, OM_TABLE] as const;
```
Default indexes created by the memory domain:
```typescript
{ collection: mastra_threads,  keys: { id: 1 }, options: { unique: true } },
{ collection: mastra_threads,  keys: { resourceId: 1, createdAt: -1 } },
{ collection: mastra_threads,  keys: { resourceId: 1, updatedAt: -1 } },
{ collection: mastra_messages, keys: { id: 1 }, options: { unique: true } },
{ collection: mastra_messages, keys: { thread_id: 1, createdAt: 1 } },
{ collection: mastra_messages, keys: { resourceId: 1, createdAt: 1 } },
{ collection: mastra_resources, keys: { id: 1 }, options: { unique: true } },
```
[VERIFIED: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mastra-ai/mastra/main/stores/mongodb/src/storage/domains/memory/index.ts]

### `MongoDBVector` — genuinely sophisticated, and the most interesting thing in the whole repo for a MongoDB engineer
```typescript
const store = new MongoDBVector({
  id: 'mongodb-vector',
  uri, dbName,
  embeddingFieldPath: 'text.contentEmbedding', // default: 'embedding'; dotted paths supported
})
```
Notable capabilities [all VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/reference/vectors/mongodb.md]:
- **`createIndex({ indexName, dimension, metric = 'cosine', filterFields, collectionName, searchIndexName, allowWrites })`**
  - `searchIndexName` defaults to **`` `${indexName}_vector_index` ``**.
  - **`filterFields`** declares metadata fields as vectorSearch filter fields (registered as `metadata.<field>`) so filters get **pushed into `$vectorSearch`** instead of pre-filtering candidate `_id`s — explicitly to avoid "the 16 MB BSON limit on large result sets". Undeclared fields silently fall back to the pre-filter.
  - **Bring-your-own (BYO) collections**: pass `collectionName` to index an existing operational collection. **BYO is read-only by default** — `upsert/updateVector/deleteVector/deleteVectors` throw a USER-category error unless `allowWrites: true`. The policy is **persisted durably** and survives restarts; pre-flag entries "fail closed."
  - `deleteIndex()` on a BYO index drops the Atlas indexes but **preserves the collection and documents**. Managed indexes drop the whole collection.
- **`query({ indexName, queryVector, topK = 10, filter, documentFilter, includeVector = false, numCandidates = 20*topK capped at 10000, metadataMode = 'field' })`**
  - **`metadataMode: 'document'`** returns the full source document as `metadata` and matches filters against the **root** document (no `metadata.` prefix) — designed for BYO operational collections.
  - Native **`ObjectId` `_id`s supported**; results coerce to string per the `QueryResult.id` contract, and deletes/updates accept the string back.
- **`createSearchIndex()` / `waitForSearchIndexReady()` / `textQuery()`** — Atlas Search BM25. Managed indexes auto-create a dynamic `${collectionName}_search_index`; BYO requires explicit opt-in (billable). Field-mapped indexes get a distinct default name `${collectionName}_${indexName}_search_fields_index` to avoid being shadowed.
- **`hybridQuery({ queryVector, query, paths, topK, weights: { vector, text }, ... })`** — uses **server-side `$rankFusion`**. Documented requirement: **MongoDB ≥ 8.0, GA from 8.1**; on 8.0.x "may need a MongoDB support case to enable."
- `waitForIndexReady({ timeoutMs = 60000, checkIntervalMs = 2000 })`; `listIndexes()` returns *logical* names, with an internal registry collection that's never listed.

### MongoDB TTL as first-class retention
The retention reference has a dedicated section recommending native TTL indexes as an alternative to `prune()`:
```typescript
new MongoDBStore({
  id: 'mongodb-storage', uri, dbName,
  indexes: [
    { collection: 'mastra_messages', keys: { createdAt: 1 }, options: { expireAfterSeconds: 30*24*60*60 } },
    { collection: 'mastra_threads',  keys: { createdAt: 1 }, options: { expireAfterSeconds: 90*24*60*60 } },
    { collection: 'mastra_ai_spans', keys: { startedAt: 1 }, options: { expireAfterSeconds: 7*24*60*60 } },
  ],
})
```
[VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/reference/storage/retention.md]

## 10. Eviction / TTL / forgetting / temporal

There is **no automatic per-item TTL or decay in the memory layer**. What exists:

1. **Storage retention + `prune()`** (opt-in, age-based): declare `retention: { memory: { messages: { maxAge: '30d' }, threads: { maxAge: '90d', batchSize: 500 } } }`, then call `await storage.prune({ maxRows, pauseMs, signal, maxBatches, retention })` from *your own* scheduler — "Mastra never runs it for you." Returns `PruneResult[] = { domain, table, deleted, done }`; batched (default `batchSize: 1000`), resumable, cancellable, never VACUUMs. Anchor columns: memory.threads/messages/resources → `createdAt`. **Reference implementations: libSQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB.** Anchor indexes are created lazily on first prune. Notably: "The memory `observational_memory` table has no timestamp anchor, so it can't be age-pruned." [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/reference/storage/retention.md]
2. **MongoDB TTL indexes** as the zero-maintenance alternative (above).
3. **OM reflection = semantic compaction**: bounded memory forever, since each reflection rewrites the whole log.
4. **`deleteMessages()`**, **`cloneThread()`** (branching/checkpointing before destructive ops).
5. **Temporal model**: OM's three-date scheme (observation / referenced / relative) + `temporalMarkers: true` (≥10-min gap inserts a persisted marker + transient reminder event). Message-level date filtering via `recall({ filter: { dateRange: { start, end, startExclusive, endExclusive } } })`. That's the extent of it — no recency decay, no importance scoring beyond the Observer's 🔴/🟡/🟢 emoji priorities.

From [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/research/observational-memory], published 2026-02-09 by Tyler Barnes:

## 12. Breaking changes you'd hit migrating from pre-1.0

All [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/guides/migrations/upgrade-to-v1/memory.md]:
- `lastMessages` default **40 → 10**.
- `semanticRecall` **on by default → off by default**.
- `generateTitle` **on → off**, and moved from `threads.generateTitle` to top-level `options.generateTitle`.
- **Default scope for working memory AND semantic recall changed `'thread'` → `'resource'`.** (Big behavioral change — cross-thread by default now.)
- semanticRecall `topK` **2 → 4**; `messageRange` **{before:2,after:2} → {before:1,after:1}** ("optimized based on RAG research").
- `memory.readOnly` → `memory.options.readOnly`.
- **`Memory.query()` → `Memory.recall()`**, return shape collapsed to `{ messages: MastraDBMessage[] }`; `vectorMessageSearch` → `vectorSearchString`; `selectBy` → `page`/`perPage`/`orderBy`/`filter`/`threadConfig`.
- **`MastraMessageV2` → `MastraDBMessage`**; `MastraMessageV3` removed.
- Working memory `use: 'text-stream'` **removed** — tool-call only.
- `Memory.rememberMessages()` removed; `format` param removed from all getters (use `toAISdkV5Messages` from `@mastra/ai-sdk/ui`).
- `processors` config removed from the `Memory` constructor (now agent-level processors).

## 14. Takeaways if you're designing MongoDB-backed agent memory

1. **Mastra's memory now sits behind a processor pipeline**, not inside the storage layer. `MessageHistory` / `SemanticRecall` / `WorkingMemory` are ordinary `Processor`s that Mastra injects, and the input/output ordering (`memory → yours` on input, `yours → memory` on output) is what makes guardrail-aborts non-persisting. That's a clean, copyable pattern.
2. **The `resource` vs `thread` scope axis is the whole memory model**, and it's implemented as nothing more than a metadata filter (`{ resource_id }` vs `{ thread_id }`) plus a `mastra_resources` document for working memory. Cheap to replicate.
3. **`MongoDBVector`'s BYO-collection design is the most transferable piece**: logical index name ≠ physical collection, durable registration of write-policy and index names in a registry collection, `filterFields` to push filters into `$vectorSearch` (16MB BSON escape hatch), `metadataMode: 'document'` for operational documents, `$rankFusion` hybrid with weight tuning, and read-only-by-default with explicit `allowWrites` opt-in.
4. **Mastra has effectively deprecated semantic-recall-as-memory** in favor of an append-only, prompt-cacheable observation log with a rewrite-on-threshold compaction step. If you're building agent memory in 2026, that architectural bet (stable cacheable prefix > per-turn retrieval) is the thing to evaluate, and the 30k/40k token thresholds + 0.2/0.8 buffer ratios are concrete starting parameters.
5. **Retention is opt-in and manual** — Mastra never runs `prune()` for you, and the OM collection can't be age-pruned at all. On MongoDB they explicitly recommend native TTL indexes instead.

## 2. MEMVID — real code, but the thing it was famous for is dead; it pivoted

**Repo:** https://github.com/memvid/memvid — **16,091 stars**, created **2025-05-27**, last push **2026-07-14**, **Rust**, Apache-2.0, not archived, **23 contributors**, 29 open issues with real engineering traffic through 2026-07-28. **The key finding — the "text in video frames" thing is officially deprecated by its own authors:**

- The v2 README states verbatim: **"Memvid v1 (QR-based memory) is deprecated"** and **"if you are referencing QR codes, you are using outdated information."** v2 **abandons video encoding entirely.** [VERIFIED: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/memvid/memvid/main/README.md]
- v2 is a single-file `.mv2` format: 4KB header, embedded write-ahead log, compressed data segments, **Lex (full-text) + HNSW (vector) indices**, a chronological time index, and a TOC footer. No sidecar files. "Smart Frames" is an **append-only log structure** *inspired by* video compression concepts (I-frame/delta framing as a data-layout metaphor) — not actual video. [VERIFIED: same README]
- The GitHub description now reads "Memory layer for AI Agents. Replace complex RAG pipelines with a serverless, single-file memory layer." [VERIFIED: GitHub API]
- **Claims:** "+35% SOTA on LoCoMo", "+76% multi-hop, +56% temporal vs. the industry average", "0.025ms P50 and 0.075ms P99, with 1,372× higher throughput". [VERIFIED verbatim: same README]
- **SDKs:** Rust core, Node.js `@memvid/sdk` (npm latest **2.0.160**, modified 2026-05-27), Python `memvid-sdk`, CLI. **No MongoDB.** [VERIFIED: https://registry.npmjs.org/@memvid/sdk; README grep = 0 mongo hits]

**Criticism (the v1 era was, correctly, called out as a gimmick):**
- Critique piece: https://esoteriic.com/memvid-critique-when-ai-claims-sound-too-good-to-be-true/ — argues MP4 is *lossy* and it was never explained how that affects semantic search precision; calls the QR+embeddings combo "architecturally weird"; refutes memvid's claim that vector DBs "are online and require a server"; concludes it's a case of "bold claims that sound revolutionary but fall apart under technical scrutiny." [VERIFIED from source]
- GitHub issue #86 ("misleading compression claims", "video codecs being misused as image compressors") **has been deleted** — `gh api repos/memvid/memvid/issues/86` returns HTTP **410 "This issue was deleted."** That is itself a notable signal about criticism handling. [VERIFIED via GitHub API]
- HN thread https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46502628 (v2 launch) got only ~2 comments, one saying *"I have no idea how video relates to AI memory and I'm more confused after reading the above and the GitHub."* [VERIFIED from source]
- A 2026 technical evaluation at https://probos.dev/research/memvid-evaluation/ flags an architectural mismatch: **"synchronous Rust, single-writer"** vs. real agent workloads that are **"async Python, multi-agent concurrent reads/writes."** [snippet-verified via DDG; primary page not fetched]

**Verdict: v1 = gimmick, now disowned by the project itself. v2 = a real, actively-maintained Rust embedded hybrid-search store** (basically "SQLite for agent memory"). It is no longer a video trick. Its benchmark claims are self-reported and unaudited. The single-writer design is a genuine limitation for multi-agent use.

## 5. MongoDB SUPPORT — the standout finding for your stack

I grepped 20 leading READMEs for "mongo". **Result: 0 hits across Hindsight, Memvid, MemPalace, OpenViking, Memori, memU, TencentDB Agent Memory, memsearch, claude-mem, basic-memory, CORE, OpenMemory, ByteRover, agentmemory, powermem, hivemind, memanto, m_flow, SimpleMem.** The single hit was **EverOS**, and it was a *negative* mention (marketing that you don't need MongoDB). [VERIFIED — bulk README grep against raw.githubusercontent.com]

**The one real MongoDB-native agent memory project is Papr:**
- https://github.com/Papr-ai/memory-opensource — **73 stars**, created **2025-12-04**, last push **2026-04-16**, Python, **AGPL-3.0**. Description verbatim: *"Predictive memory layer for AI agents. **MongoDB + Qdrant + Neo4j**."* [VERIFIED via GitHub API]
- **Three-tier storage: MongoDB = primary document store** for user data/structured content; **Qdrant** = vector semantic search; **Neo4j** = auto-discovered relationship graph; **Redis** caching. Write path indexes into all three simultaneously. Retrieval = natural-language query → semantic search + graph traversal.
- Claims **"91% Stanford STARK accuracy"** and **"<100ms on-device retrieval"** (cloud only) — methodology not published. **No documented forgetting/TTL/temporal model.** Python + JavaScript client examples. Commercial cloud at platform.papr.ai (HTTP 302, live). [VERIFIED: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Papr-ai/memory-opensource/main/README.md]
- **Status: REAL and the company is operating, but the OSS repo is small (73 stars) and has been stale for ~3.5 months.** AGPL-3.0 is a licensing hazard for embedding into a commercial SaaS. No 2026 funding news found.

**Practical implication:** if you need MongoDB-backed agent memory, the market has essentially not built it. Your `@repo/knowledge` MongoDB layer is not duplicating an existing OSS project — the closest prior art is Papr (AGPL, small, stale). The dominant new-wave storage choices are **Postgres/pgvector, SQLite(+sqlite-vec/FTS5), Milvus/LanceDB/Qdrant/Chroma, and plain Markdown files.**

**TypeScript-first options (few, worth noting):** TencentDB Agent Memory (npm, Node ≥22.16), rohitg00/agentmemory, CaviraOSS/OpenMemory, RedPlanetHQ/CORE, ByteRover `brv`, activeloopai/hivemind, cortexkit/magic-context, atomicstrata/atomicmemory. ## 6. NEW BENCHMARKS IN 2026 — this is where the field actually moved

The consensus shift in 2026: **LOCOMO and LongMemEval are considered saturated and mis-specified** (they test *recall*, not whether memory helps an agent *do the task*). Five serious new benchmarks:

1. **BEAM** — *"Beyond a Million Tokens: Benchmarking and Enhancing Long-Term Memory in LLMs"*, **ICLR 2026**, Mohammad Tavakoli et al. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.27246, repo https://github.com/mohammadtavakoli78/BEAM (**115 stars**, last push **2026-02-02** — paper artifact, low activity). **100 conversations, 2,000 validated questions, contexts up to 10M tokens, 10 memory dimensions** (abstention, contradiction resolution, event ordering, instruction-following over time). Companion method **LIGHT** claims **+155.7%** over long-context baselines. **BEAM is now the de-facto hard benchmark — everyone's scores collapse on it** (Hindsight 73.9% @1M, 64.1% @10M; mem0 64.1% @1M, 48.6% @10M).

2. **STATE-Bench (Stateful Task Agent Evaluation)** — **Microsoft**, announced **May 19, 2026** by Lewis Liu (PM) and Nishant Yadav (Senior Applied Scientist). https://opensource.microsoft.com/blog/2026/05/19/introducing-state-bench-a-benchmark-for-ai-agent-memory/ · repo https://github.com/microsoft/STATE-Bench (**72 stars**, created 2026-05-11, last push 2026-07-16, MIT) · leaderboard https://microsoft.github.io/STATE-Bench/leaderboard/. **Memory-agnostic — measures whether agents *improve with experience* on realistic enterprise tasks**, not recall. **450 tasks across customer support / travel / shopping.** Four metrics: **pass@1, pass^5 (reliability — task succeeds all 5 runs), cost/task, LLM-judged UX (1–5)**. Two tracks: Main + **Agent Learning**. Baseline: **GPT-5.1 with no memory completes fewer than half of tasks reliably; only ~30% of travel tasks pass^5.** As of my fetch the leaderboard table had **no published system results yet** — it's an open challenge. **This is the most credible new benchmark and the one to watch.** [VERIFIED from both sources + GitHub API]

3. **MemoryArena** — *"Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks"*, submitted **Feb 18, 2026**. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16313. Authors incl. Zexue He, Yu Wang, Siru Ouyang, Julian McAuley, **Yejin Choi, Alex Pentland**. Human-crafted tasks with **explicitly interdependent subtasks** across web navigation, preference-constrained planning, progressive information search, sequential formal reasoning. **Headline finding: agents that are near-perfect on LoCoMo "perform poorly in our agentic setting."** A widely-cited stat from it: swapping a memory-equipped agent for long-context-only drops task completion **80% → 45%**. [VERIFIED from arXiv abstract]

4. **LifeBench** — *"A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Multi-Source Memory"*, submitted **March 4, 2026**, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03781 (Zihao Cheng et al., Cam-Tu Nguyen senior). Tests **declarative (semantic+episodic) AND non-declarative (habitual+procedural)** memory inferred from diverse digital traces; grounded in anonymized surveys, map APIs, holiday calendars. **"Top-tier SOTA memory systems reach just 55.2% accuracy."** Now appears on Hindsight's leaderboard (71.5% EN). [VERIFIED from arXiv]

5. **GateMem** — https://github.com/rzhub/GateMem, **192 stars**, created **2026-06-16**, last push 2026-06-21, MIT. *"Benchmark and evaluation toolkit for **memory governance** in multi-principal settings"* — multiple principals write to a shared memory pool and query under different **roles, scopes, relationships**. Evaluates **utility, access control, and deletion enforcement** (hospitals, workplaces, households). **Directly relevant to your GDPR Art.17 erasure work — this is the first benchmark that scores whether deletion is actually enforced.** Very new and low-activity; watch it. [VERIFIED via GitHub API]

Also active:
- **ConvoMem** — **Salesforce AI Research**, https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/ConvoMem (23 stars, created 2025-10-01, last push 2026-06-02, Apache-2.0). **75,336 QA pairs across six evidence categories.**
- **HaluMem** — `MemTensor/HaluMem`, 149 stars, created 2025-10-25, last push **2026-04-30**. *"First operation-level hallucination evaluation benchmark"* for memory systems — i.e. does the memory layer itself fabricate. Slowing.
- **PersonaMem** — `bowen-upenn/PersonaMem`, 177 stars, **COLM 2025**, dynamic user profiling. Now standard on vendor leaderboards.
- **MemBench** (ACL 2025), **MemScore** and **MemoryArena** listed at benchd.ai/benchmarks; **brv-bench** (`campfirein/brv-bench`, 14 stars, last push 2026-05-11) is ByteRover's own retrieval-quality/latency suite.

Repo `Shichun-Liu/Agent-Memory-Paper-List` (**2,279 stars**, last push 2026-03-04). **The academic reference.** Three-axis taxonomy: **Forms** (token-level / **parametric** / latent), **Functions** (factual / experiential / working), **Dynamics** (formation / evolution / retrieval). Explicitly separates agent memory from LLM memory and RAG. Frontiers named: memory automation, RL integration, multimodal, multi-agent, trustworthiness. [VERIFIED from arXiv]

## 9. The five things that actually changed in this window

1. **Vector-only memory is over.** Every serious 2026 system is hybrid: dense + BM25 + RRF + cross-encoder rerank, usually plus a graph or temporal index. Hindsight, agentmemory, TencentDB, memsearch, memvid v2 all converge on exactly this stack.
2. **Markdown/filesystem-as-memory beat databases-as-memory in the OSS wave.** EverOS, memU, memsearch, basic-memory, TencentDB's L2/L3 tiers, OpenViking's `viking://` — the source of truth is human-readable, Git-diffable files, with the vector store demoted to a *rebuildable shadow index*. This is a direct reaction to opaque DB-state memory.
3. **The benchmark center of gravity moved from recall to task outcome.** STATE-Bench (Microsoft), MemoryArena, LifeBench, GateMem all ask "does memory make the agent *succeed*/*comply*?" rather than "can it retrieve the fact?" MemoryArena's finding that LoCoMo-perfect agents fail in agentic settings is the single most important result of 2026.
4. **Forgetting is still the least-solved primitive.** Only **agentmemory** (Ebbinghaus + TTL + contradiction + importance eviction), **engram.so** (salience decay, archive below 0.05), and **YourMemory** (Ebbinghaus) have real decay models. Hindsight, MemPalace, OpenViking, memU, EverOS, memsearch, Papr, CORE all **document no forgetting mechanism at all.** GateMem is the first benchmark to test deletion enforcement.
5. **The platforms are eating the personalization tier.** OpenAI's Dreaming V3 (free tier, June 4 2026) and Anthropic's Managed Agents memory make "remember the user's preferences" a free commodity. Surviving startups are moving up-stack into *organizational* memory (Engram $98M, Jedify $24M, Interloom $16.5M) or down-stack into *infrastructure* (HydraDB, Zilliz memsearch, TencentDB, OceanBase powermem, Volcengine OpenViking) — note how many are now **cloud-vendor projects rather than startups**.

# Agent-Memory Systems Landscape — verified as of 2026-08-02

**Methodology note:** WebSearch budget was exhausted after 1 call, so everything below was verified by direct fetches of GitHub API, `raw.githubusercontent.com`, vendor docs (`llms.txt` + `.md` endpoints), npm/PyPI registries, and DNS/HTTP probes. Anything I could not verify is explicitly marked `[UNVERIFIED]`. **No claim below is from recall.**

**Headline findings:**
1. **Memobase is dead**, not just stalled — repo dormant since 2026-01-11, marketing site returns 404, cloud API load balancer unreachable.
2. **Supermemory's OSS repo does not contain the memory engine.** The engine ships as a ~200–290 MB precompiled binary attached to GitHub releases. The repo is app + SDKs + plugins.
3. **Redis relocated its entire OSS server into a `V0/` subdirectory** on 2026-07-09 and explicitly labels it "not the current supported production path." Redis is pushing hard — but toward a managed Redis Cloud service (Redis Iris).
4. **None of the five support MongoDB.** Not one. (Detail at the end.)

This is the single most important architectural finding.
- Repo top level: `apps/{browser-extension, docs, mcp, memory-graph-playground, raycast-extension, web}` and `packages/{agent-framework-python, ai-sdk, cartesia-sdk-python, hooks, lib, memory-graph, openai-sdk-python, pipecat-sdk-python, tools, ui, validation}`. **There is no server, API, or engine directory.** [VERIFIED via `gh api .../contents`]

Source is not in the repo. [VERIFIED: `gh api repos/supermemoryai/supermemory/releases/tags/server-v0.0.6`]
- Their own README says: *"We are a research lab building the engine, plugins and tools around it."* [VERIFIED: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/supermemoryai/supermemory/main/README.md]
- Docs confirm self-hosted gets the *"Full graph engine, embedded"* but **excludes** proprietary models "tuned for long-horizon data understanding," connectors, org auth/RBAC, and the dashboard. [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/self-hosting/local-vs-enterprise.md]
- **Bottom line:** 28.7k stars are attached to a repo whose crown jewel is a binary blob. You cannot audit, fork, or patch the extraction/graph logic.

### 1. What IS a memory (data structure) [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/api-reference/content-management/create-memories-directly.md, /docs/recall/memory-operations.md]
Ingestion produces three artifact classes: **document chunks** (RAG grounding), **memories** (extracted atomic facts + relations), and **profile** (sampled summaries). [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/how-it-works.md]

Memory object fields:
- `id`, `memory`/`content` (string, 1–10,000 chars, "Should be entity-centric")
- `isStatic` (bool, default `false`) — permanent traits vs. dynamic
- `metadata` (string|number|boolean|string[])
- `createdAt`, `isLatest` (bool), `isForgotten` (bool), `forgetReason` (string|null)
- **`forgetAfter`** (ISO 8601 datetime|null) — explicit TTL
- **`temporalContext`**: `{ documentDate: datetime|null, eventDate: string[]|null }`
- `containerTag` (required, ≤100 chars, `^[a-zA-Z0-9_:-]+$`) — hard tenant isolation
- Batch limit: 100 memories per call.

### 2. Write path — **async by default, LLM-extracted**
Six-stage pipeline: Queued → Extracting (OCR/transcription) → Chunking (type-aware) → Embedding → Indexing → Done. [VERIFIED: /docs/concepts/how-it-works.md]

Two "dreaming" modes:
- **Dynamic (default)** — memory extraction continues *after* indexing; groups related documents for coherent extraction.
- **Instant** — per-document, immediately available, **charges extra operations**.

"Dynamic Dreaming" (launched **2026-05-25**) uses adaptive scheduling: triggers when the user goes quiet or enough context accumulates; worst case **~15 minutes** for dreamt content to catch up. [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/blog/introducing-dynamic-dreaming-supermemory-now-connects-the-dots-for-you]

### 3. Update semantics — **supersede-and-version + typed graph edges**
- `PATCH` creates a new version; the original is preserved with **`isLatest=false`**. Full history via "List memory entries with history." [VERIFIED: /docs/recall/memory-operations.md]
- Graph relation types: **`updates`** (new fact replaces outdated, history preserved for audit), **`extends`** (enriches without invalidating), **`derives`** (inferred from patterns). No predefined entity schema; extraction is fully automatic and **default-on**. [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/graph-memory.md]
- Ordering matters: docs advise *"ingesting documents sequentially within a single containerTag… since that's how supermemory determines what came first"* — this is what drives `updates` relations. **Out-of-order ingestion degrades temporal correctness.** [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/rules.md]
- **Inferred memories are quarantined**: derived facts are flagged `inferred` with *reduced search ranking* and go into a human review queue (`GET /v3/container-tags/{tag}/inferred`, max 50, ordered by `parentCount` desc; actions `approve`/`decline`/`undo`). [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/recall/memory-review.md] This is a genuinely differentiated safety feature.

### 4. Retrieval [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/recall/search.md]
`POST https://api.supermemory.ai/v4/search`
- `searchMode`: **`"memories"` (default)** | `"hybrid"` (recommended — memories + chunks) | `"documents"`
- **`limit` default 10**
- **`threshold` default 0.5** (0–1 similarity cutoff)
- **`rerank` default `false`** (~100ms added latency when on)
- **`rewriteQuery` default `false`** (generates variants, merges)
- `containerTag` filter; `filters` object with AND/OR metadata logic
- `include`: `documents`, `summaries`, `relatedMemories`, `forgottenMemories`
- Response: `similarity` (0–1), `metadata`, `updatedAt`, version numbers.
- Underlying store described as a **"Temporal Vector-graph Engine"** combining vector + FTS + graph.

### 5. Forgetting — **strongest of the five**
- `forgetAfter` per-memory TTL at write time.
- Single forget by `id` or exact content within a `containerTag`.
- **Semantic bulk forget**: "Forget everything about a topic in one call" — semantic search bounded by `threshold` (0–1) and `maxForget` (1–500), with **`dryRun` preview**. [VERIFIED: /docs/recall/memory-operations.md]
- Soft delete via `isForgotten` + `forgetReason` (recoverable, and retrievable via `include.forgottenMemories`).
- Safety: *"Identity is server-owned: the LLM only ever references opaque handles."*
- Consolidation via dreaming: merges fragments, reweights old facts.

### 6. Temporal model
`createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `forgetAfter`, `temporalContext.documentDate`, `temporalContext.eventDate[]`, plus version chain via `isLatest`, plus graph `updates` edges. **Not formally bi-temporal** — there is no `validFrom`/`validTo` interval pair; validity is expressed structurally through supersession edges + version chain. [VERIFIED: /docs/api-reference/content-management/create-memories-directly.md]

### 7. Benchmarks [VERIFIED: README + https://supermemory.ai/research]
Claims **#1 on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, and ConvoMem**.
- **LongMemEval (May 2026): 95% Recall@15, ~720 mean tokens, 99.4% context reduction.** Per category: SS-Assistant **100%**, Knowledge Update **99%**, SS-User **97%**, Multi-session **93%**, Temporal Reasoning **91%**, SS-Preference **90%**.
- **User profiles: ~50ms** (docs elsewhere say 50–100ms with profiles vs 200–500ms search-only, 1 call vs 3–5 queries). [VERIFIED: /docs/concepts/user-profiles.md]
- SMFS (filesystem retrieval, May 2026): 24M ±1.9M tokens vs 72M ±11M standard FS on Claude = **3.0× fewer tokens**; 48M vs 84M on GPT-5.5 = 1.75×, over 110 xAFS questions.
- ⚠️ **Caveat: no published LoCoMo or ConvoMem numbers, and no competitor numbers anywhere.** Their own MemoryBench framework (https://github.com/supermemoryai/memorybench, 303 stars) ships the harness and a `compare -p supermemory,mem0,zep -b locomo` command but **contains zero populated result tables.** [VERIFIED: raw README + /docs/memorybench/overview.md + /docs/memorybench/memscore.md] The "#1 on every benchmark" claim is currently unfalsifiable from published artifacts.
- MemScore is deliberately three numbers, not one: `accuracy / search latency (p50,p95) / context tokens`, e.g. `86% / 145ms / 1823tok`.

## 2. Honcho (Plastic Labs)

**Repo:** https://github.com/plastic-labs/honcho · **Docs:** https://honcho.dev/docs (note: `docs.honcho.dev` 301s here)

### Maintenance & company [VERIFIED: https://api.github.com/repos/plastic-labs/honcho]
- **6,382 stars**, 780 forks, 27 watchers, **185 open issues**. Created 2023-09-10. **AGPL-3.0** (copyleft — material for commercial adoption). Python. `pushed_at: 2026-07-31T20:04:43Z`.
- **91 commits since 2026-05-02**; last default-branch commit 2026-07-29. Core maintainer `VVoruganti` plus outside contributors. [VERIFIED via `gh api`]
- No GitHub Releases; versioned by tag — **latest `v3.0.12`**.
- Honcho 3 shipped **2026-01-26**. [VERIFIED: https://plasticlabs.ai/blog/posts/Honcho-3]
- Funding: **not verifiable.** Blog index shows no funding post (they ran "Xeno Grant" for autonomous agents, Dec 2024). Managed platform at app.honcho.dev with paid billing. `[UNVERIFIED]` on any raise.

### 1. What IS a memory
**Peers**, not users. Hierarchy: `Workspace → Peers + Sessions → Messages` (peers↔sessions many-to-many). Everything revolves around the **peer representation** = "the collection of reasoning Honcho has done about a peer over time." [VERIFIED: https://honcho.dev/docs/v3/documentation/core-concepts/architecture.md]

Three reasoning artifacts:
- **Conclusions** — the atomic memory unit. Exact schema from the OpenAPI [VERIFIED: /docs/v3/api-reference/endpoint/conclusions/list-conclusions.md]:
  ```
  id: string
  content: string
  observer_id: string   # the peer who made the conclusion
  observed_id: string   # the peer the conclusion is about
  session_id: string | null
  level: "explicit" | "deductive" | "inductive" | "contradiction"  (default "explicit")
  created_at: date-time
  ```
  The `(observer_id, observed_id)` pair is the killer design detail — memory is **perspectival**. Alice's model of Bob is a different object from Honcho's global model of Bob.
- **Summaries** — short every **20 messages**, long every **60 messages** (defaults). [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/representation.md]
- **Peer cards** — compact biographical cache (name, occupation).

Global vs local: `observe_me` = global representation from all messages across all sessions; `observe_others` = local, built only from messages that peer actually observed. Configurable per session.

Internally, conclusions are generated as scaffolded logic: `{"explicit": [{"content": "premise n"}], "deductive": [{"premises": [...], "conclusion": "..."}]}`. [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/reasoning.md]

### 2. Write path — **sync store, async LLM reasoning, token-batched**
- Message written to PostgreSQL + reasoning task enqueued **in the same request**; API returns immediately. Two processes: **API server** and **worker**. [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/architecture.md]
- **Token batching:** the deriver does *not* run per message. It accumulates until pending tokens for a peer representation cross **~1,000 tokens**, then processes the batch in one call. Short messages ("ok", "yes") sit in queue. Applies to representation tasks only — summary and dream tasks have separate scheduling. [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/reasoning.md] **This means recent memories are not immediately queryable.**
- Session-based queues preserve chronological ordering per representation.
- Extraction uses **custom fine-tuned models (Neuromancer)**, not off-the-shelf frontier LLMs.
- Batch API: up to **100 messages per call**.

### 3. Update semantics — **append + periodic delete-and-replace via the Dreamer**
- Deriver: append-only extraction of `explicit` + `deductive` conclusions.
- **Dreamer (consolidation)** — two sequential agents [VERIFIED: /features/advanced/dreaming.md]:
  - **Deduction**: knowledge updates, logical implications, contradictions, peer card updates. On change over time (*"works at Company A"* → *"works at Company B"*), it **deletes the outdated conclusion and creates a new one**. Note: hard delete, not versioned tombstone.
  - **Induction**: patterns/tendencies/traits/correlations, **requiring evidence from ≥2 source conclusions**.
- Dream trigger — **all three must hold**: ≥**50 new conclusions** since last dream, ≥**8 hours** since previous dream, dreaming enabled. Plus an **idle timeout (default 60 min)** waiting for user inactivity; new messages cancel a pending dream and reset the timer. Manual API trigger (`schedule-dream`) bypasses threshold and cooldown but keeps dedup safeguards.

### 4. Retrieval — **hybrid + an agentic query path**
- Search is **hybrid: full-text (keyword) + semantic (vector)**. **Default limit 10, max 100.** Filters: `session_id`, `created_at` with `gte`/`lte`, `metadata` k/v. Scopes: `honcho.search()` (workspace), `session.search()`, `peer.search()`. [VERIFIED: /features/advanced/search.md]
- **Important operational gotcha, verified:** keyword matches are available **immediately** on message creation; semantic matches wait on background embedding (several seconds). Ranking fusion between BM25 and vector is **not documented**.
- **Two query paths:**
  - `context()` — cheap, ~200ms, assembles summaries + recent messages + peer representation + peer card into a token budget (`tokens`, `summary` default `true`, `peer_target`, `peer_perspective`). Returns `SessionContext` with `.to_openai()` / `.to_anthropic()`. **Free and unlimited.** [VERIFIED: /features/get-context.md]
  - `chat()` — the **Dialectic**: spawns an agent that searches conclusions semantically, pulls supporting messages, and **traces a conclusion back to the premises it was drawn from**, then synthesizes. Runs inline (accepts latency deliberately). Five reasoning levels: `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `max`, each with its own model config and tool set. [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/architecture.md + Honcho-3 post]

### 5. Forgetting
No TTL and no decay function. Forgetting is **semantic consolidation only** — the Dreamer deletes redundant/stale conclusions. Delete endpoints exist (`delete-conclusion`, `delete-session`, `delete-workspace`). No eviction budget, no recency scoring.

### 6. Temporal model — **weakest of the five**
Only `created_at` on conclusions, plus `created_at` range filters on search. **No `valid_from`/`valid_to`, no event_date, not bi-temporal.** Temporal correctness is emergent from Dreamer supersession. Docs list "multi-hop and temporal reasoning" as **future work**: *"Current areas of development include… multi-hop and temporal reasoning."* [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/reasoning.md]

### 7. Benchmarks [VERIFIED: https://honcho.dev/ and https://honcho.dev/evals meta]
- **LoCoMo 89.9%** · **LongMem S (LongMemEval-S) 90.4%** · **BEAM 100K 0.630**
- BEAM range **0.646 at 500K → 0.409 at 10M** context
- **60–90% token savings**; `context()` ~200ms
- **Neuromancer XR** (published 2025-08-18): fine-tuned **Qwen3-8B** on **~10,000 manually curated conclusion-derivation instances**. **LoCoMo: 86.9% vs Claude 4 Sonnet 80.0% vs base Qwen3-8B 69.6%.** [VERIFIED: https://plasticlabs.ai/blog/research/Introducing-Neuromancer-XR]
- ⚠️ https://honcho.dev/evals is **JS-rendered and returned an empty body** to fetch — full tables and competitor comparisons were not retrievable. Reproduction artifacts live at https://github.com/plastic-labs/honcho-benchmarks, but **that repo was last pushed 2025-12-19** and contains only a stub README pointing back at evals.honcho.dev. So the headline numbers are self-reported and the published repro artifacts are ~8 months stale.

### 8. Storage backends — **NO MongoDB** [VERIFIED: /docs/v3/contributing/configuration.md]
- **PostgreSQL only** for primary storage: `DB_CONNECTION_URI=postgresql+psycopg://...`. Docs state explicitly that MongoDB is not supported; GitHub code search for "mongodb" in the repo returns **0 hits**.
- Vector store is pluggable: `VECTOR_STORE_TYPE=pgvector|turbopuffer|lancedb` (pgvector default).
- Embeddings: OpenAI or Gemini transport, `text-embedding-3-small` default, `EMBEDDING_VECTOR_DIMENSIONS=1536` (**immutable for the life of a deployment**), `EMBEDDING_MAX_INPUT_TOKENS=8192`.
- Optional Redis cache: `CACHE_ENABLED=false`, `CACHE_DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS=300`.
- Worker knobs: `DERIVER_WORKERS=1`, `DERIVER_POLLING_SLEEP_INTERVAL_SECONDS=1.0`, backoff max 30s. Dreaming: `DREAM_ENABLED=true`, `DREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MINUTES=60`, `DREAM_MIN_HOURS_BETWEEN_DREAMS=8`, `DREAM_MAX_TOOL_ITERATIONS=20`.

### 9. Language/SDK — **TypeScript is first-class and current**
- **npm `@honcho-ai/sdk` v2.2.0, published 2026-07-02** ("Official DX Optimized TypeScript SDK"); `@honcho-ai/core` v2.2.0 is the generated low-level client. [VERIFIED: npm registry]
- **PyPI `honcho-ai` v2.2.0, 2026-07-02** — Python and TS versions released in lockstep, a good sign.
- Ecosystem: `@honcho-ai/openclaw-honcho` (2026-07-30), opencode, codex, cursor, sillytavern, Vercel AI SDK, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP, Discord/Telegram guides.
- TS API mirrors Python exactly: `honcho.peer("alice")`, `session.addMessages([alice.message("Hello")])`, `alice.chat(...)`, `session.context({summary: true, tokens: 10_000})`.

### 10. Pricing [VERIFIED: https://honcho.dev/]

### 1. What IS a memory — three tiers [VERIFIED: https://docs.memmachine.ai/open_source/memory_types.md]
- **Working memory** — short-term session context.
- **Episodic memory**, split in two:
  - *Short-term*: "a raw episode consists of 1 message" plus summaries of episodic memory.
  - *Long-term*: "a batch of episodes generated from the short-term memories. The Episode batch is then ranked using a Reranker and deduplicated for the most frequent hits."
- **Semantic / Profile memory** — "information specific to the user and their experience," in Postgres with vector embeddings.

**Profile schema is a real relational table (`prof`)** — the most inspectable schema of the five:
```
id, set_id (user/role grouping), category (e.g. user_profile),
tag (Preferences | Skills | Background), feature (executive summary),
value (detailed content), create_at, update_at, embedding, metadata (JSONB)
```
Plus a **`citations` table**: `profile_id → episode_id`, linking every profile fact back to the source episode. **Provenance is first-class and queryable** — the only system of the five with an explicit citation join table.

### 2. Write path — async, LLM-extracted
Raw messages → LLM analysis → structured knowledge extraction → `prof` table + embeddings → citations. Semantic memory ingestion triggers on **configurable message-count or time-interval thresholds**. Short-term episodic uses LLM-based summarization. [VERIFIED: memory_types.md + /open_source/configuration.md]

### 3. Update semantics
Profile rows carry `create_at`/`update_at` — **mutate-in-place** with LLM-driven merge into `feature`/`value`. Long-term episodic dedupes "for the most frequent hits" after reranking. No version chain, no supersession edges, no contradiction agent documented. **⚠️ Notable constraint verified:** *"Vector dimensions cannot change; dimension mismatches cause search failures."*

### 4. Retrieval — **agentic multi-hop, the most sophisticated query planner here** [VERIFIED: /api-reference/memories/search-memories.md + /open_source/retrieval_agent_architecture.md]
`SearchMemoriesSpec`:
- `query` (required)
- `org_id` default `"universal"`, `project_id` default `"universal"`
- **`top_k` default 10**
- `filter` default `''` — structured expression language; user metadata needs `m.` or `metadata.` prefix (`metadata.user_id=123`), conditions AND-combined
- `expand_context` default **0**, `score_threshold` default `null`
- `types` default `[]` (= all; options `semantic`, `episodic`)
- **`agent_mode` default `false`**

With `agent_mode=true`, a `ToolSelectAgent` routes to one of:
- `MemMachineAgent` — single-step retrieval
- `SplitQueryAgent` — multiple independent entities
- `ChainOfQueryAgent` — sequential multi-hop ("What is the current company of the spouse of the CEO of Acme?")

Then aggregation + reranking. Tunable via `extra_params`: `max_attempts` (hop limit), `confidence_score` (stop threshold). Returns transparency metrics: `selected_tool`, `queries`, `memory_search_called`, `llm_time`, `confidence_scores`.

**Rerankers are pluggable and composable**: BM25, Cross-Encoder, Identity, **RRF-Hybrid**, Amazon Bedrock. [VERIFIED: /open_source/configuration.md]

### 5. Forgetting
Explicit deletes only (`Delete Episodic Memory`, `Delete Semantic Memory`). Long-term episodic dedupe. **No TTL, no decay, no eviction budget, no consolidation agent documented.** Weakest forgetting story of the five.

### 6. Temporal model
`create_at`/`update_at` on profile rows; episodes are chronologically ordered. **No validity intervals, not bi-temporal.**

### Design (still worth studying — the schema ideas are good)

**1. What IS a memory — structured profile "slots," not free text** [VERIFIED: /features/profile/profile.md]
Three-level hierarchy `topic → sub_topic → content`:
```
- basic_info
    - name
    - gender
    - language_spoken
- education
    - school
    - major
- demographics / interest / psychological / work
```
Content carries creation timestamps and IDs. Extensible via `additional_user_profiles`, or fully replaceable via `overwrite_user_profiles` in `config.yaml`.

Second primitive: **user events** — `{ event_summary (optional), event_tags (optional, e.g. emotion::happy, goal::buy_a_house), profile_delta (required — which slots were created/updated), created_at (required) }`. Later versions added **event gists** (fine-grained, added in 0.0.37, required a DB migration). [VERIFIED: /features/event/event.md + Changelog.md]

Raw inputs are **blobs** (ChatBlob, SummaryBlob). *"By default, Memobase will remove the blobs once they're processed"* unless `persistent_chat_blobs` is on. [VERIFIED: readme.md]

**2. Write path — buffered async, LLM-extracted** [VERIFIED: /references/local_config.md]
Recent blobs sit in a **buffer zone**, flushed when either:
- **`max_chat_blob_buffer_token_size` = 1024 tokens** (default), or
- **`buffer_flush_interval` = 3600 seconds** (default, 1 hour)

Manual `flush(sync=True)` forces processing (recommended at end of chat session). Higher buffer = cheaper LLM cost, staler profile.

**3. Update semantics — LLM-driven merge into slots (mutate-in-place)**
The LLM updates the profile slot given new memory. Maintainer, on a dedup complaint: *"We let the llm to update the profile slot based on the new-coming memory, so if the LLM is unable to understand the prompt, it may perform badly."* [VERIFIED: issue #143] Reorganization triggers: **`max_profile_subtopics` = 15** (exceeding forces reorg), **`max_pre_profile_token_size` = 128** (exceeding forces re-summarization). Validation: `profile_validate_mode = true`, `profile_strict_mode = false`. v0.0.40 switched to "YOLO profile merge instead of multiple profile merges, reduce tokens cost ~30%." [VERIFIED: Changelog.md]

**4. Retrieval — precompiled profile, not search-first**
The core value prop: *"Queries are extremely fast because Memobase returns a pre-compiled user profile."* `get_context` API packs profile + events into a prompt; supports `time_range_in_days`, custom prompt templates, and (0.0.36+) search over context taking **500–1000ms** depending on embedding API. Event search: `search_events`, `search_event_gists`, `search_events_by_tags`, plus context-aware profile search and retrieval-time profile filtering. Embeddings: OpenAI or Jina, `text-embedding-3-small`, `embedding_dim=1536`, `enable_event_embedding=true`. [VERIFIED: /references/local_config.md + llms.txt]

**5. Forgetting — ⚠️ the "time-decay" premise does not hold up.** GitHub code search for **"decay" across the repo returns 0 hits.** [VERIFIED] What exists is: profile cache TTL (`cache_user_profiles_ttl = 1200s`), blob deletion after processing, `time_range_in_days` recency *filtering* at retrieval, and slot-count-driven reorganization. There is **no decay function, no memory TTL, no eviction.**

**6. Temporal model** — event timeline with `created_at`, `use_timezone` config (UTC / America-New_York / Europe-London / Asia-Tokyo / Asia-Shanghai), `time_range_in_days` filters, per-message timestamps. **Timeline-based, not interval-based; not bi-temporal.**

### The big structural change [VERIFIED: `gh api .../commits` + raw README]
On **2026-07-09**, commit *"Relocate project into `V0/` and add Redis Agent Memory landing layer (#319)"* moved the entire OSS server into a `V0/` subdirectory. Repo root is now just `.devcontainer/`, `.github/`, `V0/`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `LICENSE`, `README.md`, `_typos.toml`. [VERIFIED: `gh api .../contents/`]

The new root README states, in Redis's own words:
- V0 is *"the original Redis Agent Memory Server: an open-source reference implementation"* that *"serves as the research foundation and architectural starting point"* — but **"it is not the current supported production path."**
- Redis Agent Memory in **Redis Iris** is *"Redis's official managed path for teams that want agent memory as a service, not another subsystem to build and operate themselves."*

### Is Redis actively pushing it? — **Yes, aggressively — but as a commercial managed service.**
[VERIFIED: https://redis.io/iris/ + https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/context-engine/]
**Redis Iris** is a four-service managed context engine on Redis Cloud:
1. **Redis Data Integration (RDI)** — CDC from Oracle/MySQL/PostgreSQL/MariaDB/SQL Server/Aurora into Redis "within seconds"
2. **Redis Context Retriever** — generates governed tools over business entities; agents never touch the DB directly
3. **Redis Agent Memory** — the subject here
4. **Redis LangCache** — semantic response cache

Availability [VERIFIED: /develop/ai/context-engine/agent-memory/]:
- **Redis Cloud: generally available** via REST API + Python SDK
- **Redis Software: private preview**, self-managed on Kubernetes, **license key required**, contact sales
- **Open source: still on GitHub**, pointed at the V0 docs

Managed API is a **completely different surface** from the OSS one:
```
POST /v1/stores/{storeId}/session-memory/events
{ "sessionId", "actorId", "role": "USER", "content": [{"text": "..."}], "createdAt", "metadata": {...} }

POST /v1/stores/{storeId}/long-term-memory
{ "memories": [{ "id", "text", "memoryType": "episodic", "sessionId", "ownerId" }] }
```
**⚠️ Migration risk:** OSS uses `POST /v1/long-term-memory` with snake_case (`memory_type`, `user_id`); managed uses `/v1/stores/{storeId}/...` with camelCase (`memoryType`, `ownerId`). These are not drop-in compatible.

### 1. What IS a memory — two tiers [VERIFIED: V0/docs/long-term-memory.md]
`MemoryRecord`: `text`, `id`, `memory_type`, `topics[]`, `entities[]`, `user_id`, `namespace`, **`event_date` (datetime, temporal context for episodic)**, `session_id`.

Memory types: **`semantic`** (facts, preferences, general knowledge) · **`episodic`** (events with temporal context) · **`message`** (auto-generated conversation records). Docs elsewhere also list `preference` and `summary` types.

**Working memory** = session-scoped: live messages, structured memories, message summaries, metadata. **Long-term memory** = persistent, cross-session, text + vector embeddings.

### 2. Write path — sync store, async extract-and-promote
*"Automatically extracts important information and promotes it to long-term memory in the background, so memory accumulates without slowing down the live agent loop."* Non-blocking, driven by a **separate task worker** (Docket, a Redis task scheduler). Direct long-term creation is also supported for bulk import. [VERIFIED: root README + redis.io docs]

**Extraction strategies — the most explicitly configurable of the five** [VERIFIED: V0/docs/memory-extraction-strategies.md]:
- **`discrete` (default)** — individual semantic + episodic facts, no config needed
- **`summary`** — one durable session/thread summary; `max_summary_length` **default 500**, `summary_version`, optional `topics`
- **`preferences`** — user preferences/settings/traits, minimal config
- **`custom`** — domain-specific prompt (technical/legal/medical); docs warn *"always validate prompts before deployment"* (prompt-injection risk)

All emit JSON with `type`, `text`, `topics`, `entities`. Also does automatic topic extraction, entity recognition, and conversation summarization.

### 3. Update semantics — **dedup + compaction, not versioning**
- **Hash-based**: identical text auto-deduplicated.
- **Semantic**: vector similarity identifies near-duplicates, merged in background.
- Background **compaction** via Docket: `COMPACTION_EVERY_MINUTES` **default 10** — dedup, merge, index optimization. [VERIFIED: V0/docs/memory-lifecycle.md]
- No version chain, no supersede-with-history.

### 4. Retrieval — **three modes with explicit, tunable defaults** [VERIFIED: V0/docs/long-term-memory.md]
```
POST /v1/long-term-memory/          # create
POST /v1/long-term-memory/search    # search
POST /v1/memory/prompt              # memory-enriched prompt
```
- **`semantic` (default)** — vector, **`distance_threshold: 0.8`**
- **`keyword`** — full-text BM25
- **`hybrid`** — **`hybrid_alpha` default 0.7** (range 0.0–1.0)

Filters: `user_id`, `memory_type`, `topics`, `entities`, timestamps, `namespace`, `session_id`, plus `limit`.

**Recency boost — a real, documented ranking formula. Nobody else publishes one this precisely** [VERIFIED: V0/docs/recency-boost.md]:
```python
final_score = semantic_weight * semantic_similarity + recency_weight * recency_score
recency_score = freshness_weight * freshness_score + novelty_weight * novelty_score
freshness_score = exp(-ln(2) * days_since_creation / freshness_half_life)
novelty_score   = exp(-ln(2) * days_since_last_access / novelty_half_life)
```
Defaults: `recency_semantic_weight` **0.8** · `recency_recency_weight` **0.2** · `recency_freshness_weight` **0.6** · `recency_novelty_weight` **0.4** · `recency_half_life_created_days` **30.0** · `recency_half_life_last_access_days` **7.0**.

### 5. Forgetting — **the most complete lifecycle model of the five** [VERIFIED: V0/docs/memory-lifecycle.md]
Stages: creation → promotion → access → aging → forgetting → compaction.
- **Working memory TTL: 1 hour by default**, configurable, enforced by Redis expiry.
- Long-term forgetting (**off by default**): `FORGETTING_ENABLED`, `FORGETTING_EVERY_MINUTES`, **`FORGETTING_MAX_AGE_DAYS` = 90**, **`FORGETTING_MAX_INACTIVE_DAYS` = 30**, `FORGETTING_BUDGET_KEEP_TOP_N`.
- Four strategies: age-based, inactivity-based, combined, **budget-based (keep top-N by access)**.
- Decay (recency boost) demotes without deleting; forgetting actually deletes.
- Client-side: `delete_long_term_memories()` by ID or search criteria; `delete_working_memory()`.
- **⚠️ Critical operational gotcha, verified:** *"Without a running task worker, automatic forgetting will not occur regardless of configuration settings."*

### 6. Temporal model
`event_date` on episodic memories (distinct from creation time — a genuine **event-time vs system-time separation**), creation timestamps, last-access tracking feeding novelty decay, TTL expiry. Richer than Honcho/MemMachine/Memobase, but **still not bi-temporal** (no `valid_from`/`valid_to` pair).

### 7. Benchmarks — **none. Zero published numbers.**
No LOCOMO, no LongMemEval, no comparison tables in the repo, OSS docs, or redis.io product pages. **[VERIFIED by absence across all fetched sources.]** Redis markets on latency/infra credibility, not memory-quality benchmarks. If benchmark parity matters to you, this is a real gap.

### 8. Storage backends — **Redis only. NO MongoDB.** [VERIFIED: V0/docs/advanced-memory-vector-db.md]
- *"Only Redis is explicitly mentioned as a supported backend."* Factory: `BACKEND_TYPE=[redis|custom]` (**default `redis`**), `MEMORY_VECTOR_DB_CONFIG={json}`, resilient fallback to `create_redis_memory_vector_db` on custom-backend failure.

## 1. Knowledge conflict taxonomy

**"Knowledge Conflicts for LLMs: A Survey"** — Rongwu Xu, Zehan Qi, Zhijiang Guo, Cunxiang Wang, Hongru Wang, Yue Zhang, Wei Xu. arXiv:2403.08319 (v1 2024-03-13, v2 2024-06-22). Repo: https://github.com/pillowsofwind/Knowledge-Conflicts-Survey **[V]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08319 · https://arxiv.org/html/2403.08319v2

Three-way taxonomy **[V]**:

| Type | Definition | Causes | Relevance to your system |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Context-Memory (CM)** | Retrieved/prompt context vs. the LLM's parametric knowledge | Temporal misalignment; misinformation pollution | Your extractor's priors fighting the meeting transcript |
| **Inter-Context (IC)** | Contradiction *among* pieces of context (retrieved docs, dialogue history) | Misinformation; outdated info mixed with fresh in the same corpus | **This is your core problem**: two meeting notes disagreeing about a person's role |
| **Intra-Memory (IM)** | Model gives divergent answers to semantically equivalent inputs | Training corpus bias; stochastic decoding; knowledge editing that doesn't generalize | Your extractor emitting different facts from paraphrases of the same utterance |

Solution families the survey catalogs **[V]**: for CM — *faithful-to-context* (KAFT, CAD decoding, OPIN prompting, ICLM), *discriminating misinformation* (defense prompting, query augmentation/CAR, discriminator training), *disentangling sources* (DisentQA — generate separate context-answer and memory-answer), *improving factuality* (COMBO, CD²). For IC — *eliminating conflict* (PCNN, LLM fact-checking with external tools) and *improving robustness* (discriminator+decoder fine-tuning, confidence-scored query augmentation). For IM — consistency loss fine-tuning, ConCoRD output ensembling, DoLa contrastive decoding, ITI.

Reported behavioral findings (relayed by extraction from the HTML — spot-check before quoting) **[V, extraction-relayed]**: LLMs show significant bias toward evidence aligned with parametric memory ("confirmation bias"); contradiction-detection accuracy is characterized as "subpar"; BERT/RoBERTa ~50–60% knowledge-consistency accuracy; GPT-4 ~13% inconsistency on commonsense; ~40% gap between knowledge-probe accuracy and generation accuracy. The survey's own conclusion: **no one-size-fits-all solution**; the mitigation objectives literally conflict (be faithful to context vs. protect parametric knowledge).

**Design takeaway.** Your review queue is essentially a human-in-the-loop *inter-context conflict* resolver. The survey says machines are bad at this; that justifies the queue.
