### 5.5 TOKI — the theory that types all four heuristics (best formal treatment)

"TOKI: A Bitemporal Operator Algebra for Contradiction Resolution in LLM-Agent Persistent Memory," Ziming Wang (HKUST), arXiv 2606.06240 **[V — read the full 43-page PDF]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06240 · code https://github.com/ZenAlexa/toki-bitemporal-memory

**Core reframing: contradiction resolution *is* write-time concurrency control.**

**Contradiction predicate [V]:** two facts contradict (`f₁ # f₂`) when they *"agree on subject and predicate, disagree on object, and their valid-time periods share a common instant."* Under closed-open `[t_from, t_to)` this holds for **9 of Allen's 13 base interval relations** — all except *before, after, meets, met-by* (the four sharing no interior instant).

**The four production heuristics, typed [V]:**

| Operator | Production strategy | Isolation precondition | Winner selector (source line) | Admitted anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `⊕t` | Last-writer-wins | Read-Committed | larger `(system_time_start, fact_id)` | P4 lost update |
| `⊕p` | Evidence-weighted | Snapshot Isolation | larger `(confidence, system_time_start, fact_id)` | A5B write skew |
| `⊕?` | Await-confirmation | RC + callback | external callback returns 0/1 | none |
| `⊕c` | Per-rule policy | SR on policy table | policy oracle returns 0/1 | precludes P3 phantom |

`⊕?` is literally your human review queue. `⊕c` is your rule table ("job title from HR system beats job title from a voice note").

**Dual-row schema (12 columns) [V]** — table `agent_memory`:

| # | Column | Role |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `fact_id` | PK part (with col. 7) |
| 2–4 | `subject`, `predicate`, `object` | fact content |
| 5–6 | `valid_from`, `valid_to` | valid-time period |
| 7–8 | `system_time_start`, `system_time_end` | system-time period (7 is PK part) |
| 9 | `provenance_id` | K-relation annotation `p ∈ P` |
| 10 | `confidence` | `[0,1]` |
| 11 | `resolution_strategy_id` | `∈ {⊕t, ⊕p, ⊕?, ⊕c}` |
| 12 | `row_kind` | hidden CHECK-constrained discriminator `∈ {current, audit}` |

Integrity constraints **[V]**: `CHECK (confidence BETWEEN 0.0 AND 1.0)`; `CHECK (row_kind IN ('current','audit'))`; PK `(fact_id, system_time_start)` so two system-time versions of one fact coexist; `CHECK (valid_from < valid_to)`; `CHECK (system_time_start < system_time_end)`. Open upper bound sentinel = `9999-12-31`. `as_of` predicate is closed-open (`system_time_start ≤ t < system_time_end`), defaults `row_kind='current'`, accepts `kind='audit'|'all'`.

**Algorithm 1 — the write path, verbatim [V]:**

```
Require: fact f with strategy stamp strat(f), write time t_s, judge parameter pin θ;
         oracle ρ for ⊕? / ⊕c
 1: O ← open current rows on (subj,pred) with Ts end open      # row_kind = current
 2: if ∃ r ∈ O with r.obj = f.obj and overlap(r, f) then
 3:     return                                                  # duplicate confirmation
 4: end if
 5: C ← { r ∈ O : r # f }                                       # Allen overlap, differing object
 6: if C = ∅ then
 7:     insert f as a fresh current row; return
 8: else if |C| > 1 then
 9:     raise                                                   # binary operators need one incumbent
10: end if
11: r ← the single incumbent in C
12: select operator ⊕ by strat(f): ⊕t|RC, ⊕p|SI, ⊕?|RC+cb, ⊕c|SR_policy
13: if ⊕ ∈ {⊕?, ⊕c} then
14:     v ← ρ(r, f); append v to judge_log[(R,θ)]                # BEFORE the operator commit
15: end if
16: (w, l) ← ⊕(r, f)
17: p_merge ← p_w ⊕ p_l                                         # exact K-semiring merge
18: if l = r then                                               # incumbent lost
19:     close r at Ts end t_s; insert w stamped with t_s and p_merge
20: end if
21: insert audit row (p_merge, strat(f), t_s, witness)          # row_kind = audit; defends N3
22: commit at the operator's isolation pin
23: return (w, audit)
```

Judge pinning: the decoder tuple is `θ = (prompt, seed, model, temperature, tool_hash)`; the judge verdict is logged **before** the operator commit, keyed by `(R, θ)`. That's what makes re-adjudication replay consistently.

**Three named agent-memory anomalies [V]:**
- **N1 replay inconsistency** — re-adjudicating a contradiction returns a different winner. Defence: **SR on a keyed judge log**.
- **N2 belief-drift skew** — write skew specialised to a `(subj, pred)` partition. Defence: **SR on the partition**.
- **N3 audit erasure** — loss of the overwritten fact. Defence: **the audit row**.

**Verdict matrix over 8 systems [V]** (A = admits, X = excludes, − = n/a; T = transcribed design, I = shipped code):

| System | N1 (T/I) | N2 (T/I) | N3 (T/I) |

| mem0 v3 | **A / A** | **A** / X | **A / A** |

### 5.6 Consolidated decision table

| Signal | Decision |
|---|---|
| Same `(subj,pred)`, same object, overlapping valid-time | **Duplicate confirmation** — merge provenance, bump confidence, no new row |
| Same `(subj,pred)`, different object, **non-overlapping** valid-time (Allen: before/after/meets/met-by) | **COEXIST** — two historical intervals, both true, no conflict |
| Same `(subj,pred)`, different object, overlapping valid-time, **temporally ordered** | **SUPERSEDE** — `old.invalid_at ← new.valid_at`; `new.supersedes ← old.id`; emit audit row. *No LLM call.* |
| Same slot, one object **subsumes** the other | **MERGE/elaborate** (Mem0's "keep the fact with the most information") |
| Different free-form predicate but high embedding sim + same subject | run the slot test on the resolved canonical predicate |
| Different objects, overlapping time, **not temporally ordered** (same timestamp, or both `valid_at` null) | **ESCALATE** → NLI, then LLM judge, then human queue |
| Multi-valued predicate by schema (e.g. `attended`, `skill`) | **COEXIST always** — never invalidate |
| Incoming fact is **older** than an existing candidate | insert **already invalidated** (`invalid_at ← candidate.valid_at`, `expired_at ← now`) |
| >1 incumbent on the partition | **raise** rather than guess (TOKI line 8–9) |

## 6. Truth discovery / source reliability — implementable algorithms

### 6.1 The universal skeleton

From "A Survey on Truth Discovery," Li, Gao, Meng, Li, Su, Zhao, Fan, Han (SIGKDD Explorations 2016), arXiv 1505.02463 **[V — read the PDF]** https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.02463

```
Algorithm 1  General Procedure of Truth Discovery
Input:  claims {v_o^s} for objects o ∈ O from sources s ∈ S
Output: truths {v*_o}, source weights {w_s}
1: Initialize source weights {w_s}
2: repeat
3:   for o ← 1 to |O| do
4:     Truth computation: infer truth for object o given current {w_s}
5:   end for
6:   Source weight estimation: update {w_s} given current {v*_o}
7: until stop criterion satisfied
8: return {v*_o}, {w_s}
```

Three formalizations of the same fixed point **[V]**:
- **Iterative** (TruthFinder, Investment, Sums/Hubs-Authorities) — most interpretable.
- **Optimization**: `min_{ {w_s},{v*_o} } Σ_o Σ_s w_s · d(v_o^s, v*_o)` subject to a regularizer on `w`, solved by **coordinate descent** (→ the same two alternating steps). Distance `d` = 0-1 loss for categorical, L2 for continuous.
- **PGM**: likelihood `Π_s p(w_s|β) · Π_o [ p(v*_o|α) · Π_s p(v_o^s | v*_o, w_s) ]`, inferred by EM. With Gaussian `p(·)`, `v*_o` is the mean and `w_s` is the **precision** (1/variance).

Common stop criterion: change in `{v*}` or `{w}` below a threshold; TruthFinder/the QCRI benchmark use **cosine similarity between successive source-trust vectors ≤ δ**.

### 6.2 TruthFinder (Yin, Han, Yu — KDD 2007), exact equations

**[V — read the PDF]** http://hanj.cs.illinois.edu/pdf/kdd07_xyin.pdf

Four heuristics **[V]**: (1) usually only one true fact per property; (2) the true fact looks the same/similar across sites; (3) false facts on different sites are less likely to be similar; (4) a site that provides mostly true facts for many objects likely provides true facts for others.

```
(1)  t(w)  = Σ_{f ∈ F(w)} s(f) / |F(w)|                       # site trustworthiness
(2)  s(f)  = 1 − Π_{w ∈ W(f)} (1 − t(w))                      # naive-Bayes independence
(3)  τ(w)  = −ln(1 − t(w))                                    # trustworthiness SCORE, ∈ [0,∞)
(4)  σ(f)  = −ln(1 − s(f))                                    # confidence SCORE
(5)  σ(f)  = Σ_{w ∈ W(f)} τ(w)                                # Lemma 1: score is ADDITIVE
(6)  σ*(f) = σ(f) + ρ · Σ_{o(f')=o(f)} σ(f') · imp(f' → f)    # similar-fact influence
(7)  s*(f) = 1 − e^(−σ*(f))          → with damping: 1 − e^(−γ·σ*(f))
(8)  s(f)  = 1 / (1 + e^(−γ·σ*(f)))                           # logistic, keeps s(f) > 0
```

Why (3)/(5) matter for implementation: the log transform turns a product into a **sum**, avoiding underflow *and* making trust differences meaningful — `t=0.9` vs `t=0.99` differ by 1.1× in `t` but **2×** in `τ`. **[V]**

- `ρ ∈ [0,1]` weights related-fact influence; **`imp(f' → f) < 0` when `f` conflicts with `f'`** — this is where "contradicting evidence subtracts confidence" lives.
- `γ ∈ (0,1)` is the dampening factor compensating for **source dependence/copying** ("if a fact `f` is provided by five web sites with trustworthiness of 0.6, `f` will have confidence of 0.99!"). **[V]**
- The logistic in (8) prevents negative confidence when a fact is contradicted by trustworthy sources.

Initialization/convergence **[V]**: all sites start at uniform `t₀ = 0.9` (estimated average trustworthiness); stop when the cosine similarity between successive `t⃗` vectors changes by less than δ. Paper's params: **ρ = 0.5, γ = 0.3, δ = 0.001%**. Book-authors dataset: 894 bookstores, 1,265 books, 34,031 listings, avg **5.4 distinct author sets per book**. **TruthFinder reaches ~95% accuracy after the 3rd iteration and stabilizes; Voting is materially lower.** Timing: 8.73 s to pre-compute implications + 4.43 s for four iterations; Voting 1.22 s. Error breakdown on 100 books: correct — Voting 71, TruthFinder 85, Barnes & Noble 64; missed author(s) — 12 / 2 / 4; incomplete names — 18 / 5 / 6. **[V]**

Implication function used: `imp(f₁→f₂) = z/x − base_sim` with `base_sim = 0.5` (partial-credit set overlap). **[V]**

### 6.3 CRH — the optimization framework (SIGMOD 2014)

Li, Li, Gao, Zhao, Fan, Han. **[V — read the PDF]** https://www.cse.buffalo.edu/~jing/doc/sigmod14_crh.pdf

```
min_{X*, W}  f(X*, W) = Σ_k w_k Σ_i Σ_m d_m(v*_im, v_im^(k))
             s.t.  δ(W) = 1,  W ∈ S
```

With regularizer `δ(W) = Σ_k exp(−w_k)`, **Theorem 1**: the problem is convex in `W` and the global optimum is

```
              (   Σ_i Σ_m d_m(v*_im, v_im^(k))          )
w_k = − log ( ─────────────────────────────────────────  )
              ( Σ_{k'} Σ_i Σ_m d_m(v*_im, v_im^(k'))    )
```

i.e. **a source's weight is the negative log of its share of total error.** Truth step: `v*_im ← argmin_v Σ_k w_k · d_m(v, v_im^(k))`. Block coordinate descent between the two. Different `d_m` per data type (0-1 for categorical, normalized L2 for continuous) is exactly the "heterogeneous" contribution — **and it's why CRH fits your schema, where a person has both categorical facts (employer) and numeric ones (headcount).** **[V]**

### 6.4 CATD — the fix for long-tail sources (VLDB 2015)

Li, Li, Gao, Su, Zhao, Demirbas, Fan, Han. **[V — read the PDF]** http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p425-li.pdf

Problem: most sources make very few claims, so a point estimate `σ̂²_s` of a source's error variance is unreliable. CATD uses the **upper bound of the (1−α) chi-squared confidence interval** for `σ²_s` instead (minimax: minimize the worst plausible variance).

```
Σ_{n ∈ N_s} (x_n^s − x*_n)² / σ²_s  =  |N_s|·σ̂²_s / σ²_s  ~  χ²(|N_s|)

(1−α) CI for σ²_s = [ Σ(x_n^s − x*_n)² / χ²_(1−α/2,|N_s|) ,  Σ(x_n^s − x*_n)² / χ²_(α/2,|N_s|) ]

min_W Σ_s w_s² u_s²   s.t. Σ_s w_s = 1, w_s ≥ 0    ⟹    (7)  w_s ∝ 1/u_s² = χ²_(α/2,|N_s|) / Σ_{n ∈ N_s} (x_n^s − x*_n)²

x*_n = Σ_{s ∈ S_n} w_s · x_n^s / Σ_{s ∈ S_n} w_s
```

Their worked example, α = 0.05 **[V]**:

| Source | #claims | σ̂²_s | 95% CI | weight from σ̂² | **weight from u²** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 200 | 0.1 | (0.0830, 0.1229) | 0.4839 | **0.9385** |
| B | 200 | 3 | (2.4890, 3.6871) | 0.0161 | 0.0313 |
| C | **2** | 0.1 | (0.0271, **3.9498**) | 0.4839 | **0.0292** |
| D | **2** | 3 | (0.8133, **118.49**) | 0.0161 | 0.0010 |

Source C looks as good as A on the point estimate but gets 32× less weight once you account for its two observations. **This is exactly the correction you need**: a one-off voice note should not get the same source weight as a 200-fact email history. Categorical claims are one-hot encoded and squared L2 gives the error. Note: CATD's Algorithm 1 as published is **non-iterative** — remove outliers, initialize truths, compute weights via Eq(7), compute truths via Eq(1), return.

### 6.5 Dawid–Skene (1979) — confusion-matrix EM

**[V, via "Truth Inference in Crowdsourcing: Is the Problem Solved?" Zheng, Li, Li, Shan, Cheng, VLDB 2017]** http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol10/p541-zheng.pdf

Each worker/source `w` is an **ℓ×ℓ confusion matrix** `q^w`, where `q^w_{j,k} = Pr(worker answers k | truth is j)`. Answer likelihood `Pr(v_i^w | q^w, v*_i) = q^w_{v*_i, v_i^w}`. Objective:

```
Pr(V | {q^w}) = Π_{i=1..n} Σ_{z=1..ℓ}  Pr(v*_i = z) · Π_{w ∈ W_i} q^w_{z, v_i^w}
```

maximized by **EM** — E-step: posterior over each `v*_i` given current `{q^w}`; M-step: re-estimate each `q^w` from soft-labeled counts. Extensions: **LFC** adds Beta/Dirichlet priors `α^w_{j,k}` on `q^w`; **LFC_N** handles numeric tasks with `v_i^w ~ N(v*_i, σ²_w)`; **BCC/CBCC** are Bayesian versions (CBCC assigns each *community* a representative confusion matrix). **[V]**

Why D&S matters for you specifically: unlike TruthFinder's single scalar trust, **a confusion matrix captures directional bias** — e.g. an email-signature parser that's great at emails but systematically wrong about job titles. If your sources are heterogeneous (meeting transcript vs. email vs. voice note vs. CRM), model reliability **per (source-type × predicate-type)**, not per source.

### 6.6 Knowledge-Based Trust (Google) — separating extraction error from source error

**[V, abstract]** arXiv 1502.03519, Dong, Gabrilovich, Murphy, Dang, Horn, Lugaresi, Sun, Zhang.

> "We propose a way to distinguish errors made in the **extraction process** from **factual errors in the web source per se**, by using joint inference in a novel **multi-layer probabilistic model**. We call the trustworthiness score we computed Knowledge-Based Trust (KBT). … applied to a database of **2.8B facts** extracted from the web, and thereby estimate the trustworthiness of **119M webpages**."

The multi-layer trick is the important one for you: when a fact turns out to be wrong, you must decide whether *the source lied* or *your extractor misread it* — and you must estimate both jointly, or your source-reliability scores absorb your extractor's bugs. **Model `(source_reliability, extractor_precision)` as separate latent variables.**

Knowledge Vault (Dong et al., KDD 2014) is the companion system, fusing extractors + priors from an existing KB into calibrated per-triple probabilities. **[R, unverified — I did not fetch it.]**

### 6.7 Empirical reality check: how much does any of this beat Voting?

"Truth Discovery Algorithms: An Experimental Evaluation," Waguih & Berti-Équille (QCRI TR, May 2014), arXiv 1409.6428 **[V — read the PDF]** https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.6428

Same convergence test for all (cosine similarity of successive source-trust vectors ≤ δ); all initialized `T_S = 0.8`.

**Book dataset** (877 sources, 33,235 claims, 1,263 objects, 1 attribute, gold on 100 objects):

| Method | Precision | Accuracy | Recall | Specificity | Iter | Time (s) | Mem (MB) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MajorityVoting | 0.9804 | 0.8664 | 0.7979 | 0.9748 | 1 | 0.009 | 41 |
| TruthFinder | 0.9777 | 0.9387 | 0.9211 | 0.9667 | 5 | 0.359 | 618 |
| Cosine | 0.9769 | 0.9279 | 0.9037 | 0.9661 | 8 | 0.312 | 165 |
| 2-Estimates | 0.9812 | 0.8893 | 0.8351 | 0.9748 | 4 | 0.193 | 124 |
| 3-Estimates | **0.9935** | 0.8849 | 0.8172 | **0.9915** | 42 | 1.474 | 1117 |
| SimpleLCA | 0.9758 | 0.9023 | 0.8610 | 0.9667 | 5 | 0.136 | 82 |
| GuessLCA | 0.9808 | 0.8820 | 0.8226 | 0.9748 | 17 | 0.566 | 82 |
| **AccuSim** | 0.9730 | **0.9516** | **0.9474** | 0.9583 | 3 | 10.092 | 2072 |
| Depen | 0.9814 | 0.8889 | 0.8360 | 0.9744 | 5 | 9.650 | 1879 |
| Accu | 0.9809 | 0.8852 | 0.8280 | 0.9748 | 4 | 9.463 | 1451 |
| LTM | 0.8551 | 0.8885 | **0.9839** | 0.7395 | 500 | 4.273 | 1049 |

**Flight** (38 sources, 2.86M claims): MajorityVoting 0.8205 precision; best is Accu 0.9111, AccuSim 0.9049, Cosine 0.8825; **TruthFinder 0.7970 — *worse* than voting**; 3-Estimates 0.7028, SimpleLCA 0.6802.

**Weather** (16 sources, 365,890 claims): MajorityVoting 0.6305; best TruthFinder 0.6443, AccuNoDep 0.6442, SimpleLCA 0.6421; **AccuSim 0.5079 and Accu 0.5231 — well *below* voting.**

**Read that carefully.** No algorithm dominates. Voting's precision is within a couple of points of the best method on two of three datasets, and the sophisticated methods sometimes *lose*. The authors also found the tuned params from Book don't transfer: "parameters selected to maximize precision for the Book data set do not maximize precision of the algorithms when they are applied to other data sets." Runtime is brutal too: Depen/Accu/AccuSim scale **quadratically in #sources** (5,492–5,788 s in the scaling experiment) vs. MajorityVoting at 438–528 ms and TruthFinder at 1.912 s.

Pseudocode for TruthFinder, Cosine, 2-Estimates, 3-Estimates, LTM, MLE, Depen/Accu/AccuSim is all in that paper (Algorithms 2.1–2.7) — best single source if you want to implement more than one. Params they settled on: TruthFinder ρ=.5, γ=.1, T_S=.8, δ=.001; Depen α=.2, T_S=.8, c=.8; Accu c=.1; AccuSim c=.05; MLE β₁=.5, r=.5. **Ordering instability warning [V]:** Depen-family results fluctuate run-to-run because sources with equal dependence probability get arbitrary order (Depen precision .9814±.0002, Accu .9741±.0061, AccuSim .9413±.0051); they fixed it by using **lexical ordering** instead of dependence-probability ordering.

**Recommendation for you: start with confidence-weighted voting (`⊕p`), add CATD's chi-squared long-tail correction, and only reach for a full fixed-point iteration if you measure a gap.** Your source count is small (a handful of channel types), which is exactly the long-tail regime CATD targets and the regime where TruthFinder-style trust estimation is noisiest.

## 7. 2025–2026: confidence scoring, provenance-weighted fusion, consolidation conflict handling

**"Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs," arXiv 2605.12978** **[V, abstract-level]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12978 — **the single most important paper for your nightly consolidation job.**
- Memory utility follows a **U-shape**: "first rises, then degrades, and **can fall below the no-memory baseline**."
- **GPT-5.4 fails on 54% of a set of ARC-AGI problems it had previously solved without memory.**
- The fault is in **consolidation, not the experiences**: "the same trajectories yield qualitatively different memories under different update schedules."
- Mitigations: **treat raw episodes as first-class evidence** and **gate consolidation explicitly rather than firing it after every interaction**; an episodic-only control that just retains trajectories "remains competitive with the consolidators."

Cross-corroborated by Engram's facts-only ablation finding. **Do not let your nightly job rewrite/overwrite atomic facts in place; make it emit new versions with supersession links, and keep the source blobs retrievable.**

**"STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid?", arXiv 2605.06527** **[V, abstract]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06527
- Names the failure mode you'll hit most: **Implicit Conflict** — "a later observation invalidates an earlier memory **without explicit negation**, requiring contextual inference and commonsense reasoning to detect." (Your NLI model will miss most of these: no antonym, no negation, no numeric mismatch.)
- 400 expert-validated conflict scenarios, 1,200 queries, >100 everyday topics, contexts to 150K tokens.
- Three probing dimensions: **State Resolution** (detect the belief is outdated), **Premise Resistance** (reject queries that falsely presuppose stale state), **Implicit Policy Adaptation** (apply the update to future behavior).
- **Best evaluated model: 55.2% overall.** Models frequently accept outdated assumptions embedded in the user's query.
- Prototype **CUPMem** uses "structured state consolidation and propagation-aware search"; conclusion: **explicit state adjudication** is the promising direction.

**BeliefShift, arXiv 2603.23848** **[V, abstract]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23848 — 2,400 human-annotated multi-session trajectories (health, politics, personal values, product preferences); 7 models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, LLaMA-3, Mistral-Large) zero-shot + RAG. Metrics: **Belief Revision Accuracy (BRA), Drift Coherence Score (DCS), Contradiction Resolution Rate (CRR), Evidence Sensitivity Index (ESI)**. Core finding: "models that personalize aggressively resist drift poorly, while factually grounded models miss legitimate belief updates." Up to **42% of cross-session contradictions left unresolved**.

**TSM — "Beyond Dialogue Time: Temporal Semantic Memory for Personalized LLM Agents," arXiv 2601.07468** **[V, abstract]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07468 — two named problems: **temporal inaccuracy** ("memories are organized by dialogue time rather than their actual occurrence time") and **temporal fragmentation** (missing durative/persistent-state info). Fix: semantic timelines + **durative memory** consolidating temporally continuous, semantically related info + query-aware retrieval with temporal intent. **Up to 12.2% absolute accuracy improvement** on LongMemEval and LoCoMo. → **Your `occurred_at` must be distinct from your `captured_at`.** A meeting on Tuesday discussing something that happened last March produces a fact with `valid_at = March`, not Tuesday.

**ODKE+ (Apple), arXiv 2509.04696** **[V, abstract]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04696 — production open-domain KG extraction pipeline with the exact stage decomposition you want: (1) **Extraction Initiator** detects missing/stale facts, (2) **Evidence Retriever**, (3) hybrid extractors (pattern rules + ontology-guided LLM prompting), (4) **lightweight Grounder validates extracted facts using a second LLM**, (5) **Corroborator ranks and normalizes candidates for ingestion**. Numbers: **9M+ Wikipedia pages, 19M high-confidence facts, 98.8% precision, 195 predicates, up to 48% overlap improvement with third-party KGs, ~50-day average reduction in update lag.** (Formulas/thresholds are in the full paper, not the abstract.)

**"Always-On Agents: A Survey of Persistent Memory, State, and Governance in LLM Agents," arXiv 2606.30306** **[V — read the PDF]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30306 — best synthesis of this whole space.
- "The failure modes of semantic facts are **staleness, contradiction, and authority confusion**."
- The deepest problem it names is **authority confusion**: "a benchmark that scores recall rewards an agent for retrieving a fact regardless of whether it **still carries a current, unrevoked authority to influence action**. … an agent can top a preference-following benchmark and still have no mechanism to revoke a fact the user has retracted." Directly relevant to your GDPR erasure work — *revocation is not deletion.*
- **DynamicMem** (Wang, Braverman, Payani, Zheng, Liu, 2026) shows user attributes/habits/preferences drift on **different timelines** driven by external events, "so a single decay rate cannot keep a semantic store current."
- **CarMem** (Kirmayr, Stappen, Schneider, Matthes, André, 2025), arXiv 2501.09645 **[V, abstract]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09645 — category-bounded preference memory for voice assistants; **bounding facts to declared categories lets scheduled maintenance sharply cut redundant and contradictory stored preferences**, and it's motivated by EU privacy/transparency requirements. **This is the closest published analogue to your typed people/orgs/engagements schema plus nightly consolidation.**
- On the imports: "**Park [2026] builds a graph-native versioned memory whose update and contraction operations are proven to satisfy the AGM and Hansson belief-base postulates, importing rationality guarantees that the heuristic consolidation literature lacks entirely, and Wang [2026b] recasts contradiction resolution as write-time concurrency control** … giving the both-truths representation an always-on agent needs to mark a fact superseded rather than delete it."
- On graph substrates generally: "few works address edge deletion, node versioning, graph-integrity validation under concurrent agent-driven updates, or **who is authorized to rewrite a relation**."

Others worth a look, verified only as titles/abstracts:
- **Governed Shared Memory for Multi-Agent LLM Systems**, arXiv 2606.24535 — names four failure modes (unauthorized leakage, stale propagation, **contradiction persistence**, provenance collapse) and four primitives (scoped retrieval, **temporal supersession**, provenance tracking, policy-governed propagation); production service MemClaw reconstructed 100% of depth-four derivation chains. **[V, abstract]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24535
- **ShadowMerge**, arXiv 2605.09033 — poisoning attack on graph memory via **relation-channel conflicts**: a poisoned relation shares the same query-activated anchor and canonicalized relation channel as benign evidence while carrying a conflicting value. Your `(subject, predicate)` partition key is also an attack surface. **[V, abstract]** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09033
- **MemLineage** (2605.14421), **HaluMem** (2511.03506), **Memanto** (2604.22085), **APEX-MEM** (2604.14362), **WorldDB** (2604.18478), **MIRIX/MMA** (2602.16493). **[V, citations from TOKI's bibliography]**

## 8. Concrete recommendation for your MongoDB knowledge brain

Synthesizing across TOKI (formal contract), Engram (cost cascade), Memanto (three-way resolution + typed categories), Nous (reliability signals), CATD (long-tail weighting), and Graphiti (temporal guards):

**Schema.** On your facts collection, per fact document: `subject`, `predicate`, `object`, `valid_from`, `valid_to`, `system_time_start`, `system_time_end` (sentinel `9999-12-31`), `confidence ∈ [0,1]`, `provenance[]` (source ids + channel tier), `resolution_strategy`, `supersedes` (fact_id), `row_kind ∈ {current, audit}`. Unique index on `(fact_id, system_time_start)`. Partial index on `{subject:1, predicate:1}` **filtered to `row_kind:'current'` and open `system_time_end`** — that's your partition-scan index for the write path. Add a partial index on `{row_kind:'current', valid_from:1, valid_to:1}` for as-of queries.

**Predicate cardinality declaration.** Tag each predicate in your schema as `single_valued` (employer, title, email) vs `multi_valued` (attended, skill, mentioned_topic). **Multi-valued predicates never conflict.** This one declaration kills the majority of spurious conflict work.

**Write path.** Implement TOKI Algorithm 1 verbatim. Use `⊕p` (evidence-weighted, `(confidence, system_time_start, fact_id)`) as your default operator, `⊕?` (await-confirmation) as your review-queue operator, `⊕c` (per-rule policy) for hard rules (e.g. CRM/HR-sourced fields always win over voice notes). Always emit the audit row — five of six shipped systems get this wrong.

**Conflict cascade.** Engram's ordering: slot match → embedding sim on the predicate → subsumption test → Allen-overlap test → (only if still ambiguous) NLI → (only in the ambiguous band) LLM judge → (only if the judge is low-confidence or the rule table says so) human queue. Most facts should reach a decision with **zero model calls**.

**Confidence.** `r = min(channel_tier, content_confidence)` (Nice's provenance cap; content-only trust is 100%-poisonable). Weight sources with CATD's `w_s ∝ χ²_(α/2,|N_s|) / Σ(error²)` so a source with 3 facts can't outvote one with 300. Track reliability **per (channel × predicate-type)** à la Dawid–Skene, not per channel.

**Retrieval.** Enforce the exclusion at the query layer, not the app layer — Kumiho's mandatory `WHERE NOT deprecated` clause on **both** the text and vector branches. In Mongo that means the `row_kind`/`system_time_end` filter must live inside the `$search`/`$vectorSearch` `filter` stage, not in a downstream `$match` you might forget.

**Nightly consolidation.** Gate it (2605.12978: firing after every interaction is what breaks it). Never overwrite atomic facts in place — emit versions. Keep raw episodes/blobs first-class and retrievable alongside facts (Engram: facts-only loses recall). Consider running your consolidation only on partitions that received writes since the last run, and log a before/after diff so a bad run is revertible via as-of read.

**Evaluation.** Build a small internal analogue of STALE: 50–100 hand-built implicit-conflict scenarios from your own domain (someone changes job, an engagement ends, a preference is retracted). The published numbers say the best frontier models sit at ~55% here; assume yours will too until measured. Watch the **knowledge-update** and **temporal-reasoning** slices specifically — Zep's own data shows knowledge-update can *regress* with a weaker model.

# Agent-Memory Systems Landscape — verified as of 2026-08-02

**Methodology note:** WebSearch budget was exhausted after 1 call, so everything below was verified by direct fetches of GitHub API, `raw.githubusercontent.com`, vendor docs (`llms.txt` + `.md` endpoints), npm/PyPI registries, and DNS/HTTP probes. Anything I could not verify is explicitly marked `[UNVERIFIED]`. **No claim below is from recall.**

**Headline findings:**
1. **Memobase is dead**, not just stalled — repo dormant since 2026-01-11, marketing site returns 404, cloud API load balancer unreachable.
2. **Supermemory's OSS repo does not contain the memory engine.** The engine ships as a ~200–290 MB precompiled binary attached to GitHub releases. The repo is app + SDKs + plugins.
3. **Redis relocated its entire OSS server into a `V0/` subdirectory** on 2026-07-09 and explicitly labels it "not the current supported production path." Redis is pushing hard — but toward a managed Redis Cloud service (Redis Iris).
4. **None of the five support MongoDB.** Not one. (Detail at the end.)

## 1. Supermemory

**Repo:** https://github.com/supermemoryai/supermemory · **Docs:** https://supermemory.ai/docs

### Maintenance & company [VERIFIED: https://api.github.com/repos/supermemoryai/supermemory]
- **28,741 stars**, 2,503 forks, 104 watchers, 83 open issues. Created 2024-02-27. **MIT.** Primary language TypeScript. `pushed_at: 2026-08-02T07:47:28Z` — pushed *today*.
- 100+ commits since 2026-05-02 (API page cap). Last commits 2026-08-02 (`feat(web): company brain trial visibility`). Very active, multi-contributor. [VERIFIED via `gh api repos/supermemoryai/supermemory/commits`]
- **Funding: $3M pre-seed, announced 2025-10-06, led by Susa Ventures, with Browder Capital and SF1.** [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/blog/supermemory-raises-3-million] No later round found; I could not run news searches, so a 2026 round is `[UNVERIFIED]`.
- Release cadence: self-hosted server binaries `server-v0.0.3` (2026-06-13) → `v0.0.4`, `v0.0.5` (2026-07-10) → `v0.0.6` (2026-07-19) → `v0.0.7-rc.2` (2026-07-22). Roughly weekly. [VERIFIED via `gh api .../releases`]

### Is the OSS repo the real product or a shell? — **Mostly a shell around a closed engine** [VERIFIED]
This is the single most important architectural finding.
- Repo top level: `apps/{browser-extension, docs, mcp, memory-graph-playground, raycast-extension, web}` and `packages/{agent-framework-python, ai-sdk, cartesia-sdk-python, hooks, lib, memory-graph, openai-sdk-python, pipecat-sdk-python, tools, ui, validation}`. **There is no server, API, or engine directory.** [VERIFIED via `gh api .../contents`]
- The self-hosted "server" ships as prebuilt platform binaries attached to releases: `supermemory-server-linux-x64` (242 MB), `-darwin-arm64` (203 MB), `-windows-x64.exe` (292 MB), plus `install.sh`. Source is not in the repo. [VERIFIED: `gh api repos/supermemoryai/supermemory/releases/tags/server-v0.0.6`]
- Their own README says: *"We are a research lab building the engine, plugins and tools around it."* [VERIFIED: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/supermemoryai/supermemory/main/README.md]
- Docs confirm self-hosted gets the *"Full graph engine, embedded"* but **excludes** proprietary models "tuned for long-horizon data understanding," connectors, org auth/RBAC, and the dashboard. [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/self-hosting/local-vs-enterprise.md]
- **Bottom line:** 28.7k stars are attached to a repo whose crown jewel is a binary blob. You cannot audit, fork, or patch the extraction/graph logic.

### 1. What IS a memory (data structure) [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/api-reference/content-management/create-memories-directly.md, /docs/recall/memory-operations.md]
Ingestion produces three artifact classes: **document chunks** (RAG grounding), **memories** (extracted atomic facts + relations), and **profile** (sampled summaries). [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/how-it-works.md]

Memory object fields:
- `id`, `memory`/`content` (string, 1–10,000 chars, "Should be entity-centric")
- `isStatic` (bool, default `false`) — permanent traits vs. dynamic
- `metadata` (string|number|boolean|string[])
- `createdAt`, `isLatest` (bool), `isForgotten` (bool), `forgetReason` (string|null)
- **`forgetAfter`** (ISO 8601 datetime|null) — explicit TTL
- **`temporalContext`**: `{ documentDate: datetime|null, eventDate: string[]|null }`
- `containerTag` (required, ≤100 chars, `^[a-zA-Z0-9_:-]+$`) — hard tenant isolation
- Batch limit: 100 memories per call.

### 2. Write path — **async by default, LLM-extracted**
Six-stage pipeline: Queued → Extracting (OCR/transcription) → Chunking (type-aware) → Embedding → Indexing → Done. [VERIFIED: /docs/concepts/how-it-works.md]

Two "dreaming" modes:
- **Dynamic (default)** — memory extraction continues *after* indexing; groups related documents for coherent extraction.
- **Instant** — per-document, immediately available, **charges extra operations**.

"Dynamic Dreaming" (launched **2026-05-25**) uses adaptive scheduling: triggers when the user goes quiet or enough context accumulates; worst case **~15 minutes** for dreamt content to catch up. [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/blog/introducing-dynamic-dreaming-supermemory-now-connects-the-dots-for-you]

### 3. Update semantics — **supersede-and-version + typed graph edges**
- `PATCH` creates a new version; the original is preserved with **`isLatest=false`**. Full history via "List memory entries with history." [VERIFIED: /docs/recall/memory-operations.md]
- Graph relation types: **`updates`** (new fact replaces outdated, history preserved for audit), **`extends`** (enriches without invalidating), **`derives`** (inferred from patterns). No predefined entity schema; extraction is fully automatic and **default-on**. [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/graph-memory.md]
- Ordering matters: docs advise *"ingesting documents sequentially within a single containerTag… since that's how supermemory determines what came first"* — this is what drives `updates` relations. **Out-of-order ingestion degrades temporal correctness.** [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/rules.md]
- **Inferred memories are quarantined**: derived facts are flagged `inferred` with *reduced search ranking* and go into a human review queue (`GET /v3/container-tags/{tag}/inferred`, max 50, ordered by `parentCount` desc; actions `approve`/`decline`/`undo`). [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/recall/memory-review.md] This is a genuinely differentiated safety feature.

### 4. Retrieval [VERIFIED: https://supermemory.ai/docs/recall/search.md]
`POST https://api.supermemory.ai/v4/search`
- `searchMode`: **`"memories"` (default)** | `"hybrid"` (recommended — memories + chunks) | `"documents"`
- **`limit` default 10**
- **`threshold` default 0.5** (0–1 similarity cutoff)
- **`rerank` default `false`** (~100ms added latency when on)
- **`rewriteQuery` default `false`** (generates variants, merges)
- `containerTag` filter; `filters` object with AND/OR metadata logic
- `include`: `documents`, `summaries`, `relatedMemories`, `forgottenMemories`
- Response: `similarity` (0–1), `metadata`, `updatedAt`, version numbers.
- Underlying store described as a **"Temporal Vector-graph Engine"** combining vector + FTS + graph.

### 5. Forgetting — **strongest of the five**
- `forgetAfter` per-memory TTL at write time.
- Single forget by `id` or exact content within a `containerTag`.
- **Semantic bulk forget**: "Forget everything about a topic in one call" — semantic search bounded by `threshold` (0–1) and `maxForget` (1–500), with **`dryRun` preview**. [VERIFIED: /docs/recall/memory-operations.md]
- Soft delete via `isForgotten` + `forgetReason` (recoverable, and retrievable via `include.forgottenMemories`).
- Safety: *"Identity is server-owned: the LLM only ever references opaque handles."*
- Consolidation via dreaming: merges fragments, reweights old facts.

### 6. Temporal model
`createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `forgetAfter`, `temporalContext.documentDate`, `temporalContext.eventDate[]`, plus version chain via `isLatest`, plus graph `updates` edges. **Not formally bi-temporal** — there is no `validFrom`/`validTo` interval pair; validity is expressed structurally through supersession edges + version chain. [VERIFIED: /docs/api-reference/content-management/create-memories-directly.md]

## 2. Honcho (Plastic Labs)

**Repo:** https://github.com/plastic-labs/honcho · **Docs:** https://honcho.dev/docs (note: `docs.honcho.dev` 301s here)

### Maintenance & company [VERIFIED: https://api.github.com/repos/plastic-labs/honcho]
- **6,382 stars**, 780 forks, 27 watchers, **185 open issues**. Created 2023-09-10. **AGPL-3.0** (copyleft — material for commercial adoption). Python. `pushed_at: 2026-07-31T20:04:43Z`.
- **91 commits since 2026-05-02**; last default-branch commit 2026-07-29. Core maintainer `VVoruganti` plus outside contributors. [VERIFIED via `gh api`]
- No GitHub Releases; versioned by tag — **latest `v3.0.12`**.
- Honcho 3 shipped **2026-01-26**. [VERIFIED: https://plasticlabs.ai/blog/posts/Honcho-3]
- Funding: **not verifiable.** Blog index shows no funding post (they ran "Xeno Grant" for autonomous agents, Dec 2024). Managed platform at app.honcho.dev with paid billing. `[UNVERIFIED]` on any raise.

### 1. What IS a memory
**Peers**, not users. Hierarchy: `Workspace → Peers + Sessions → Messages` (peers↔sessions many-to-many). Everything revolves around the **peer representation** = "the collection of reasoning Honcho has done about a peer over time." [VERIFIED: https://honcho.dev/docs/v3/documentation/core-concepts/architecture.md]

Three reasoning artifacts:
- **Conclusions** — the atomic memory unit. Exact schema from the OpenAPI [VERIFIED: /docs/v3/api-reference/endpoint/conclusions/list-conclusions.md]:
  ```
  id: string
  content: string
  observer_id: string   # the peer who made the conclusion
  observed_id: string   # the peer the conclusion is about
  session_id: string | null
  level: "explicit" | "deductive" | "inductive" | "contradiction"  (default "explicit")
  created_at: date-time
  ```
  The `(observer_id, observed_id)` pair is the killer design detail — memory is **perspectival**. Alice's model of Bob is a different object from Honcho's global model of Bob.
- **Summaries** — short every **20 messages**, long every **60 messages** (defaults). [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/representation.md]
- **Peer cards** — compact biographical cache (name, occupation).

Global vs local: `observe_me` = global representation from all messages across all sessions; `observe_others` = local, built only from messages that peer actually observed. Configurable per session.

Internally, conclusions are generated as scaffolded logic: `{"explicit": [{"content": "premise n"}], "deductive": [{"premises": [...], "conclusion": "..."}]}`. [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/reasoning.md]

### 2. Write path — **sync store, async LLM reasoning, token-batched**
- Message written to PostgreSQL + reasoning task enqueued **in the same request**; API returns immediately. Two processes: **API server** and **worker**. [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/architecture.md]
- **Token batching:** the deriver does *not* run per message. It accumulates until pending tokens for a peer representation cross **~1,000 tokens**, then processes the batch in one call. Short messages ("ok", "yes") sit in queue. Applies to representation tasks only — summary and dream tasks have separate scheduling. [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/reasoning.md] **This means recent memories are not immediately queryable.**
- Session-based queues preserve chronological ordering per representation.
- Extraction uses **custom fine-tuned models (Neuromancer)**, not off-the-shelf frontier LLMs.
- Batch API: up to **100 messages per call**.

### 3. Update semantics — **append + periodic delete-and-replace via the Dreamer**
- Deriver: append-only extraction of `explicit` + `deductive` conclusions.
- **Dreamer (consolidation)** — two sequential agents [VERIFIED: /features/advanced/dreaming.md]:
  - **Deduction**: knowledge updates, logical implications, contradictions, peer card updates. On change over time (*"works at Company A"* → *"works at Company B"*), it **deletes the outdated conclusion and creates a new one**. Note: hard delete, not versioned tombstone.
  - **Induction**: patterns/tendencies/traits/correlations, **requiring evidence from ≥2 source conclusions**.
- Dream trigger — **all three must hold**: ≥**50 new conclusions** since last dream, ≥**8 hours** since previous dream, dreaming enabled. Plus an **idle timeout (default 60 min)** waiting for user inactivity; new messages cancel a pending dream and reset the timer. Manual API trigger (`schedule-dream`) bypasses threshold and cooldown but keeps dedup safeguards.

### 4. Retrieval — **hybrid + an agentic query path**
- Search is **hybrid: full-text (keyword) + semantic (vector)**. **Default limit 10, max 100.** Filters: `session_id`, `created_at` with `gte`/`lte`, `metadata` k/v. Scopes: `honcho.search()` (workspace), `session.search()`, `peer.search()`. [VERIFIED: /features/advanced/search.md]
- **Important operational gotcha, verified:** keyword matches are available **immediately** on message creation; semantic matches wait on background embedding (several seconds). Ranking fusion between BM25 and vector is **not documented**.
- **Two query paths:**
  - `context()` — cheap, ~200ms, assembles summaries + recent messages + peer representation + peer card into a token budget (`tokens`, `summary` default `true`, `peer_target`, `peer_perspective`). Returns `SessionContext` with `.to_openai()` / `.to_anthropic()`. **Free and unlimited.** [VERIFIED: /features/get-context.md]
  - `chat()` — the **Dialectic**: spawns an agent that searches conclusions semantically, pulls supporting messages, and **traces a conclusion back to the premises it was drawn from**, then synthesizes. Runs inline (accepts latency deliberately). Five reasoning levels: `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `max`, each with its own model config and tool set. [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/architecture.md + Honcho-3 post]

### 5. Forgetting
No TTL and no decay function. Forgetting is **semantic consolidation only** — the Dreamer deletes redundant/stale conclusions. Delete endpoints exist (`delete-conclusion`, `delete-session`, `delete-workspace`). No eviction budget, no recency scoring.

### 6. Temporal model — **weakest of the five**
Only `created_at` on conclusions, plus `created_at` range filters on search. **No `valid_from`/`valid_to`, no event_date, not bi-temporal.** Temporal correctness is emergent from Dreamer supersession. Docs list "multi-hop and temporal reasoning" as **future work**: *"Current areas of development include… multi-hop and temporal reasoning."* [VERIFIED: /core-concepts/reasoning.md]

### 7. Benchmarks [VERIFIED: https://honcho.dev/ and https://honcho.dev/evals meta]
- **LoCoMo 89.9%** · **LongMem S (LongMemEval-S) 90.4%** · **BEAM 100K 0.630**
- BEAM range **0.646 at 500K → 0.409 at 10M** context

So the headline numbers are self-reported and the published repro artifacts are ~8 months stale.

### Maintenance [VERIFIED: `gh api`]
- **3,342 stars**, 202 forks, 16 watchers, 89 open issues. Created **2025-08-15** (youngest of the five). **Apache-2.0.** Python. `pushed_at: 2026-07-31T18:07:06Z`.

### 1. What IS a memory — three tiers [VERIFIED: https://docs.memmachine.ai/open_source/memory_types.md]
- **Working memory** — short-term session context.
- **Episodic memory**, split in two:
  - *Short-term*: "a raw episode consists of 1 message" plus summaries of episodic memory.
  - *Long-term*: "a batch of episodes generated from the short-term memories. The Episode batch is then ranked using a Reranker and deduplicated for the most frequent hits."
- **Semantic / Profile memory** — "information specific to the user and their experience," in Postgres with vector embeddings.

**Profile schema is a real relational table (`prof`)** — the most inspectable schema of the five:
```
id, set_id (user/role grouping), category (e.g. user_profile),
tag (Preferences | Skills | Background), feature (executive summary),
value (detailed content), create_at, update_at, embedding, metadata (JSONB)
```
Plus a **`citations` table**: `profile_id → episode_id`, linking every profile fact back to the source episode. **Provenance is first-class and queryable** — the only system of the five with an explicit citation join table.

### 2. Write path — async, LLM-extracted
Raw messages → LLM analysis → structured knowledge extraction → `prof` table + embeddings → citations. Semantic memory ingestion triggers on **configurable message-count or time-interval thresholds**. Short-term episodic uses LLM-based summarization. [VERIFIED: memory_types.md + /open_source/configuration.md]

### 3. Update semantics
Profile rows carry `create_at`/`update_at` — **mutate-in-place** with LLM-driven merge into `feature`/`value`. Long-term episodic dedupes "for the most frequent hits" after reranking. No version chain, no supersession edges, no contradiction agent documented. **⚠️ Notable constraint verified:** *"Vector dimensions cannot change; dimension mismatches cause search failures."*

### 4. Retrieval — **agentic multi-hop, the most sophisticated query planner here** [VERIFIED: /api-reference/memories/search-memories.md + /open_source/retrieval_agent_architecture.md]
`SearchMemoriesSpec`:
- `query` (required)
- `org_id` default `"universal"`, `project_id` default `"universal"`
- **`top_k` default 10**
- `filter` default `''` — structured expression language; user metadata needs `m.` or `metadata.` prefix (`metadata.user_id=123`), conditions AND-combined
- `expand_context` default **0**, `score_threshold` default `null`
- `types` default `[]` (= all; options `semantic`, `episodic`)
- **`agent_mode` default `false`**

With `agent_mode=true`, a `ToolSelectAgent` routes to one of:
- `MemMachineAgent` — single-step retrieval
- `SplitQueryAgent` — multiple independent entities
- `ChainOfQueryAgent` — sequential multi-hop ("What is the current company of the spouse of the CEO of Acme?")

Then aggregation + reranking. Tunable via `extra_params`: `max_attempts` (hop limit), `confidence_score` (stop threshold). Returns transparency metrics: `selected_tool`, `queries`, `memory_search_called`, `llm_time`, `confidence_scores`.

**Rerankers are pluggable and composable**: BM25, Cross-Encoder, Identity, **RRF-Hybrid**, Amazon Bedrock. [VERIFIED: /open_source/configuration.md]

### 5. Forgetting
Explicit deletes only (`Delete Episodic Memory`, `Delete Semantic Memory`). Long-term episodic dedupe. **No TTL, no decay, no eviction budget, no consolidation agent documented.** Weakest forgetting story of the five.

### 6. Temporal model
`create_at`/`update_at` on profile rows; episodes are chronologically ordered. **No validity intervals, not bi-temporal.**

### 7. Benchmarks [VERIFIED: memmachine.ai blog]
- **LoCoMo, v0.2, 2025-12-01, gpt-4.1-mini judge** [VERIFIED: https://memmachine.ai/blog/2025/12/memmachine-v0.2-delivers-top-scores-and-efficiency-on-locomo-benchmark/]:

### 4. Retrieval — **three modes with explicit, tunable defaults** [VERIFIED: V0/docs/long-term-memory.md]
```
POST /v1/long-term-memory/          # create
POST /v1/long-term-memory/search    # search
POST /v1/memory/prompt              # memory-enriched prompt
```
- **`semantic` (default)** — vector, **`distance_threshold: 0.8`**
- **`keyword`** — full-text BM25
- **`hybrid`** — **`hybrid_alpha` default 0.7** (range 0.0–1.0)

Filters: `user_id`, `memory_type`, `topics`, `entities`, timestamps, `namespace`, `session_id`, plus `limit`.

**Recency boost — a real, documented ranking formula. Nobody else publishes one this precisely** [VERIFIED: V0/docs/recency-boost.md]:
```python
final_score = semantic_weight * semantic_similarity + recency_weight * recency_score
recency_score = freshness_weight * freshness_score + novelty_weight * novelty_score
freshness_score = exp(-ln(2) * days_since_creation / freshness_half_life)
novelty_score   = exp(-ln(2) * days_since_last_access / novelty_half_life)
```
Defaults: `recency_semantic_weight` **0.8** · `recency_recency_weight` **0.2** · `recency_freshness_weight` **0.6** · `recency_novelty_weight` **0.4** · `recency_half_life_created_days` **30.0** · `recency_half_life_last_access_days` **7.0**.

### 5. Forgetting — **the most complete lifecycle model of the five** [VERIFIED: V0/docs/memory-lifecycle.md]
Stages: creation → promotion → access → aging → forgetting → compaction.
- **Working memory TTL: 1 hour by default**, configurable, enforced by Redis expiry.
- Long-term forgetting (**off by default**): `FORGETTING_ENABLED`, `FORGETTING_EVERY_MINUTES`, **`FORGETTING_MAX_AGE_DAYS` = 90**, **`FORGETTING_MAX_INACTIVE_DAYS` = 30**, `FORGETTING_BUDGET_KEEP_TOP_N`.
- Four strategies: age-based, inactivity-based, combined, **budget-based (keep top-N by access)**.
- Decay (recency boost) demotes without deleting; forgetting actually deletes.
- Client-side: `delete_long_term_memories()` by ID or search criteria; `delete_working_memory()`.
- **⚠️ Critical operational gotcha, verified:** *"Without a running task worker, automatic forgetting will not occur regardless of configuration settings."*

All six research streams have reported (the OSS-framework parent is still finishing, but its conflict-resolution sub-agent delivered the substance). Here's the synthesis.

---

# Part 1 — What I found

## Hermes Agent (your actual question)

**Nous Research's Hermes Agent** — MIT, self-hosted, first released 2026-02-25, `NousResearch/hermes-agent`. Model-agnostic across any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Not to be confused with the Hermes *model* family, which ships no agent harness.

Your hunch about "options you can use by providers" is a real, named feature: `memory.provider` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` selects one of **nine pluggable memory backends** — honcho, openviking, mem0, hindsight, holographic, retaindb, byterover, supermemory, memori. One external provider at a time; the built-in memory stays active alongside it with writes mirrored.

The architecture underneath the plugin slot is the interesting part, and it's three tiers:

| Tier | Mechanism | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Curated prompt memory | `MEMORY.md` (2,200 chars) + `USER.md` (1,375 chars), auto-injected, **frozen at session start** to preserve prefix cache | Fixed, ~1,300 tok |
| Episodic recall | `session_search` over SQLite **FTS5**, unlimited, ~20ms | Zero standing |
| Procedural | Skills as `SKILL.md` files, three-tier progressive disclosure, background Curator ages them active→stale→archived | ~3k tok summaries |

The design decision worth stealing: the memory write tool has `add`/`replace`/`remove` and **no `read` action** — because it's already in the prompt. At the cap the tool *errors* and forces consolidation within the same turn. A hard bound plus a forcing function, rather than an unbounded store with a hopeful prompt.

Hermes deliberately uses **none** of the provider-native memory APIs. Anthropic context editing is an open, unimplemented issue (#526, filed March, still open). Its only provider integration is prompt caching.

## Garry Tan's gbrain

Public, MIT, `garrytan/gbrain`, 269K LOC. Explicitly aimed at YC's "company brain" RFS. Three things matter for you:

**Markdown-in-git is the system of record; Postgres is a derived cache.** Disaster recovery is `DELETE FROM facts; ...` then re-sync. Enforced by a CI check and an invariant test. Everything else follows from this.

**Facts vs takes.** Two separate stores with a strictly one-way bridge. *Facts* are hot, single-user, decaying. *Takes* are cold epistemic claims carrying `holder` (`world` | `brain` | `people/<slug>`), `weight ∈ [0,1]`, `since/until`, `superseded_by`. Consolidation promotes hot→cold and **never deletes** — facts stay stamped with `consolidated_at`/`consolidated_into`.

**Confidence is part of the answer.** The synthesis prompt says: mark low-weight claims explicitly in prose ("has a hunch (w=0.4) that…"), surface *both* sides of a contradiction in a Conflicts section and never silently pick, and return a structured `gaps[]` array of what the brain couldn't answer. Plus a Brier score on the owner's own predictions, fed back as bias correction at answer time.

Two things not to copy: guardrails ship **observe-only and fail-open**, and `SECURITY.md` contains zero mentions of prompt injection despite ingesting untrusted email. And the complexity budget — 22 dream phases, 125 migrations, 106 operations — is what a full-time agent swarm produces in four months.

## Provider-native memory — the state of the art

Only four vendors ship genuine model-extracted long-term memory: Anthropic (memory stores + dreams), Google (Memory Bank), AWS (AgentCore), Microsoft (Foundry). OpenAI, xAI, Mistral and Cohere give you *transcript persistence*, not memory — and OpenAI bills every prior token again on each turn.

Corrections to what I had cached, both verified independently by two agents:

- Anthropic's memory tool went **GA 2026-02-17** (no beta header).
- Memory stores moved to header **`agent-memory-2026-07-22`**; sending it together with `managed-agents-2026-04-01` is a 400.
- Google's Memory Bank is **GA** since 2025-12-16.

The eight mechanisms worth knowing about, ranked by relevance to you:

1. **Immutable version-per-mutation that outlives its parent** (Anthropic `memver_...`, with `created_by` actor and a `/redact` that scrubs content while keeping the trail). Google goes further: revisions carry a `context` field recording *why* each fact was extracted.
2. **`content_sha256` optimistic concurrency** on memory writes. Nobody else ships this.
3. **Consolidation that writes to a new store and never mutates the input** (Anthropic dreams). Makes the scariest operation in a memory system safe to run and A/B-testable.
4. **`scope` as one exact-match KV dict doing three jobs** (Google): isolation boundary, consolidation candidate set, retrieval predicate — with IAM enforceable per scope.
5. **A consolidation partition key** (AWS `STRICTLY_CONSISTENT`, Google `REQUIRE_EXACT_MATCH`) guaranteeing the merge step cannot cross a boundary you care about.
6. **Progressive disclosure with a machine-enforced index cap.** Claude Code measures `MEMORY.md` after each write and *returns an error* past 200 lines / 25 KB. The enforcement is what makes it work.
7. **`access: read_only` as injection containment.** Anthropic's warning is the clearest anyone publishes: a successful injection writes to the store, and "later sessions then read that content as trusted memory."
8. **Dry-run deletion** (Google `:purge{filter, force:false}`).

Two vendor anti-patterns to avoid: `DELETE /v1/conversations/{id}` on OpenAI does not delete the items inside it, and AWS AgentCore's TTL covers raw events only — extracted records have no auto-expiry and there's no per-actor purge.

## Claude Code's memory helper

Four mechanisms, not two. The two you drew on:

**The `remember` plugin** — episodic, hook-driven. PostToolUse counts transcript-line delta > 50, cooldown 120s, then Haiku writes one sentence. Four lossy tiers: `now` → `today` (hourly) → `recent` (3d, ≤600 tok) → `archive` (weekly, ≤400 tok) → rotated slices, which are **named but not injected** ("these files were rotated BECAUSE they were too large to fit a prompt"). Note: `core-memories.md` is read at session start and **written by nothing** — the promotion tier was never implemented.

**Auto-memory** — semantic, model-decided, one fact per file with typed frontmatter (`user|feedback|project|reference`) and `[[wiki-links]]`. Recall is **index-then-fetch with an LLM reranker**: a manifest of `name + description + type + date` is a cached prompt prefix, each query appends a turn, and a cheap model returns ≤5 filenames as JSON schema. No embeddings anywhere.

Three details worth lifting verbatim:
- The `description` field is written **for the retriever**, not the reader.
- Type-conditioned retrieval conservatism: "Be especially conservative with `[user]`/`[project]` memories… Match on what the question IS ABOUT, not on surface keyword overlap." Broad-scope facts are high-recall poison.
- The **do-not-save list**, where every exclusion names a more authoritative source: "git history — `git log` is authoritative"; "debugging solutions — the fix is in the code." A knowledge base earns its keep only on what cannot be derived from a live source.

The "dream" runs as a **forked agent with a narrowed tool grant** (read-only shell + `.md` delete, no edit), gated on `{minHours: 24, minSessions: 5}` — time *and* activity.

## Research: conflict resolution is the unsolved part

The literature is blunt about how badly this works today. **BeliefShift**: up to 42% of cross-session contradictions left unresolved across seven LLM families. **STALE**: best frontier model scores 55.2% at knowing when its own memories are stale. MemoryAgentBench: *all* evaluated methods fail on multi-hop conflict.

The single most important paper for your nightly job — **"Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs"** (arXiv 2605.12978): memory utility follows a **U-shape** and can fall *below the no-memory baseline*. GPT-5.4 failed 54% of ARC-AGI problems it had previously solved without memory. The fault is in consolidation, not the experiences: "the same trajectories yield qualitatively different memories under different update schedules." An episodic-only control that just retains trajectories stays competitive with the consolidators.

**Zep/Graphiti** is the reference bi-temporal implementation. Four timestamps: `t_valid`/`t_invalid` (world) and `t'_created`/`t'_expired` (system). Contradiction handling now lives fused into the dedupe prompt, and the temporal guard is a pure function — no LLM call:

```python
# skip if intervals cannot conflict; only invalidate a STRICTLY OLDER edge
elif edge.valid_at < resolved_edge.valid_at:
    edge.invalid_at = resolved_edge.valid_at
    edge.expired_at = edge.expired_at or utc_now()
```

It also handles out-of-order ingestion by inserting a fact **already invalidated** when a newer candidate exists — essential once you ingest email, which arrives out of chronological order constantly.

**Engram** contributes the cost cascade: slot match → embedding similarity → subsumption → Allen-overlap → NLI → LLM judge → human. Most facts decide with zero model calls. Its load-bearing negative result: a **facts-only read path loses recall** — you must retrieve conflict-resolved facts *plus* raw source chunks. "We caution against shipping facts-only QA."

**TOKI** reframes contradiction resolution as write-time concurrency control, and its audit of eight shipped systems is damning: **five of six agent-memory systems admit audit erasure** — the overwritten fact is simply gone. Graphiti sets `invalid_at` and emits no audit edge; mem0 v2's DELETE branch removes the loser with no audit row.

And **the reliability finding that changes how you'd spend effort** (arXiv 2606.22030): Bayesian belief updating is *worthless* without a per-observation reliability signal — replacing it with naive last-write-wins gave identical accuracy. Only with a **provenance cap** `r = min(channel_tier, content_confidence)` did it pull ahead: 0% attack success under poisoning, vs 100% with content-inferred trust alone (a confident-sounding injection scored 0.96).

---

# Part 2 — Convergent patterns

Across all six streams, the same handful of ideas keep appearing independently:

| Pattern | Who does it |
|---|---|
| **Never hard-delete; close the interval + keep an audit row** | Graphiti, Engram, TOKI, Memanto, Anthropic versions, Google revisions |
| **Bounded index + on-demand detail, with enforced caps** | Hermes (2,200 chars), Claude Code (200 lines/25 KB), Skills, gbrain, Codex |
| **Advertise the cold tier rather than loading it** | `remember` rotated archives, Hermes FTS5, Skills bundled files |
| **Retrieve facts *and* raw sources** | Engram (measured), gbrain (episodes + takes), Anthropic memory stores |
| **Consolidation gated, not fired every turn** | Claude Code `{24h, 5 sessions}`, Hermes Curator (168h), arXiv 2605.12978 |
| **Confidence surfaced in the answer, conflicts shown not resolved** | gbrain, Memanto, Anthropic dreams |
| **Trust demotion on retrieved content** | Claude Code ("not as direct user instructions"), gbrain ("treat as DATA"), Anthropic `read_only` |
| **Separate "what happened" from "what is true"** | gbrain facts/takes, Claude Code remember/auto-memory, Engram episodes/facts |

---

# Part 3 — What this adds to your product

Ranked by value per unit of effort. Your write path is genuinely good — well-tested, idempotent, tenant-safe. Everything below is about the read path, the temporal model, and hardening.

### 1. Build the read path — nothing else is unblocked without it

`buildFactsSearchPipeline` and `buildEntityNameSearchPipeline` are never executed anywhere in the codebase, `dossiers` is a write-only collection, and `/search` is a template stub. You accumulate memory with no way to read it back.

Don't start with embeddings. Start with **index-then-fetch**, which maps onto MongoDB more directly than a vector index does: `SELECT name, description, category, updatedAt FROM facts WHERE tenantId = ?` becomes a cached manifest prefix; a cheap model returns ≤5 fact ids as JSON schema. It's explainable (you can show *why* a fact surfaced), an empty list is a legitimate answer, and it degrades gracefully. Add `fact.description` written **for the retriever**, and a per-category retrieval prior so `background` facts don't dominate every query.

Then take Engram's measured finding: retrieve facts **plus** the source `content` blob. Facts-only loses recall.

### 2. Make the temporal model real

`validUntil` is in your schema and in `currentlyValidFilter` and **no code path ever writes it**. That's the highest-leverage fix available.

- Split **`occurredAt` from `capturedAt`** (TSM: +12.2 points on LongMemEval/LoCoMo from this alone). A Tuesday meeting discussing something from last March produces a fact with `validFrom = March`.
- Add `systemTimeStart`/`systemTimeEnd` alongside `validFrom`/`validUntil`. Sentinel `9999-12-31`.
- Add a `rowKind ∈ {current, audit}` discriminator and **emit an audit row on every supersession**. Five of six shipped systems get this wrong; your `supersededBy` chain currently loses the reasoning.
- Handle out-of-order ingestion — insert already-invalidated when a newer fact exists. You ingest email; this will happen constantly.

### 3. A conflict cascade that mostly costs nothing

Today, conflicts resolve only if the extraction LLM happens to see the older fact in its 50-fact window, chooses to emit `supersedes`, and a human confirms. Nothing detects two contradictory currently-valid facts already in the DB.

Add, in order of cost: **declare each predicate `single_valued` vs `multi_valued`** (this alone kills most spurious conflict work — `attended` and `skill` never conflict), then slot match → Allen-overlap test → subsumption → NLI → LLM judge → your existing review queue. Steal Graphiti's coexist rule verbatim: *"Bob ran 5 miles on Tuesday" / "Bob ran 3 miles on Wednesday" → not a contradiction.*

Your review queue is already the right shape — it's TOKI's `⊕?` await-confirmation operator. Add a `⊕c` rule table for cases where a policy should decide without a human.

### 4. Make `confidence` load-bearing, or delete it

It's model-generated, stored, rendered as a percentage in the review UI, and used for nothing. Right now it's a number that looks meaningful and isn't.

Wire it as `r = min(channel_tier, content_confidence)` — channel tier assigned by *source type*, not learned. This is the difference between 0% and 100% poisoning success in the measured result, and it matters directly because you ingest inbound email. Weight sources with CATD's chi-squared correction so a one-off voice note can't outvote a 200-fact email history.

### 5. Fix the extraction context before it silently degrades

`gatherContext` feeds the model the 50 most-recently-updated facts **across the entire tenant**. Past ~50 facts the model stops seeing the relevant ones, so it stops proposing supersessions and starts proposing duplicates — with no error, just growing redundancy and review load. This is your primary scaling failure mode and the strongest argument for retrieval-selected context.

### 6. Harden the dream cycle

Your consolidation is dedup-by-merge only, time-gated, `minFacts: 8` (so long-tail anchors never consolidate at all). Three changes:

- **Gate on time *and* activity**, per Claude Code's `{minHours, minSessions}` and the U-shape paper. Only run on anchors that received writes since the last run.
- **Run it under a scoped identity** with a narrowed grant — Claude Code's dream gets read-only shell plus `.md` delete and no edit. Your consolidation should not be able to do anything except propose.
- **Add a consolidation partition key** so the merge LLM structurally cannot blend across a boundary. You're multi-tenant; `tenantId` is the obvious one, but consider per-organization too.

Your fact-set-hashed proposal id is already excellent — it makes a reviewer's "no" durable. Keep that.

### 7. Close the GDPR gaps

Three concrete holes, in severity order:

- **`erasePerson` never redacts the `facts` collection.** A fact anchored to an *organization* whose `text` names the erased person survives verbatim — and the dossier wipe is a cache drop, so the next `refreshDossier` recomposes the name straight back in. The existing 11-test suite doesn't catch it because the fixture's surviving fact deliberately contains no name.
- **Adopt redact-not-delete for derived facts**, per Anthropic's `/redact`: scrub content, preserve who-did-what-when. It's the correct primitive, and it's compatible with your audit-trail philosophy in `review.ts`.
- **Add a dry-run mode** to the erasure cascade (Google's `:purge{force: false}`). For a predicate-based cascade this is the difference between a workflow people run and one nobody dares run.

Also worth internalizing gbrain's hardest-won lesson: **forgetting must be expressible in whatever you treat as canonical.** If erasure only touches derived state, a rebuild resurrects it.

### 8. An eval harness — because every prompt change is currently unfalsifiable

168 tests, all against mocked `generate` functions. Nothing measures extraction precision/recall, correct anchoring, correct supersession, or information loss on merge — the one property the consolidation prompt most insists on.

Build a small internal STALE analogue: 50–100 hand-built implicit-conflict scenarios from your own domain (someone changes job, an engagement ends, a preference is retracted). Assume you'll score around 55% until measured — that's where the best frontier models sit. gbrain publishes its bad benchmark numbers next to the good ones; that's the right posture.

### Concrete bugs the codebase agent found along the way

Not research findings, but they're blocking and worth fixing first:

- **`event.data.from` in the inbound-email webhook is the raw `From` header** (`"Anna Nordwind <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>"`), matched verbatim against a map of plain addresses. If a display name is present — which is the normal case — **every inbound email is silently dropped** as "sender not allowlisted." Fails closed, so not a security hole, but potentially a 100% drop rate that no test catches.
- **`parseInboundSenderMap` throws and the route doesn't catch it** — a typo in the env var makes every delivery 500, and Resend retries forever.
- **Cron routes fail open**: `if (secret && ...)` means an unset `CRON_SECRET` leaves `/cron/knowledge-pipeline` publicly reachable, burning AssemblyAI and gateway spend across every tenant. `CRON_SECRET` is in no `keys()` schema.
- **The supersession race in `review.ts:178`** no-ops silently, leaving both facts valid with no error surfaced. Anthropic's `content_sha256` precondition is exactly the fix.

---

**One structural framing to carry forward.** The two Claude Code systems disagree about what a memory *is*, and both are right: `remember` stores *what happened*, compressed by age, never retrieved by topic; auto-memory stores *what is true*, indexed by relevance, never retrieved by time. gbrain draws the same line as episodes-vs-takes. You need both stores and both retrieval paths — and the mistake to avoid is running the episodic firehose through the semantic pipeline. The "what NOT to save" list is precisely the filter that keeps the second store from filling up with the first.

# Agent-Memory Landscape for a MongoDB + TypeScript Knowledge Brain
**Compiled 2026-08-02. Everything below is from primary sources fetched today unless marked [RECALLED].**

> **Methodology caveat:** the session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted early, so ~95% of this was gathered by direct fetches of docs (`.md` endpoints), the GitHub REST API, npm/PyPI registries, and raw source files. That's actually *higher* fidelity than search snippets, but it means a few discovery-only items are flagged.

---

## PART 1 — MongoDB-Native Agent Memory (highest value for you)

### 1.1 The headline: MongoDB shipped three new retrieval primitives in 2026

This is the biggest change since your cutoff, and it directly changes how you should build retrieval for `@repo/knowledge`.

| Stage | Min version | Status | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `$rankFusion` | **MongoDB 8.0+** | **GA 2026-06-30** | Native RRF over N sub-pipelines |
| `$scoreFusion` | **MongoDB 8.3+** | **GA 2026-06-30** | Score-based fusion w/ normalization + custom expression |
| `$score` | 8.3+ (companion) | GA | Compute/normalize an arbitrary score as `$meta:"score"` |
| `$rerank` | **MongoDB 8.3+, Atlas cloud only** | **Preview** (shipped 2026-06-30) | Cross-encoder rerank via Voyage AI, in-pipeline |

[VERIFIED: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/rankFusion/ · https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/scoreFusion/ · https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/score/ · https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/query/aggregation-stages/rerank/ · https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/search-changelog/ · https://www.mongodb.com/blog/post/product-release-announcements/boost-search-relevance-mongodb-atlas-native-hybrid-search]

#### `$rankFusion` — exact syntax [VERIFIED]

```javascript
{
  $rankFusion: {
    input: {
      pipelines: {
        <name1>: [ ...stages ],
        <name2>: [ ...stages ]
      }
    },
    combination: { weights: { <name1>: <number>, <name2>: <number> } },  // default 1 each
    scoreDetails: <bool>   // default false
  }
}
```

- **RRF formula, verbatim:** `RRFscore(d) = Σ(r∈R) w(r) / (60 + r(d))` — the rank constant is **hardcoded 60**, not configurable.
- Result score lands in the **`score`** metadata field. `scoreDetails` populates a nested per-pipeline breakdown (`inputPipelineName`, `rank`, `weight`, `value`) — retrieve with `{$meta: "scoreDetails"}`.
- **Input pipeline restrictions:** each must be a *Selection* AND *Ranked* pipeline. Allowed stages only: `$match`, `$search`, `$vectorSearch`, `$sample`, `$geoNear`, `$sort`, `$skip`, `$limit`. Must either begin with `$search`/`$vectorSearch`/`$geoNear` or contain an explicit `$sort`.
- Pipeline names: non-empty, no leading `$`, no `.`, no `\0`.
- De-duplicates: a doc appears at most once regardless of how many pipelines return it.
- Single collection only; no database scope.
- ⚠️ On 8.0.X you must **open a support case** to enable it. Fine from 8.1+.

**Real working example from MongoDB's own hybrid tutorial** [VERIFIED: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/hybrid-search/vector-search-with-full-text-search.md]:

```javascript
[
  { "$rankFusion": {
      "input": { "pipelines": {
          "vectorPipeline": [{ "$vectorSearch": {
              "index": "hybrid-vector-search",
              "path": "plot_embedding_voyage_4_large",
              "queryVector": [...],
              "numCandidates": 500,
              "limit": 50 }}],
          "fullTextPipeline": [
              { "$search": { "index": "hybrid-full-text-search",
                  "text": { "query": "charming animal", "path": "fullplot", "fuzzy": {} }}},
              { "$limit": 50 }
          ]
      }},
      "combination": { "weights": { "vectorPipeline": 0.5, "fullTextPipeline": 0.5 }},
      "scoreDetails": true
  }},
  { "$project": { "_id":1, "title":1, "fullplot":1, "scoreDetails": {"$meta":"scoreDetails"} }},
  { "$limit": 10 }
]
```

#### `$scoreFusion` + `$score` — the recency/importance lever you want [VERIFIED]

```javascript
{
  $scoreFusion: {
    input: {
      pipelines: { <name>: [...] },
      normalization: "none" | "sigmoid" | "minMaxScaler"
    },
    combination: {
      weights: { <name>: <number> },
      method: "avg" | "expression",       // default "avg"
      expression: { $sum: [ {$multiply: ["$$pipeA", 10]}, "$$pipeB" ] }
    },
    scoreDetails: <bool>
  }
}
```

- `sigmoid` = `1/(1+e^-x)`; `minMaxScaler` = `(s - min_s)/(max_s - min_s)`.
- **Key insight for a knowledge brain:** input pipelines that don't natively produce a score can supply one via the new **`$score` stage** — `{$score: {score: <expression>, normalization: "sigmoid", weight: <n>}}`. This is how you fold **recency decay** or **importance/confidence** into hybrid ranking *inside the database*, alongside vector and text, rather than re-sorting in Node. That's the single most directly applicable new capability for your `facts`/`sources` collections.
- Docs note: **8.3+** (the GA blog post says 8.2+ — trust the manual).

#### `$rerank` — native Voyage cross-encoder [VERIFIED]

```json
{ "$rerank": {
    "query": { "text": "<query-text>" },
    "path": "<field>" | ["<f1>","<f2>"],
    "numDocsToRerank": <int, max 1000>,
    "model": "rerank-2.5" | "rerank-2.5-lite" | "rerank-2" | "rerank-2-lite"
}}
```

- Score via `{$addFields: {rerankScore: {$meta: "score"}}}`. **`$rerank` overwrites `$meta:"score"`** — project the prior `$rankFusion` score into a named field *before* `$rerank` if you need both.
- **Errors if any `path` field is missing on any input doc.** Mitigate with a prior `$set` to `""` or `$match` with `$exists`.
- **Hard limitations:** cannot be used on self-managed or **Atlas Local** deployments; cannot appear inside `$rankFusion`/`$scoreFusion` input pipelines; not on Views. Must be enabled per-project by a Project Owner (org-level Cedar `forbid` policy available to block it).
- Runs off-cluster on MongoDB's infra — does not consume your cluster CPU, but adds real latency. Docs: "best suited for workloads where retrieval quality is prioritized over ultra-low latency, such as RAG and agentic AI."
- **Pricing:** `rerank-2.5` $0.05/1M tokens, `rerank-2.5-lite` $0.02/1M. **200M free tokens one-time per org.** Billing formula: `(query_tokens × numDocsToRerank) + sum(document_tokens)`. Rate limits 4,000 RPM / 4M TPM (`2.5`) or 8M TPM (`2.5-lite`). [VERIFIED: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/query/native-reranking/billing.md · .../managing.md]

**The canonical full-stack memory retrieval pipeline is now: `$rankFusion`(vector + text [+ `$score` recency]) → `$rerank` → `$limit`.** MongoDB documents exactly this composition.

### 1.2 Automated Embedding — you may not need to embed in app code anymore

Public Preview announced **2026-05-11** ("AI Search for Agents: Announcing Automated Embedding in MongoDB Atlas"). [VERIFIED: https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/channel/artificial-intelligence]

**Index definition** — new `autoEmbed` field type [VERIFIED: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/index/vector-search-type.md]:
```json
{ "fields": [
    { "type": "autoEmbed", "modality": "text", "path": "<field>",
      "model": "voyage-4-large | voyage-4 | voyage-4-lite | voyage-code-3",
      "numDimensions": 256 | 512 | 1024 | 2048,
      "quantization": "float | scalar | binary | binaryNoRescore",
      "similarity": "dotProduct | cosine | euclidean",
      "indexingMethod": "flat | hnsw",
      "hnswOptions": { "maxEdges": <n>, "numEdgeCandidates": <n> } },
    { "type": "filter", "path": "<field>" }
]}
```

**Query** — pass text, not vectors:
```json
{ "$vectorSearch": { "index": "<name>", "path": "<field>",
    "query": "<query-text>", "model": "<embedding-model>" }}
```

Mechanics [VERIFIED: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/crud-embeddings/automated-embedding/overview.md]:
- Initial sync scans the collection, embeds via Voyage, stores vectors in a **separate internal system collection** (`__mdb_internal_search`, naming format `<index_id>-<hash>-<mv_version>-<def_version>` since 2026-06-30) — **your documents stay clean, no `embedding: number[]` field bloating them**. This is a genuinely nice property for a document-model knowledge brain.
- Ongoing sync via **change streams** on insert/update/delete. Updates to non-indexed fields do not trigger re-embedding.
- Self-managed Community/Enterprise supported by supplying a Voyage API key; Atlas uses MongoDB-hosted multi-tenant inference (GCP, US region).
- **Pricing / 1M tokens:** `voyage-4-lite` $0.02 · `voyage-4` $0.06 (recommended) · `voyage-4-large` $0.12 · `voyage-code-3` $0.18. **200M free tokens per org, one-time, non-refreshing.** Index rate limits 2,000 RPM; TPM 3M/8M/16M/3M respectively. [VERIFIED: .../automated-embedding/models.md]

**Trade-off for you:** you lose control of chunking and input_type asymmetry, and you pay per query. For a knowledge brain where facts are short and writes are bursty, it removes a whole embedding pipeline. For high-QPS retrieval it may be cheaper to keep embedding yourself.
