### 1.4 Is there an official `mongodb-agent-memory` package? — **No, but there's something better for you**

**Nothing named `mongodb-agent-memory` exists on npm or PyPI** [VERIFIED]. Instead MongoDB DevRel shipped a family of framework-specific memory integrations in Q2 2026:

#### ⭐ `@mongodb-developer/vercel-ai-memory` — the most directly relevant artifact in this entire survey

- npm **v0.4.2, published 2026-06-25**; repo https://github.com/mongodb-developer/vercel-ai-memory (⭐2, pushed 2026-06-25, Apache-2.0); author **Pavel Duchovny** (MongoDB DevRel). Peers: `ai ^6||^7`, `mongodb ^6||^7`, `zod ^3.25||^4`. Tracks AI SDK v7 and driver v7 actively.
- **It is listed as a first-class memory provider in the official Vercel AI SDK v7 docs** alongside Letta, Mem0, Supermemory, and Hindsight — so despite 2 GitHub stars, it's the canonical MongoDB path. [VERIFIED: https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/agents/memory]

**Five memory tiers, each a collection** [VERIFIED from `src/types.ts`]:

| Type | Collection | Vector index | Default retention |
|---|---|---|---|
| session | `session_memory` | — | TTL 86,400s on `created_at` |
| semantic | `semantic_memory` | `semantic_vector_index` | none |
| procedural | `procedural_memory` | `procedural_vector_index` | none |
| episodic | `episodic_memory` | `episodic_vector_index` | TTL 31,536,000s on **`stats.last_retrieved`** |
| scratchpad | `scratchpad_memory` | — | TTL 3,600s on `created_at` |

The `SemanticMemory` document shape, verbatim:
```ts
interface SemanticMemory {
  _id: ObjectId
  user_id: string
  name: string                    // entity name
  category: 'semantic'
  description: string
  embedding: number[]
  importance: number              // LLM-assigned 1–10
  stats: { retrieval_ct: number; avg_importance: number; last_retrieved: Date }
  timestamp: Date
  is_latest: boolean              // ← temporal versioning
  tags?: string[]
  expire_at?: Date | null         // ← TTL index expireAfterSeconds: 0
}
```

Mechanisms worth stealing:
- **Temporal versioning via `is_latest`**: `semanticSave` does `updateMany({user_id, name}, {$set:{is_latest:false}})` then `insertOne({..., is_latest:true})` when `keepHistory`, else an in-place upsert. Retrieval pre-filters `is_latest: {$eq: true}` **inside `$vectorSearch.filter`**.
- **Four retention modes:** `none` | `ttl` | **`ttl+importance`** (TTL only applies below `minImportance` — important memories immune) | **`dynamic`** (`computeExpireAt({importance, stats, createdAt})` per doc, backed by an `expire_at` TTL index with `expireAfterSeconds: 0`, recomputed on read when `refreshOnRead: true`). That last one is a **real forgetting curve**, e.g. `2^importance` hours, or `24 * 1.5^importance + retrieval_ct * 12`.
- **`memory_forget` tool**: sets `expire_at = now`; TTL monitor reaps within ~60s. A clean agent-driven GDPR-adjacent delete.
- **Retrieval-time filters:** `minImportance`, `recencyWindowHours` (applied as `$match` on `stats.last_retrieved` after `$vectorSearch`), `numCandidatesMultiplier` (default 10 → `numCandidates = limit * 10`).
- **Read-side write-back:** every search `$inc`s `stats.retrieval_ct` and `$set`s `stats.last_retrieved` (bulk-written), which is what feeds decay.
- **Hook-driven vs tool-driven session persistence.** The README is refreshingly honest that tool-driven is "**not deterministic**: the model sometimes skips writes." Production mode uses `prepareCall` + `onFinish` hooks with `topology.hideToolCommands: ['session']` so the runtime persists every turn exactly once. **This is the right lesson: don't let the LLM decide whether to persist the transcript.**
- Multi-tenant via `topology.extraFilterFields: { semantic: ['tenant_id'] }` → registered as `{type:'filter'}` paths in the vector index.

⚠️ **Gap:** it uses **plain `$vectorSearch` only** — no `$rankFusion`, no `$search`, no `$rerank`. Given your Atlas Search setup in `packages/knowledge/search.ts`, you're already ahead of it on retrieval.

https://github.com/RichmondAlake/memorizz · **⭐757**, pushed **2026-07-19**, PyPI v0.4.0 (2026-07-19). ## PART 2 — Mastra (the other Priority 1)

**Status: very healthy, and its memory model changed fundamentally since your cutoff.** ⭐26,828, pushed 2026-08-02, Apache-2.0 (© Kepler Software). `@mastra/core` **1.55.0** (2026-07-30), `@mastra/memory` **1.24.0** (2026-07-28). 1.0 shipped 2026-01-20. **$22M Series A led by Spark Capital, 2026-04-09** ($35M total; Gradient, basecase, YC W25). Weekly npm downloads: core 1.36M, memory 851K. [VERIFIED: GitHub API, npm registry, https://mastra.ai/blog/series-a]

### 2.1 The big shift: Observational Memory replaced the old model

Since `@mastra/memory@1.1.0` (Feb 2026), the flagship is **Observational Memory (OM)**, and the docs now say verbatim: *"In practical terms, OM replaces both working memory and message history, and has greater accuracy (and lower cost) than Semantic Recall."* [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/observational-memory.md]

**Mechanism:** two background agents — an **Observer** and a **Reflector** — maintain a dense, **append-only** observation log that substitutes for raw history.
- Observer fires when unobserved messages cross **30,000 tokens**; Reflector fires when the observation log crosses **40,000 tokens**.
- **Reflection rewrites the *entire* log**, so memory stays bounded forever rather than accumulating a third layer.
- Buffering ratios: `bufferTokens: 0.2` (background pass every 20% of threshold), `bufferActivation: 0.8` (drop ~80% of history on activation), `blockAfter: 1.2` (hard sync ceiling at 36k / 48k).
- Observation format: two-level Markdown bullets with **emoji priority + timestamps** (`- 🔴 12:10 User is building a Next.js app…`).
- **Three-date temporal model:** *observation date*, *referenced date* ("my flight is January 31"), *relative date* ("2 days from today"). This is the only real temporal model in Mastra.
- **The architectural bet: an append-only, prompt-cacheable prefix beats per-turn retrieval.** That's the opposite of RAG-style memory and worth serious consideration for your design.
- Storage support for OM: `@mastra/pg`, `@mastra/libsql`, `@mastra/mysql`, **`@mastra/mongodb`**, `@mastra/convex`.
- **Extractors** (1.22.0+) piggyback typed Zod extraction on the Observer's already-primed context — cheap structured extraction as a side effect of observation.

### 2.2 Working memory — exact mechanism

- Markdown **template** (REPLACE semantics — agent emits the whole blob) **XOR** Zod/Standard-Schema **`schema`** (**MERGE semantics** — deep-merge, `null` deletes, **arrays replaced wholesale**). Mutually exclusive at the type level.
- Tool name is **`updateWorkingMemory`** (or `setWorkingMemory` when `useStateSignals: true`).
- Config: `{ enabled, template | schema, scope: 'thread'|'resource' (default **'resource'**), useStateSignals: false, agentManaged: true }`.
- Injected into the **system message** wrapped in `<working_memory_template>` / `<working_memory_data>` tags; tag parsing is `indexOf`-based specifically to avoid ReDoS.
- Experimental `version: 'vnext'` swaps full-rewrite for a **search-and-replace edit** tool taking `{newMemory, searchString, updateReason: 'append-new-memory'|'clarify-existing-memory'|'replace-irrelevant-memory'}`.
- `useStateSignals` moves WM out of the system prompt into a state signal — motivated purely by **prompt-cache invalidation**.
- Resource-scoped WM requires **libSQL, Postgres, Upstash, or MongoDB**.

### 2.3 Semantic recall — exact mechanism and defaults

```ts
semanticRecall: {
  topK: 4,                                    // default
  messageRange: { before: 1, after: 1 },      // default
  scope: 'resource',                          // default
  filter?: VectorFilter,                      // MongoDB-style $and/$or/$eq/$in/...
  indexConfig?: VectorIndexConfig
}
```
- **`messageRange` is a hydration window, not a vector setting.** After top-K, each hit's `metadata.message_id` + `thread_id` is turned into a relational re-fetch with `withPreviousMessages`/`withNextMessages`. That's a clean pattern: vector index finds anchors, relational store supplies contiguous context.
- Scope is implemented as **nothing more than a metadata filter**: `{resource_id}` vs `{thread_id}`. Embedding metadata written on save is `{message_id, thread_id, resource_id}`. Resource-scoped recall **throws** without a `resourceId` — "a missing ID never expands the search."
- Index naming: **`memory_messages`** at 1536 dims, `memory_messages_<dim>` otherwise; requests `metadataIndexes: ['thread_id','resource_id']`.
- **Disabled by default** (`semanticRecall: false`); `lastMessages` default **10**.

### 2.4 Memory processors — the pattern worth copying

Memory is now *implemented as* processors in the agent pipeline: `MessageHistory`, `SemanticRecall`, `WorkingMemory` (all `@mastra/core/processors`). Execution order:

```
Input:  [Memory Processors] → [Your inputProcessors]
Output: [Your outputProcessors] → [Memory Processors]
```

**Rationale: an output guardrail that calls `abort()` runs *before* persistence, so nothing gets written to memory.** That's a genuinely good design constraint for a system with GDPR/PII concerns. If you place one manually, Mastra won't auto-add its own.
- `TokenLimiter` and `ToolCallFilter` are **generic** processors, not memory processors: `TokenLimiterProcessor {limit, strategy:'truncate'|'abort', countMode:'cumulative'|'part', trimMode:'best-fit'|'contiguous'}`; `ToolCallFilter {exclude, filterAfterToolSteps, preserveModelOutput}`.

### 2.5 MongoDB support — yes, and `MongoDBVector` is the most transferable code in the repo

**`@mastra/mongodb` v1.15.1 (2026-07-30)** ships **both** `MongoDBStore` (storage domains) and `MongoDBVector` (Atlas Vector Search). Requires Atlas cloud or **Atlas Local via Docker**; MongoDB 7.0+ recommended. [VERIFIED: https://mastra.ai/reference/storage/mongodb.md · .../vectors/mongodb.md · GitHub `stores/mongodb/src/{storage,vector}`]

Collections: `mastra_threads`, `mastra_messages`, `mastra_resources`, `mastra_observational_memory`, plus workflow/trace/scorer tables. Default indexes include `{resourceId:1, createdAt:-1}`, `{thread_id:1, createdAt:1}`, unique `{id:1}`.

`MongoDBVector` capabilities that are directly worth stealing:
- **`filterFields`** declares metadata fields as vector-index filter paths (`metadata.<field>`) so filters get **pushed into `$vectorSearch`** instead of pre-filtering candidate `_id`s — explicitly to dodge **the 16 MB BSON limit on large result sets**. Undeclared fields silently fall back to slow pre-filtering.
- **BYO-collection mode**: index an existing operational collection; **read-only by default**, writes require explicit `allowWrites: true`, and the policy is **persisted durably** and "fails closed." `deleteIndex()` on a BYO index drops Atlas indexes but preserves documents.
- **`metadataMode: 'document'`** returns the whole source document as metadata and matches filters against the **root** (no `metadata.` prefix) — for operational collections.
- **`hybridQuery({queryVector, query, paths, weights: {vector, text}})`** uses **server-side `$rankFusion`**; docs state MongoDB ≥8.0, GA from 8.1.
- `numCandidates` defaults to `20 × topK`, capped 10,000; native `ObjectId` `_id`s supported.
- **Retention:** `@mastra/mongodb` has a real `retention.ts` with age-based `prune()` (batched, resumable, cancellable, lazy anchor-index creation), but Mastra **never runs it for you** — and the OM collection has no timestamp anchor so **cannot be age-pruned**. Docs recommend **native MongoDB TTL indexes** instead, via `indexes: [{collection:'mastra_messages', keys:{createdAt:1}, options:{expireAfterSeconds: 30*86400}}]`.

**LongMemEval-S: OM + gpt-5-mini = 94.87%**, claimed "highest score ever recorded on this benchmark, by any system, with any model." Oracle gpt-4o baseline 82.40%; full-context gpt-4o 60.20%; average context ~30k tokens; 3–6× text compression. [VERIFIED as a claim: https://mastra.ai/research/observational-memory, 2026-02-09] Self-published, self-run, mixed actor models across the leaderboard rows — treat accordingly.

### 3.2 Honcho — healthy, uniquely *perspectival*, AGPL

⭐**6,382**, **AGPL-3.0**, Python, pushed 2026-07-31, 91 commits since May, latest tag **v3.0.12**. Honcho 3 shipped 2026-01-26. Funding not verifiable. [VERIFIED: GitHub API, https://plasticlabs.ai/blog/posts/Honcho-3]

- **Model:** `Workspace → Peers + Sessions → Messages`. **Peers, not users** (agents are peers too; peers↔sessions many-to-many).
- **Memory unit = "conclusion":**
  ```
  id, content, observer_id, observed_id, session_id,
  level: "explicit" | "deductive" | "inductive" | "contradiction", created_at
  ```
  **The `(observer_id, observed_id)` pair is the differentiator — memory is perspectival.** Alice's model of Bob is a distinct object from the system's global model of Bob. Nobody else in this survey has this. Directly relevant if your knowledge brain ever needs "what does person X believe about person Y."
- `observe_me` (global rep from all messages) vs `observe_others` (local, only from messages that peer actually saw).
- **Write path:** message + task enqueued synchronously; reasoning async. **Token-batched:** the deriver accumulates until ~**1,000 tokens** pending per representation, then processes in one call. **Recent memories are not immediately queryable.** Extraction uses their fine-tuned **Neuromancer** models, not frontier LLMs.
- **Consolidation — "the Dreamer":** two sequential agents. *Deduction* handles knowledge updates/contradictions and **hard-deletes the outdated conclusion, creating a new one** (no tombstone). *Induction* finds patterns requiring **≥2 source conclusions**. Trigger requires **all three**: ≥50 new conclusions, ≥8 hours since last dream, enabled — plus a **60-min idle timeout**; new messages cancel and reset.
- **Retrieval — two paths:** `context()` (~200ms, **free and unlimited**, packs summaries + recent messages + representation + peer card into a token budget, `.to_openai()`/`.to_anthropic()`); and `chat()` — **the Dialectic** — which spawns an agent that searches conclusions, **traces a conclusion back to the premises it was drawn from**, and synthesizes. Five reasoning levels `minimal→max`, each with its own model and tools. Search is hybrid BM25 + vector, limit 10/max 100; ⚠️ keyword hits are available immediately, semantic hits lag embedding by seconds; **fusion method undocumented**.
- Summaries: short every 20 messages, long every 60.
- **Forgetting:** none — no TTL, no decay. Only Dreamer consolidation + explicit deletes.
- **Temporal: weakest here.** `created_at` only. Docs list "multi-hop and temporal reasoning" as **future work**.
- **Benchmarks:** LoCoMo **89.9%**, LongMemEval-S **90.4%**, BEAM-100K **0.630** (0.646 @500K → 0.409 @10M), 60–90% token savings. Neuromancer XR (Qwen3-8B fine-tuned on ~10,000 curated conclusion-derivations): LoCoMo **86.9%** vs Claude 4 Sonnet 80.0% vs base Qwen3-8B 69.6%. ⚠️ `honcho.dev/evals` is JS-rendered and returned empty; the repro repo `plastic-labs/honcho-benchmarks` was last pushed **2025-12-19** and is a stub.
- **Storage: PostgreSQL only, no MongoDB** (docs say so explicitly; 0 code hits). Vector pluggable: `pgvector|turbopuffer|lancedb`. `EMBEDDING_VECTOR_DIMENSIONS=1536` is **immutable for the life of a deployment**.
- **TS SDK: excellent** — `@honcho-ai/sdk` **v2.2.0 (2026-07-02)**, released in lockstep with Python.
- **Pricing:** ingest **$2.00/M tokens**; `context()` **free/unlimited**; per-query reasoning $0.001 (minimal) → **$0.50 (max)**. Startups <$5M raised get $1,000 credits.

### 3.5 Redis Agent Memory Server — **repositioned, not abandoned**

⭐**301** (far smaller than the others), Apache-2.0, Python.

**The structural change:** on **2026-07-09** commit *"Relocate project into `V0/` and add Redis Agent Memory landing layer (#319)"* moved the whole OSS server into a `V0/` subdirectory. The new root README says in Redis's own words that V0 *"serves as the research foundation and architectural starting point"* but **"it is not the current supported production path"** — supported teams use **Redis Cloud**, not the OSS version. [VERIFIED: GitHub API + raw README]

**Redis is pushing hard, but commercially.** **Redis Iris** is a four-service managed context engine: RDI (CDC from Oracle/MySQL/Postgres/etc.), Context Retriever, **Redis Agent Memory** (GA on Redis Cloud, private preview on Redis Software w/ license key), and LangCache. The managed API surface is **not drop-in compatible** with OSS: `/v1/stores/{storeId}/long-term-memory` with camelCase (`memoryType`, `ownerId`) vs OSS `/v1/long-term-memory` with snake_case (`memory_type`, `user_id`). [VERIFIED: https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/context-engine/agent-memory/]

OSS momentum has stopped: last release **server/v0.15.2, 2026-04-10** (~4 months); 32 commits since May of which **10 of the last 15 are Dependabot**; npm `agent-memory-client` **0.3.1, 2026-01-31** (~6 months stale).

**But the design is the best-specified forgetting model in the entire survey, and it's Apache-2.0 so you can lift it freely:**

- **`MemoryRecord`:** `text, id, memory_type, topics[], entities[], user_id, namespace, event_date, session_id`. Types `semantic` | `episodic` | `message` (+ `preference`, `summary`). **`event_date` is distinct from creation time — a genuine event-time vs system-time separation.**
- **Four named extraction strategies:** `discrete` (default, individual facts), `summary` (`max_summary_length` 500), `preferences`, `custom` (domain prompt; docs warn about prompt injection).
- **Retrieval:** `semantic` (default, `distance_threshold: 0.8`) | `keyword` (BM25) | **`hybrid` (`hybrid_alpha` default 0.7)**.
- **⭐ Recency boost — a real published ranking formula:**
  ```python
  final_score   = semantic_weight * semantic_similarity + recency_weight * recency_score
  recency_score = freshness_weight * freshness_score + novelty_weight * novelty_score
  freshness     = exp(-ln(2) * days_since_creation    / freshness_half_life)
  novelty       = exp(-ln(2) * days_since_last_access / novelty_half_life)
  ```
  Defaults: semantic **0.8** / recency **0.2**; freshness **0.6** / novelty **0.4**; half-lives **30 days** (created) and **7 days** (last access). **Nobody else publishes numbers this precise.** This maps directly onto a `$score` stage inside `$scoreFusion` on your stack.
- **Forgetting lifecycle:** working memory **TTL 1 hour** default; long-term forgetting **off by default** (`FORGETTING_MAX_AGE_DAYS` 90, `FORGETTING_MAX_INACTIVE_DAYS` 30, `FORGETTING_BUDGET_KEEP_TOP_N`); four strategies — age, inactivity, combined, **budget-based keep-top-N by access**. Compaction every 10 min. ⚠️ *"Without a running task worker, automatic forgetting will not occur regardless of configuration settings."*
- **Benchmarks: none. Zero published numbers** anywhere. Redis markets on latency/infra credibility.
- **Storage: Redis only. No MongoDB.** `BACKEND_TYPE=[redis|custom]`; custom requires subclassing `MemoryVectorDatabase` and no other production-ready backend is documented.
- Native **MCP server** alongside REST (port 8000) is a real differentiator.

- Memory store (`memstore_…`) = workspace-scoped collection of **path-addressed text documents**, **mounted as a real directory** in the session sandbox at `/mnt/memory/<slug>/`; attached at session creation only, max 8 per session, `access: read_write|read_only` enforced at the filesystem level. Lifecycle `pending→running→completed/failed/canceled`, runtime "minutes to a few hours." Nuance: `instructions` steers *synthesis*, not editing — "imperative directives that target specific lines generally produce no change."

[VERIFIED: https://docs.crewai.com/en/concepts/memory · https://pypi.org/project/crewai/] Note MongoDB DevRel independently built `crewai-mongodb-memory` implementing the `StorageBackend` protocol.

[VERIFIED: https://eve.dev/docs/patterns/multi-tenant-memory · https://eve.dev/docs/guides/state]

[VERIFIED: https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/api-reference/sessions/ · .../store-and-sync-state/]

### 5.6 New benchmarks — the field moved from recall to task outcome

This is the most important intellectual shift of 2026. **LOCOMO and LongMemEval are now widely considered saturated and mis-specified** — they test recall, not whether memory helps an agent *do the task*.

1. **BEAM** — ICLR 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.27246. **100 conversations, 2,000 validated questions, contexts up to 10M tokens, 10 memory dimensions** (abstention, contradiction resolution, event ordering, instruction-following over time). **Everyone's scores collapse on it** (Hindsight 73.9% @1M → 64.1% @10M). This is now the de-facto hard benchmark.
2. **STATE-Bench** — **Microsoft**, 2026-05-19, https://opensource.microsoft.com/blog/2026/05/19/introducing-state-bench-a-benchmark-for-ai-agent-memory/ · https://github.com/microsoft/STATE-Bench (⭐72, MIT — I re-verified). **Memory-agnostic: measures whether agents *improve with experience*** on 450 realistic enterprise tasks (support/travel/shopping). Metrics: **pass@1, pass^5 (succeeds all 5 runs), cost/task, LLM-judged UX**. Baseline: **GPT-5.1 with no memory completes fewer than half of tasks reliably; only ~30% of travel tasks pass^5.** Leaderboard currently **has no published system results** — it's an open challenge. **The most credible new benchmark and the one to watch.**
3. **MemoryArena** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16313 (Feb 2026; authors incl. Yejin Choi, Alex Pentland). Human-crafted **interdependent** multi-session tasks. **Headline finding: agents near-perfect on LoCoMo "perform poorly in our agentic setting."** Swapping memory-equipped for long-context-only drops task completion **80% → 45%**.
4. **LifeBench** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03781 (Mar 2026). Declarative **and** non-declarative (habitual/procedural) memory from diverse digital traces. **"Top-tier SOTA memory systems reach just 55.2% accuracy."**
5. **⭐ GateMem** — https://github.com/rzhub/GateMem (⭐192, Jun 2026, MIT). *"Benchmark and evaluation toolkit for **memory governance** in multi-principal settings"* — multiple principals write to a shared pool and query under different roles/scopes/relationships. **Evaluates utility, access control, and deletion enforcement.** **This is the first benchmark that scores whether deletion is actually enforced — directly relevant to your GDPR Art. 17 erasure cascade.** Very new, low activity, but worth tracking.

## PART 7 — Synthesis for Your Stack

**Five things that actually changed in this window:**

1. **Vector-only memory is over.** Every serious 2026 system is hybrid: dense + BM25 + RRF + cross-encoder rerank, usually plus a graph or temporal index. **MongoDB just made that entire stack a native aggregation pipeline** — you're one of the few people who can implement it without a second datastore.
2. **Filesystem/Markdown-as-memory beat database-as-memory in the OSS wave.** Anthropic's `/memories` and `/mnt/memory/`, AG2's `KnowledgeStore`, OpenViking's `viking://`, EverOS, memU, memsearch, basic-memory — human-readable, Git-diffable files as the source of truth, with the vector store demoted to a **rebuildable shadow index**. Worth considering for auditability even on a Mongo backbone.
3. **"Dream"/consolidation passes are now a named pattern at both major labs** within a month of each other. Your `09c49c6` "dream cycle" is aligned. Copy Anthropic's non-destructive variant: write consolidation output to a *new* store, review, then swap.
4. **Benchmarks moved from recall to task outcome.** STATE-Bench, MemoryArena, LifeBench, GateMem. MemoryArena's "LoCoMo-perfect agents fail in agentic settings" is the single most important result of 2026.
5. **Forgetting is still the least-solved primitive**, and prompt-injection-into-memory is now an explicitly documented threat (Anthropic, eve, Microsoft all warn about it in different ways).

**Concrete mechanisms worth stealing, ranked by fit:**

1. **Redis's recency-boost formula** (exp half-life on freshness + novelty, 0.8/0.2 and 0.6/0.4 weights, 30d/7d half-lives) implemented as a **`$score` pipeline inside `$scoreFusion`** alongside your `$vectorSearch` and `$search`. Apache-2.0, so lift it freely. This is the highest-leverage single change.
2. **`@mongodb-developer/vercel-ai-memory`'s retention model** — `ttl+importance` (important memories immune to TTL) and `dynamic` with a per-doc `computeExpireAt` backed by an `expire_at` TTL index at `expireAfterSeconds: 0`. Plus `memory_forget` = set `expire_at = now`. This is a complete, tested forgetting curve on MongoDB.
3. **Supermemory's soft-delete + semantic bulk-forget with `dryRun`** (`isForgotten`, `forgetReason`, `maxForget` 1–500) — a much better UX than hard deletes, and it composes with your erasure cascade.
4. **Anthropic's memory-version `redact` endpoint** — immutable version history plus a redaction primitive that preserves the audit trail. That's the published state of the art for GDPR-with-audit, and the closest analogue to `erasePerson`.
5. **Mastra's processor ordering** — memory processors run *before* your input processors and *after* your output processors, so an aborting guardrail prevents persistence entirely. Cheap to replicate, and it's the right safety property for a PII-bearing knowledge brain.
6. **MemMachine's `citations` table** (`profile_id → episode_id`) — you already have `sources ↔ facts`; note that it's the only one of the five that makes provenance a first-class queryable join, which validates your design.
7. **`is_latest` temporal versioning pre-filtered inside `$vectorSearch.filter`** — cheap supersession semantics that keep history without polluting retrieval.
8. **Hook-driven, not tool-driven, transcript persistence.** MongoDB's own package documents that LLM-controlled session writes are "not deterministic — the model sometimes skips writes." Persist from the runtime.
9. **`voyage-context-4`** for chunk embeddings if your facts carry document context — it removes the manual context-augmentation step entirely.
10. **`filterFields` pushed into `$vectorSearch`** (from Mastra's `MongoDBVector`) to avoid the 16 MB BSON limit on pre-filtered `_id` lists at scale.

**And the reassuring finding:** across ~25 verified OSS projects and 5 commercial systems, **essentially nobody has built MongoDB-native agent memory.** The only one is Papr (⭐73, AGPL, stale). | 2 | temporal | 321 |
| 3 | open-domain | 96 |
| 4 | single-hop | 841 |
| 5 | **adversarial** | **446** |
| | **Total** | **1,986** |
| | **Excluding cat 5** | **1,540** |

This confirms the ubiquitous "1,540 questions" figure: it is cats 1–4 of the **10‑conversation public subset**, not the 50‑conversation paper set. Zep's current 94.7% is reported as **1,459/1,540**, which cross-validates the denominator [V].

**The category‑5 defect, mechanically explained** [V-mine]. Category‑5 items have **no `answer` field** (only 2 of 446 do). They carry `adversarial_answer` instead — and that field holds *the answer to the wrong-speaker version of the question*, i.e. the thing the model must **not** say:

- cat 4: *"What did **Melanie** realize after the charity race?"* → `answer`: "self-care is important"
- cat 5: *"What did **Caroline** realize after her charity race?"* → `adversarial_answer`: "self-care is important"

So **444 of 1,986 questions (22.4%) have a null gold answer**. A harness keying on `answer` silently drops them; a harness keying on `adversarial_answer` as gold **rewards hallucination**. This is the precise mechanism behind the Zep↔Mem0 dispute (§A.6).

**Other data defects I measured** [V-mine]: 9/2,815 evidence pointers (0.32%) dangle to non-existent `dia_id`s; 12 duplicate question strings.

**Gold-answer errors** [V-mine]: I located Letta's cited example verbatim in the released file — *"What might John's degree be in?"* → `answer`: "Political science, Public administration, Public affairs" (category 3, evidence `D9:6`).

**Published criticisms:**
- **Zep** ([blog](https://blog.getzep.com/lies-damn-lies-statistics-is-mem0-really-sota-in-agent-memory/)) [V]: conversations are only **16k–26k tokens** — inside every modern context window; **"lacks questions designed to test knowledge updates"**; category 5 unusable; questions about images whose info isn't in the descriptions; **incorrect speaker attribution**; ambiguous questions with multiple defensible answers. Their falsification test is worth adopting verbatim: *"If simply providing all the text yields better results than the specialized memory system, the benchmark isn't adequately stressing memory capabilities."*
- **LongMemEval's own comparison table** confirms LoCoMo does **not** cover Knowledge Update (✗ in the KU column) [V].
- **ConvoMem** ([arXiv:2511.10523](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10523), Salesforce) [V]: *"sample sizes per category often fall below 100 questions … making statistical comparisons unreliable; synthetic data generation introduces detectable patterns that models exploit rather than demonstrating genuine memory."*
- **LoCoMo‑Plus** ([arXiv:2602.10715](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10715v1)) [V]: task-disclosed prompting and string-matching metrics "conflate memory fidelity with prompt adaptation"; metrics show length bias, "peaking near the average ground-truth length." Every system drops when re-tested on beyond-factual cognitive memory: Gemini‑2.5‑Pro 71.78→45.72, GPT‑4o 62.99→41.94, Mem0 57.24→41.44, A‑Mem 59.64→42.44 (gaps 9.6–26.1 pts).
- **Letta** ([blog](https://www.letta.com/blog/benchmarking-ai-agent-memory/)) [V]: a plain **filesystem** with `grep`/`search_files`/`open`/`close` on **gpt‑4o‑mini** scores **74.0%**, beating Mem0's best graph variant at **68.5%**. *"Simpler tools are more likely to be in the training data of an agent."*

**Verdict:** LoCoMo is a *smoke test*, not a benchmark. Useful only for catching gross regressions.

### A.2 LongMemEval — the best-designed of the classic benchmarks

[V] [arXiv:2410.10813](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.10813v2) (Wu et al., UCLA + Tencent AI Lab, ICLR 2025) · [repo](https://github.com/xiaowu0162/longmemeval)

**Five abilities** (verbatim): Information Extraction, Multi-Session Reasoning, **Knowledge Updates** ("recognize the changes in the user's personal information and update the knowledge of the user dynamically over time"), Temporal Reasoning, **Abstention** ("identify questions seeking unknown information … and answer 'I don't know'").

**Exact composition — I downloaded the dataset and counted** [V-mine]:

| Question type | Total | answerable | `_abs` |
|---|---|---|---|
| temporal-reasoning | 133 | 127 | 6 |
| multi-session | 133 | 121 | 12 |
| **knowledge-update** | **78** | 72 | 6 |
| single-session-user | 70 | 64 | 6 |
| single-session-assistant | 56 | 56 | 0 |
| single-session-preference | 30 | 30 | 0 |
| **Total** | **500** | 470 | **30** |

**Construction** [V]: ontology of **164 user attributes** in 5 categories → LLM-generated background paragraphs → evidence statements → 8–10-turn sessions. Haystack: *"we sample a number of unrelated user-AI chat sessions, randomly insert the evidence sessions in the middle, and assign a plausible timestamp."* Distractors come from **(1) self-chat on non-conflicting attributes and (2) ShareGPT + UltraChat**. Variants: **_S** ≈115k tokens (~40–50 sessions); **_M** = 500 sessions, ~1.5M tokens; **_oracle** = evidence sessions only.

**Evaluation** [V]: prompt-engineered **GPT‑4o judge**, separate prompts per question type; **>97% agreement with human experts** overall, ≥90% in all settings, deviating most on single-session-preference and abstention. Intermediate retrieval metrics: **Recall@k and NDCG@k** against human-annotated answer-location labels.

**The four design findings — the most directly implementable results in the whole field** [V]:

1. **Round-level > session-level** granularity. But *"replacing sessions or rounds with extracted summaries or facts negatively impacts QA performance due to information loss. The only exception is … multi-session reasoning questions, where fact decomposition consistently improves performance."*
2. **Fact-augmented key expansion** — index the verbatim round *plus* extracted facts. Table 3, value = round:

| Key design | Recall@5 | NDCG@5 | Recall@10 | QA (GPT‑4o, top‑5) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K = V (round text) | 0.582 | 0.481 | 0.692 | 0.615 |
| K = fact **only** | 0.530 | 0.411 | 0.654 | 0.588 |
| K = keyphrase only | 0.282 | 0.159 | 0.392 | 0.425 |
| **K = V + fact** | **0.644** | **0.498** | **0.784** | **0.657** |

   +9.4% recall@k, +5.4% accuracy. **Facts belong in the index, not in place of the source.**
3. **Time-aware indexing + query expansion**: +6.8%–11.3% recall on temporal questions.
4. **Chain-of-Note + structured JSON** in the reading step: up to **+10 absolute points**, even with perfect recall.

**Known issue:** there is now an official **[longmemeval-cleaned](https://huggingface.co/datasets/xiaowu0162/longmemeval-cleaned)** dataset (3.03 GB, 12,260 downloads) whose card states it *"removes noisy history sessions that interfere with the answer correctness"* [V] — i.e. the original haystack contained sessions that contradicted the gold answers. **Check which variant any quoted score used.**

**ConvoMem's methodological critique** [V]: LongMemEval *"sources filler conversations from other benchmarks rather than generating them within the same framework … This creates a stylistic mismatch that potentially allows systems to identify evidence conversations based on their different characteristics rather than through genuine memory retrieval."* Given the fillers are ShareGPT/UltraChat, this is a real style-shortcut risk.

### A.3 The statistical-power problem — original computation

I computed Wilson 95% CIs and minimum detectable differences (two-proportion, α=.05, 80% power) on the verified counts [V-mine]:

| Slice | n | 95% CI half-width | Min detectable diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| LongMemEval overall | 500 | ±4.4 pts | 8.7 pts |
| temporal-reasoning | 133 | ±8.4 | 16.8 |
| multi-session | 133 | ±8.4 | 16.8 |
| **knowledge-update** | **78** | **±10.8** | **22.0** |
| single-session-user | 70 | ±11.4 | 23.2 |
| single-session-assistant | 56 | ±12.7 | 25.9 |
| **single-session-preference** | **30** | **±16.8** | **35.4** |
| **abstention (all `_abs`)** | **30** | **±16.8** | **35.4** |
| LoCoMo cat 3 (open-domain) | 96 | ±9.8 | 19.8 |
| LoCoMo cats 1–4 | 1,540 | ±2.5 | 4.9 |

ConvoMem independently reports the same thing [V]: *"the Preferences category contains merely 30 questions, yielding approximately ±18% margin of error … Some multi-session subgroups contain as few as 6 questions, resulting in error margins approaching ±40%."*

**Consequences for claims you will read:**
- Zep's headline "single-session-preference +184% (20.0→56.7)" is on **n=30**. The delta (36.7 pts) does clear the 35.4-pt bar — barely.
- Zep's "knowledge update +6.52%" and "−3.36%" are on **n=78**. Both are **noise**.
- **The two categories that map most directly onto your problem — knowledge-update and abstention — are the two least statistically powered in the benchmark.**

**Golden-set sizing for your own evals** [V-mine, computed]:

| Lift to detect | n per arm @ p≈0.5 | @ p≈0.7 |
|---|---|---|
| 20 pts | 93 | 62 |
| 15 pts | 170 | 121 |
| 10 pts | 388 | 294 |
| 5 pts | 1,565 | 1,251 |

Use a **paired design** (same questions, both configs, McNemar) — it's 2–4× cheaper. For per-category readouts across 7 fact categories at 10‑pt sensitivity you'd need ~2,700 questions; at 20‑pt, ~650.

### A.4 The 2026 successors — what's actually current

**BEAM** — *Beyond a Million Tokens*, ICLR 2026 [V] ([arXiv:2510.27246](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.27246) · [site](https://mohammadtavakoli78.github.io/beam-light/) · [code](https://github.com/mohammadtavakoli78/BEAM)). **100 conversations up to 10M tokens, 2,000 validated questions**, ten abilities: Abstention, **Contradiction Resolution**, Event Ordering, Information Extraction, Instruction Following, Knowledge Update, Multi-Hop Reasoning, Preference Following, Summarization, Temporal Reasoning. The BEAM paper's own best average at 1M is **0.336**. That is a ~2× discrepancy under a strict nugget rubric. Either the protocol differs materially or the numbers aren't comparable.

**MemoryAgentBench** — ICLR 2026 [V] ([arXiv:2507.05257](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.05257v1) · [repo](https://github.com/HUST-AI-HYZ/MemoryAgentBench) · [HF](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai-hyz/MemoryAgentBench)). CR is tested via **FactConsolidation**, built from **MQUAKE counterfactual edit pairs**: original fact then contradictory rewrite, ordered so the newer fact appears later, at 32K/64K/262K context. Metric: Substring Exact Match. Results:

| System | FactConsolidation‑SH | ‑MH |
|---|---|---|
| GPT‑4o (long-context) | 60% | 5% |
| Claude‑3.7‑Sonnet | — | 2% |
| Cognee | 28% | — |
| Mem0 | 18% | 2% |
| most RAG/agentic | 2–7% | ≤6% |

*"All methods fail on the multi-hop situation."* Also: Mem0 needed **14,644 seconds** for memory construction on small datasets.

**ConvoMem** [V] ([arXiv:2511.10523](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10523), Pakhomov/Nijkamp/Xiong, Salesforce). **75,336 QA pairs** (150× LongMemEval), six categories (user facts, assistant recall, abstention, preferences, temporal changes, implicit connections), 1k–3M tokens, configurable 2–300 conversations, **40% single-message / 60% multi-message evidence (2–6 messages)**. Explicit **"design emphasis on enterprise scenarios like customer relationship management, technical support, and business process automation."**

The decision-relevant finding, verbatim: *"simple full-context approaches achieve **70‑82%** accuracy even on our most challenging multi-message evidence cases, while sophisticated RAG-based memory systems like Mem0 achieve only **30‑45%** when operating on conversation histories under 150 interactions … long context excels for the first **30** conversations, remains viable with manageable trade-offs up to **150** conversations, and typically requires hybrid or RAG approaches beyond that point."* Also: *"medium-tier models deliver equivalent memory performance to premium models at **8x lower cost**."*

**MemoryArena** — ICML 2026 [V] ([site](https://memoryarena.github.io/)). Human-crafted **multi-session agentic tasks with interdependent subtasks** — bundled web shopping, group travel planning with preferences, progressive web search, sequential math/physics reasoning. Measures whether memory improves *task completion*, not recall. *"Agents with near-saturated performance on existing long-context memory benchmarks like LoCoMo perform poorly in our agentic setting."* Reported elsewhere [V-2nd]: models near-perfect on LoCoMo fall to **40–60%**; swapping an active memory agent for long-context-only dropped completion from >80% to ~45%.

**ForgetEval / Control-Plane Placement** — [arXiv:2606.15903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15903), **VERIFIED REAL**, Dongxu Yang, v1 14 Jun 2026 [V]. This is the benchmark you most need and almost nobody runs. Thesis, verbatim: ***"Production failures are predominantly forgetting failures rather than recall failures, yet existing benchmarks measure only recall."*** 1,000 templated cases + 385 adversarial (132 hand-crafted + 253 LLM-drafted, oracle-validated), 10-annotator **Fleiss' κ = 0.958**, MIT-licensed with a 6-method adapter protocol (~130 lines to onboard a store). Five forgetting families: **Supersession, Decay, Amnesia, Purge (explicitly GDPR Art. 17), Drift**. Ten adversarial categories including `prefix_collision`, `shared_attribute` (over-deletion), `compound_fact`, `identifier_obfuscation`, `cross_lingual_identifier`. Results: Mem0 v2.0.2 `infer=False` 68.3% / `infer=True` **43.6%**; LangGraph InMemoryStore 62.9%; A‑MEM 70.6%; Letta 65.5%; **Graphiti 7.0%**; **HippoRAG 9.5%**; **MemPalace 0/385**; Lethe+mutation-time LLM hook **91.7%**.

**Others worth knowing** [V, abstracts verified]: **MemBench** ([arXiv:2506.21605](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21605)) — factual vs reflective memory, participation vs observation, scored on effectiveness/**efficiency**/**capacity** (degradation as the store grows). **EvoMemBench** ([arXiv:2605.18421](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18421)) — 15 memory approaches, organized by scope (in-episode vs cross-episode) × content (knowledge vs execution). **StreamMemBench** ([arXiv:2606.14571](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14571)) — streaming/future-oriented assistance over EgoLife streams, four metrics (evidence recall, initial evidence use, feedback incorporation, follow-up reuse). **FiFA / MaRS** ([arXiv:2512.12856](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12856)) — privacy-aware forgetting, six policies, 300 runs, scored on narrative coherence + goal completion + social recall + privacy preservation + cost.

**Long-context benchmarks are a different thing** — don't confuse them: **HELMET** ([site](https://princeton-nlp.github.io/HELMET/), [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/forum?id=293V3bJbmE)) [V], 7 application-centric categories, 8k–128k, 59 models, key finding *"synthetic tasks like NIAH are not good predictors of downstream performance."* **PrefEval** ([site](https://prefeval.github.io/)) [V] — 3,000 curated preference/query pairs, 20 topics, 3 preference forms (explicit, implicit choice-based, implicit persona-driven), gaps to 100k tokens; *"preference following accuracy falls below 10% at merely 10 turns (~3k tokens) across most evaluated models."* Also ∞Bench, RULER, BABILong, LongBench, NIAH — single-pass attention, not cross-session memory.

### A.5 Enterprise / team / multi-user — the benchmarks that actually match your product

**GroupMemBench** — [arXiv:2605.14498](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14498), UCSB + Microsoft, May 2026 [V]. **This is the closest published benchmark to your system.** Multi-party workplace threads with a graph-grounded synthesis pipeline: Projects → Topics → **Phases** (progress category ∈ {RISKS, MILESTONE, WORKITEMS}, status goal, start/target dates, owner) → per-user Personas (role, tone, style, expertise, sampled without replacement so every user has a distinct voice) → Messages (post / reply / cross_project_reply). Four domains: Technology, Healthcare, Manufacturing, Finance. Injected realism: ~25% disagreement turns, ~20% stylistic imperfections, and — critically — ***"decision changes (~5% of eligible phases) in which a previously committed decision is deliberately reversed mid-phase, with the reversal recorded as ground-truth metadata for downstream evaluation."***

Difficulty is *enforced* via a **Solve–Judge–Refine loop**: a baseline agent attempts each query; if it succeeds the query is refined harder; if it fails it's accepted. Synthetic quality validated with **G‑Eval on 6 dimensions** (Naturalness, Coherence, Diversity, Contextual Relevance, Momentum, Engagingness) against a real-group-chat upper bound.

**GateMem** — [arXiv:2606.18829](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18829), Jun 2026 [V]. **Memory governance for multi-principal shared memory** — hospitals, workplaces, campuses, households. **91 long-form multi-party episodes, 2,218 hidden checkpoints** (728 utility / 727 access-control / 763 forgetting), 4 domains, avg 223 turns/episode, **13.4 principals** and **11.6 roles** per episode. Includes indirect inference, delegated requests, and **socially engineered recovery attempts**.

**The metric is directly implementable and exactly what a team knowledge base needs** [V, verbatim]:

- **Utility** `U = (1/N_u) Σ 1[â_n = a*_n ∧ Satisfies(r̂_n, J_n)]` — correct answer AND judge-confirmed factual coverage. Track **over-refusal rate** `OR` separately.
- **Access-Control Violation** `A = (1/N_a) Σ 1[Leaks(r̂_n, Λ_n) ∨ â_n ∉ {refuse, answer_redacted}]`
- **Active Forgetting Failure** `F = (1/N_f) Σ 1[Recovered(r̂_n, Λ_n) ∨ â_n ≠ no_memory]`
- **Memory Governance Score** `MGS = U · (1 − A) · (1 − F)` — *multiplicative on purpose*: *"a system cannot obtain a high overall score merely by being highly useful if it leaks protected information, nor by being perfectly secure if it paralyzes legitimate authorized queries."*

Headline: *"no method simultaneously achieves strong utility, robust access control, and reliable forgetting. Long-context prompting often yields the best governance score at high token cost, while retrieval-based and external-memory methods reduce cost yet still leak unauthorized or deleted information."*

**Adopt MGS as your top-line metric.** It is the only published metric that jointly scores usefulness, tenant isolation, and GDPR erasure — the three things your product is actually judged on.

That survey also proposes a **four-layer metric stack** which is the best available answer to your literal question [V]:
- **L1 Task effectiveness** — success rate, factual correctness, plan completion
- **L2 Memory quality** — retrieved-record precision/recall, **contradiction rate**, **staleness distribution**, coverage of task-relevant facts
- **L3 Efficiency** — latency/op, prompt tokens, retrieval calls/step, storage growth
- **L4 Governance** — privacy leakage rate, deletion compliance, access-scope violations

## B. Memory conflict / contradiction resolution

### B.1 Taxonomy

[V] **Knowledge Conflicts for LLMs: A Survey** — [arXiv:2403.08319](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08319), Xu, Qi, Guo, Wang, Wang, Zhang, Xu (Mar 2024, rev. Jun 2024). Three types:

- **Context‑memory conflict** — context vs parametric knowledge. Causes: *temporal misalignment* and *misinformation pollution*.
- **Inter-context conflict** — retrieved documents contradict **each other**. **This is your case.** Causes: misinformation, outdated information.
- **Intra-memory conflict** — the model answers semantically-equivalent-but-syntactically-distinct prompts differently. Causes: training-corpus bias, decoding strategy, knowledge editing.

**Model behaviors under inter-context conflict (all verbatim, and all bad news)** [V]:
- Chen et al. 2022: *"inconsistencies across knowledge sources exert a **minimal effect on the confidence levels** of models"* — an LLM will not flag that its sources disagree. **You must detect conflict structurally, not by asking the model how confident it is.**
- Xie et al. 2023: LLMs show *"a significant bias to evidence that aligns with the model's parametric memory"* and *"a predisposition towards emphasizing information related to entities of higher popularity and answers that are corroborated by a **larger volume of documents**."* Naive frequency bias, not evidence quality.

**Solutions the survey catalogues for inter-context conflict**, split pre-hoc/post-hoc [V]:
- *Eliminating conflict — specialized models:* **PCNN** (Pairwise Contradiction Neural Network, Hsu et al. 2021) using fine-tuned Sentence-BERT embeddings to compute pairwise contradiction probability; Pielka et al. 2022 (inject linguistic knowledge — XLM‑RoBERTa alone "struggles to effectively grasp the syntactic and semantic features that are vital for accurate contradiction detection"); Wu et al. 2022 (topological text representations, MultiNLI).
- *Eliminating conflict — general models:* Chern et al. 2023 (tool-augmented fact-checking); Leite et al. 2023 (LLM-generated weak labels over predefined **credibility signals**, aggregated by weak supervision).
- *Improving robustness:* Hong et al. 2023 (discriminator + decoder on a shared encoder); **CAR** query augmentation (Weller et al. 2022).

### B.2 NLI-based contradiction detection — the cheap, deployable primitive

[V] [cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base](https://huggingface.co/cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base): 3 labels `[contradiction, entailment, neutral]`, **SNLI 92.38**, **MNLI-mismatched 90.04**.

```python
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
model = CrossEncoder('cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base')
scores = model.predict([(fact_a.text, fact_b.text)])
label = ['contradiction','entailment','neutral'][scores.argmax(axis=1)[0]]
```

**Recommended wiring for your pipeline** (synthesizing PCNN + Graphiti's scoping trick):
1. On new fact `f_new`, retrieve currently-valid facts sharing **the same anchor and category** (your `currentlyValidFilter` + `anchors.*` + `category`) — this is the analogue of Graphiti constraining to the same entity pair, and it's what keeps this tractable.
2. Embedding-filter to top‑k (k≈10, Mem0's default) by cosine.
3. Run NLI both directions on each pair. `contradiction` → conflict; `entailment` → redundancy (route to the merge path); `neutral` → coexist.
4. Only escalate `contradiction` pairs to an LLM adjudicator. This keeps the expensive judge off the hot path for the ~95% of writes that aren't conflicts.

### B.3 Belief revision for agent memory

[V] **Kumiho — Graph-Native Cognitive Memory: Formal Belief Revision Semantics for Versioned Memory Architectures** (Kumiho Inc., 23 Feb 2026, cached PDF). Establishes a correspondence between **AGM belief revision** (Alchourrón–Gärdenfors–Makinson 1985) and property-graph memory operations, framed at the level of **belief bases** (Hansson 1999) rather than belief sets. Proves basic AGM postulates **K\*2–K\*6** plus Hansson's **Relevance** and **Core-Retainment**. Deliberately uses simple propositional logic over ground triples to *"avoid the Flouris et al. impossibility results for description logics."* K\*7/K\*8 left open. Architecture: dual-store (Redis working memory + Neo4j long-term), async consolidation extending "sleep-time compute" with safety guards.

**The load-bearing result for you: a principled *rejection* of the Recovery postulate, grounded in immutable versioning.** Recovery says contracting by φ then expanding by φ restores everything. In a memory where contraction is a pointer flip (`supersededBy`) rather than destruction, Recovery is neither needed nor meaningful. **Your design is formally defensible.**

**Relevance** and **Core-Retainment** are the two postulates that should constrain your consolidation prompt: only remove beliefs that actually contributed to the inconsistency. Your existing instruction *"never merge unrelated facts into a grab-bag sentence"* is an informal Relevance constraint — worth stating formally.

Classical ancestry: **JTMS** (Doyle 1979) with justifications + IN/OUT labels and dependency-directed backtracking; **ATMS** (de Kleer 1986) with labels as minimal environment sets — literally DNF provenance [V, [reason maintenance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_maintenance)]. ### B.4 Temporal invalidation — the Graphiti algorithm, verbatim

[V] **Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory**, [arXiv:2501.13956](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956), Rasmussen et al., 20 Jan 2025. §2.2.3, quoting:

> *"the system tracks four timestamps: t′created and t′expired ∈ T′ monitor when facts are created or invalidated in the system, while tvalid and tinvalid ∈ T track the temporal range during which facts held true."*
>
> *"The system employs an LLM to compare new edges against semantically related existing edges to identify potential contradictions. When the system identifies temporally overlapping contradictions, it invalidates the affected edges by setting their **tinvalid to the tvalid of the invalidating edge**. Following the transactional timeline T′, Graphiti consistently **prioritizes new information**."*

**Two implementation details worth stealing:**
- Edge dedup/contradiction search is *"constrained to edges existing between the same entity pairs as the proposed new edge"* — this both prevents cross-entity false merges and *"significantly reduces the computational complexity."*
- Invalidation **closes the validity window, it does not delete** — history stays auditable.

Benchmarks: DMR 94.8% vs MemGPT 93.4%; LongMemEval +18.5% accuracy, −90% latency.

> **Note for your schema:** you have `validUntil` declared in `schemas/facts.ts` and in `currentlyValidFilter`, but I grepped the whole package — **no code path ever sets it** [V-mine]. You have transaction-time supersession (`supersededBy`) but no valid-time. Adding `validFrom`/`validUntil` writes gives you "what did we believe as of date X" and "what was true as of date X" as separate queries — which is what GroupMemBench's knowledge-update category and Zep's guide both test.

### B.5 Update vs. coexist — the decision, formalized

[V] **TOKI: A Bitemporal Operator Algebra for Contradiction Resolution in LLM-Agent Persistent Memory**, Ziming Wang (HKUST), [arXiv:2606.06240](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06240), 4 Jun 2026. The best framing available. Thesis: ***contradiction resolution is write-time concurrency control.***

**Four production heuristics, typed as bitemporal operators with isolation preconditions:**

| Operator | Semantics | Isolation precondition |
|---|---|---|
| **Last-writer-wins** | newest claim wins | Read Committed |
| **Evidence-weighted merge** | combine by confidence/source weight | Snapshot Isolation |
| **Await-confirmation** | defer to a human/callback | RC + callback |
| **Per-rule policy** | domain rules decide | Serializable |

**Your review queue is the Await-confirmation operator.** That is the strongest of the four for correctness and the weakest for latency — the right trade for a knowledge base of record.

**Three write-time anomalies** [V, verbatim]: *"replay inconsistency, when re-adjudicating the same contradiction returns a different winner; belief-drift skew, when concurrent confidence revisions corrupt a subject-predicate partition; and audit erasure, when the overwritten fact becomes unrecoverable."*

**The sharp result:** *"within the relational schedule model, **keyed logging of the adjudicating judge is necessary for replay consistency**, a discipline every deployed baseline we audit omits"* — and *"every baseline that keeps a language-model judge on the write path admits at least one of three write-time anomalies."* Schema: **dual-row** — one physical schema with a hidden audit-row discriminator; the losing fact is preserved in the audit row.

**Scorecard against your system:**
- ✅ *Audit erasure* — avoided; `supersededBy` preserves losers.
- ✅ *Belief-drift skew* — you already guard it: the `openForAnchor` check in `consolidation.ts` plus the `supersededBy: null` guard in `review.ts` is exactly TOKI's "partition pin."
- ❌ *Replay inconsistency* — **open gap.** Your proposals record `resolvedBy`/`resolvedAt` but not the model, prompt, or verdict that produced the merge. Add a keyed judge log committed before the operator commits.

**Mem0's four operations** [V, [arXiv:2504.19413](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.19413v1)], for comparison: `ADD` (no semantically equivalent memory exists), `UPDATE` (augment with complementary info), `DELETE` (*"removal of memories contradicted by new information"*), `NOOP`. Config: `s = 10` similar memories retrieved, `m = 10` previous messages. The graph variant *"determines if certain relationships should be obsolete, **marking them as invalid rather than physically removing them** to enable temporal reasoning."* LoCoMo: 66.88% (Mem0) / 68.44% (Mem0^g). Latency p50/p95: search 0.148/0.200s; total 0.708/1.440s vs full-context 9.870/17.117s. Tokens/conversation: Mem0 ~7k, Mem0^g ~14k, full-context ~26k, Zep >600k.

**Decision table I'd implement:**

| NLI verdict | Temporal relation | Action |
|---|---|---|
| entailment (either direction) | any | **merge** (your dream cycle) — supersede both, `derivedFrom` = both |
| contradiction | new fact has later `validFrom` | **supersede**: set old `validUntil = new.validFrom`, `supersededBy = new._id` |
| contradiction | overlapping/unknown validity | **await-confirmation** → review queue, both stay valid, flagged `conflictsWith` |
| contradiction | different anchors/scopes | **coexist** — not a conflict; it's two people's differing views |
| neutral | any | **coexist** |

That last row matters for a *team* brain: "Anna says the deadline is tight" and "Petra says the deadline is comfortable" are **not** a contradiction to resolve — they're two attributed beliefs. GroupMemBench calls this speaker-grounded belief tracking, and it's where systems collapse to 27%.

### B.6 Truth discovery / source reliability — and why you probably shouldn't use it

**TruthFinder** (Yin, Han, Yu, KDD 2007) — full algorithm, extracted verbatim from the paper [V]:

1. `t(w) = Σ_{f∈F(w)} s(f) / |F(w)|` — source trustworthiness = mean confidence of its facts
2. `s(f) = 1 − Π_{w∈W(f)} (1 − t(w))` — fact confidence, noisy-OR over its sources
3. `τ(w) = −ln(1 − t(w))` — trustworthiness **score** (log space; avoids underflow and discriminates better: τ(0.99) = 2·τ(0.9))
4. `σ(f) = −ln(1 − s(f))` — confidence score; conveniently **= the sum of the trustworthiness scores of its sources**
5. `σ*(f) = σ(f) + ρ · Σ_{f'≠f, o(f')=o(f)} σ(f') · imp(f' → f)` — adjust by related facts about the same object; `imp ∈ [−1,1]`, positive = mutually supporting, negative = mutually exclusive. If you have a similarity function: `imp(f1→f2) = sim(f1,f2) − base_sim`
6. `s(f) = 1 / (1 + e^{−γ·σ*(f)})` — logistic squashing; γ = damping factor
7. Iterate: init all `t(w) = t₀ ≈ 0.9`; alternate (1) ↔ (2–6); stop when change < δ

**But — the experimental evidence says don't bother.** [V] *Truth Discovery Algorithms: An Experimental Evaluation* (Waguih & Berti-Équille, QCRI TR, 2014). On the Book dataset (877 sources, 33,235 claims, 1,263 objects):

| Method | Precision | Accuracy | Recall | Iter | Time (s) | Mem (MB) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **MajorityVoting** | **0.9804** | 0.8664 | 0.7979 | 1 | **0.009** | **41** |
| TruthFinder | 0.9777 | 0.9387 | 0.9211 | 5 | 0.359 | 618 |
| Cosine | 0.9769 | 0.9279 | 0.9037 | 8 | 0.312 | 165 |
| 3‑Estimates | **0.9935** | 0.8849 | 0.8172 | 42 | 1.474 | 1,117 |
| AccuSim | 0.9730 | **0.9516** | **0.9474** | 3 | 10.092 | 2,072 |
| Depen | 0.9814 | 0.8889 | 0.8360 | 5 | 9.650 | 1,879 |

Verbatim conclusions: ***"none of the methods constantly outperforms the others in terms of precision and a 'one-fits-all' approach does not seem to be achievable"*** and — decisively for you — ***"for few conflicts — i.e., less than 8 distinct values per data item … most of the methods perform worse than random guessing with precision from .1 to .4."***

**A team knowledge base is exactly the low-conflict regime.** Most facts have one source; contested facts have 2–3 variants. Truth discovery is designed for the web, where 50 sites claim a book's author. **Recommendation: do not implement TruthFinder.** Majority voting gets 98% precision at 0.009s; everything fancier buys recall you don't need and fails in your regime.

**What *is* worth taking — CATD's shrinkage idea.** [V] *A Confidence-Aware Approach for Truth Discovery on Long-Tail Data* (Li et al., SUNY Buffalo/MSR/Huawei/UIUC). The long-tail phenomenon — *"most of the sources only provide information about one or two items"* — is your exact situation. Their fix: weight sources by the **confidence interval of the variance estimate**, using the **chi-squared distribution** so sample size enters directly. *"When a source only provides very few claims, the weight is mostly dominated by the chi-squared probability value so that the source reliability degree is automatically smoothed and small sources will not affect the trustworthiness estimation heavily."*

**Practical version:** shrink source reliability toward a global prior with a pseudo-count, e.g. `reliability(s) = (accepted(s) + α·μ) / (total(s) + α)` with α ≈ 10–20. A source with 2 accepted facts must not get reliability 1.0. Your review queue gives you `accepted`/`total` for free from `resolution.status ∈ {confirmed, edited, discarded}`.

**Dawid–Skene** (1979) [R, unverified this session] — EM over per-annotator confusion matrices; the right model if you want to estimate *reviewer* reliability rather than *source* reliability. Given your review queue, that is the more valuable application.

## C. Machine unlearning / selective forgetting

*(This section is the work of a dedicated research pass; I have spot-verified several of its claims independently, noted inline.)*

### C.1 Provenance semirings — the correct cascade semantics

[V] Green, Karvounarakis, Tannen, *Provenance Semirings*, PODS 2007 — [PDF](https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf) · [ACM](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1265530.1265535). Annotate base tuples with semiring elements; `×` = joint use (join/AND), `+` = alternative use (union/OR).

The hierarchy, coarsest → finest: `B` → `N` → **`Lineage(X)`** (flat set — *cannot distinguish AND from OR*) → `Why(X)` → **`PosBool(X)`** → `Trio(X)` → `N[X]` (how-provenance polynomials).

**The operational result:** to answer *"does derived tuple t survive if I delete source s?"* — set s's variable to 0 in t's provenance polynomial and evaluate. `t` survives iff some monomial has no deleted variable. **`PosBool(X)` is the coarsest semiring that answers this correctly; `Lineage(X)` is not.**

> **Your `facts.derivedFrom: ObjectId[]` is `Lineage(X)`.** A merge of two *corroborating* facts (disjunctive — survives if one parent survives) is indistinguishable from a merge of two *complementary* facts (conjunctive — must die if either dies). Fix cheaply with a discriminator field `derivation: "merge" | "corroboration" | "inference" | "summary"`, or properly with DNF nesting: `derivedFrom: z.array(z.array(zodObjectId).min(1)).min(1)`.

Deletion propagation optimization is NP-hard in general (Buneman/Khanna/Tan, PODS 2002 — [link](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/on-the-propagation-of-deletions-and-annotations-through-views/); 2025 unified treatment: [Gatterbauer & Simons](https://gatterbauer.name/download/Gatterbauer-Simons2025-Generalized-Deletion-Propagation.pdf)) — but for GDPR you don't solve the optimization, you take the forced transitive closure.

### C.2 GDPR — what actually binds

[V] [Art. 17](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/), [Art. 19](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-19-gdpr/), [Recital 66](https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-66/). Recital 66's *"any links to, or copies or replications of those personal data"* is the textual hook. **There is no derived-data exemption internally** — embeddings, summaries, consolidated facts, dossiers and search indexes are all your processing of the same personal data. Art. 17(3)(e) (legal claims) is the usual basis for retaining a *redacted* audit trail.

[V] **EDPB Opinion 28/2024** (17 Dec 2024) — [official PDF](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2024-12/edpb_opinion_202428_ai-models_en.pdf). Two-pronged anonymity test: must be *very unlikely* to (1) extract training personal data from the model, **and** (2) extract it via queries — assessed against *"all means reasonably likely to be used."* The EDPB explicitly acknowledges personal data can be embedded in parameters as **mathematical objects**: **being a vector does not launder personal data.** Notably, facilitating erasure is listed as a *mitigating measure* in the legitimate-interest balance — your erasure work is legally load-bearing.

[V-2nd] **CJEU, *EDPS v SRB*, C‑413/23 P (4 Sep 2025)** — [press release](https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2025-09/cp250107en.pdf) · [FPF analysis](https://fpf.org/blog/rethinking-personal-data-the-cjeus-contextual-turn-in-edps-vs-srb/). "Personal" is **relative to the recipient**. Critically: **personal opinions/views are personal data** because they're "necessarily closely linked" to the person. Your facts are opinion-bearing statements about identified people ("Petra objects to the Q3 timeline") — unambiguously personal data. The relative approach only helps when shipping vectors to a third party without the key; it does not help you internally.

⚠️ EDPB anonymisation guidance is still in flight — a [stakeholder-event report](https://www.insideprivacy.com/gdpr/edpb-publishes-report-on-stakeholder-event-on-anonymisation-and-pseudonymisation/) landed 18 Feb 2026. Re-check before relying.

### C.3 Soft-delete is not erasure — the empirical proof

[V] **Ghost Vectors: Soft-Deleted Embeddings Remain Reconstructible in HNSW Vector Databases** — [arXiv:2606.18497](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.18497v1).

Threat model: read access to raw storage (insider, cloud misconfig, **backup exposure**). Pull vectors off disk (`hnswlib.get_items()`, `index.reconstruct_n()`), run **off-the-shelf Vec2Text with no fine-tuning**, then NER. 98.4% of plateau quality in one inference step at **30.7 ms/record**.

| Corpus | Metric | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Wikipedia biographies (n=98) | person names | **25.5%** |
| Wikipedia biographies | locations | 46.4% |
| Synthetic clinical (n=1000) | patient surname | **49.9%** |
| LFW faces (n=4324) | top‑1 identity | **99.17%** |

Per-store: **ChromaDB** marks deletion in SQLite while `index.bin` is physically unchanged; **FAISS** `IndexHNSWFlat` has no `delete()` at all; **Weaviate 1.26.6** *grew* on disk after deletion (52.5 → 55.4 MB).

**What worked:** epoch key rotation (AES‑256‑CTR per epoch, key discarded on deletion) → **0% PII recovery**, ~0.005 ms/record, plus an **ECDSA-signed deletion proof**. **What failed:** orthogonal transforms (attacker applies Tᵀ), differential privacy, query-side transforms. Full index rebuild works (2,250 ms) but isn't retroactive to backups.

> **Your `facts.embedding` is an inline array on the fact document** — `deleteOne` removes it atomically. That is the right design and you should keep it. If you move to Atlas Vector Search, add a **post-erasure verification query** (name search + embedding kNN, assert zero hits) rather than trusting the delete ack.

### C.4 Crypto-shredding in MongoDB

[V] [MongoDB: Implementing Right to Erasure with CSFLE](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/csfle/tutorials/right-to-erasure/). One **DEK per data subject** with `key_alt_names=[userId]`; erasure = delete the DEK; ciphertext remains but fails to decrypt. Caveats stated by MongoDB: **client DEK cache TTL is 60 seconds**; **key vault must be on a separate cluster** so restoring a data backup doesn't resurrect DEKs; oplog/transaction logs are not addressed; they recommend deleting the encrypted data too; and they explicitly disclaim regulatory sufficiency.

MongoDB-specific residue to document [R, unverified]: `deleteOne` doesn't zero WiredTiger pages; the **oplog** retains the delete and, if `changeStreamPreAndPostImages` is on, retains **full pre-images**; Atlas backups retain erased docs for the retention window. → Confirm pre/post-images are **off** for `facts`/`sources`, set backup retention shorter than your erasure SLA, and record the oplog window in your Art. 30 register.

### C.5 Weight-level unlearning: don't rely on it

[V-snippet] **MUSE** ([arXiv:2407.06460](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06460)) — six desiderata including **(5) scalability w.r.t. removal-request size** and **(6) sustainability over sequential requests**. Finding: most algorithms suppress memorization to a degree, but **only one avoids severe privacy leakage**, and existing algorithms **degrade utility and cannot sustain successive requests** — which is precisely what an ongoing GDPR stream demands.

[V] **When Machine Unlearning Meets RAG** ([arXiv:2410.15267](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15267), IEEE TDSC 2026) modifies the external knowledge base to simulate forgetting. Note the nuance: their approach injects **retrieval-time suppression instructions**. That's fine for behavior, **wrong for Art. 17** — suppression ≠ erasure.

> **Strategic conclusion: never put personal facts into weights.** Keep all subject-linked knowledge in MongoDB where erasure is a `deleteOne`, and treat the LLM as a stateless renderer. Your architecture already does this — it is your biggest compliance asset and belongs in the DPIA explicitly.

### C.6 Intentional forgetting for quality — the formulas

**Generative Agents** (Park et al., UIST 2023) — [ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2304.03442), all verbatim [V]:
- `score = α_recency·recency + α_importance·importance + α_relevance·relevance`; *"all αs are set to 1"*; each component min-max normalized to [0,1]
- *"Our decay factor is 0.995"*, exponential over hours **since the memory was last retrieved** (retrieval refreshes recency — the spacing effect)
- Importance prompt: *"On the scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is purely mundane … and 10 is extremely poignant … rate the likely poignancy"*
- **Reflection trigger:** *"we generate reflections when the sum of the importance scores for the latest events perceived by the agents exceeds a threshold (150 in our implementation)"* — roughly 2–3× per day

**MemoryBank** (Zhong et al., AAAI 2024) — [ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.10250) [V]: `R = e^(−t/S)`; init `S=1`; on recall *"we increase S by 1 and reset t to 0."* After n recalls the half-life is ~(1+n)× longer. Two integers (`strength`, `lastRecalledAt`), no ML.

**SirLLM** (ACL 2024) — [arXiv:2405.12528](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.12528) [V-snippet]: pure top-score retention produces **"rigid memory"**; fix is a **decay ratio η<1** applied multiplicatively each round. **Transferable regardless of KV caches: if your consolidation ranks by a static score, multiply by η≈0.9–0.98 per nightly run or month-one facts freeze in place forever.**

**FSFM** ([arXiv:2604.20300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20300), Apr 2026) [V for abstract; ⚠️ body constants LOW-CONFIDENCE]: abstract-verified gains of **+8.49% access efficiency, +29.2% signal-to-noise, 100% elimination of security risks**. Structure worth copying: `I = α·CQA + β·BVE + γ·TRS + δ·SRC` with α=0.4, β=0.3, γ=0.2, δ=0.1 and **negative SRC penalties (−10 dangerous, −2 sensitive)** so sensitive content sorts to the *top* of the eviction queue. Two decay rates: λ=0.05 durable, λ=0.2 transient. Cap at 70% storage, batch-prune lowest 10%.

**OSL‑MR** ([arXiv:2606.10616](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10616)) [V-mine, verified independently]: retention as constrained stochastic optimization with **miss, reacquisition, and stale penalties**; NP-hard, reduces to budgeted maximum coverage; monotone submodular so greedy gives (1−1/e) *when coverage sets are known* — but they're unobservable at deployment, hence a learning-augmented greedy with strict separation between online-observable features and offline supervision. **The three delayed-cost terms are the useful, verified contribution.**

**Auto-Dreamer** ([arXiv:2605.20616](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.20616)) [V-mine, verified — and I corrected a bad extraction]: the "merge at >90% similarity / prune below 25th percentile / 30 days" constants reported by an automated summarizer **are not in the paper**; it's a GRPO-trained learned consolidator with no such thresholds. What the paper *does* say, and it matters for you: entries have `name` (short heading) + `body` + **provenance links to source trajectories**; the consolidator selects a **working region**, treats it as read-only evidence, and **fetches the provenance-linked source trajectories** via a `get_source_trace` tool before synthesizing a replacement set.

> **Concrete improvement to your dream cycle:** `buildConsolidationPrompt` shows the model only `id | category | text`. Auto-Dreamer fetches the **original sources** during consolidation. Give your consolidator a `get_source` tool so it can check the transcript before merging — this directly mitigates the information-loss risk that your "ZERO information loss" instruction can only ask for, not enforce.

**LSCS** ([arXiv:2409.13265](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.13265v2), TMLR) [V-snippet]: the cleanest justification for a lossy dream cycle — unlike continual learning which *fights* catastrophic forgetting, lifespan cognitive systems **intend** some forgetting, aligned with abstraction and experience merging.

### D.1 The two design principles everyone converges on

1. **Separate retrieval quality from generation quality.** Chroma Context‑1 [V]: *"if the downstream model fails to answer correctly, it is ambiguous whether the search agent retrieved insufficient evidence or the reasoning model failed to use what was provided"* — so they verify the answer-bearing document appears in the output set instead of grading end-to-end. Zep makes **Context Completeness** (COMPLETE/PARTIAL/INSUFFICIENT) their *primary* metric precisely because it *"isolates memory system performance from LLM generation quality"* [V].
2. **Always report accuracy, latency and tokens together.** Zep: *"Always report accuracy alongside latency and token consumption together"* [V]. Mem0 docs: *"accuracy without a token budget is a half-finished score"* [V].

### D.3 Context Rot — why "just stuff the facts in" fails

[V] [Context Rot](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot) · [code](https://github.com/chroma-core/context-rot). **18 LLMs**, **194,480 LLM calls** across 8 input lengths × 11 needle positions; GPT‑4.1 judge at **>99% human alignment** [V-2nd].

- *"models do not use their context uniformly; instead, their performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows"* — even for verbatim replication.
- **Needle–question similarity:** performance degrades faster for low-similarity pairs (range 0.445–0.775). → *Your users will ask "what did Sarah say about pricing?" when the fact reads "S. Chen flagged margin concerns on the Q3 renewal." That's the fast-rot regime.*
- **Distractors** compound non-uniformly and worsen with length. **GPT models hallucinate most; Claude models abstain most.**
- **Counterintuitive:** across **all 18 models**, *"Models perform better on shuffled haystacks than on logically structured ones."* → **A/B test a flat list of atomic facts against a narrated memory digest. The flat list may win.**
- **LongMemEval slice:** full prompt ≈**113k tokens** vs focused prompt ≈**300 tokens**; *"significantly higher performance on focused prompts."* Difficulty order: knowledge update > multi-session > temporal reasoning. **This is the strongest quantitative case for your architecture: ~113k → ~300 tokens with accuracy going up.**
- **Refusal rates:** GPT‑3.5 Turbo refused 60.29% of the repeated-word task; Claude Opus 4 refused 2.89%.
- The money quote: *"Whether relevant information is present in a model's context is not all that matters; what matters more is **how that information is presented**."*

### D.4 Chunking metrics you're probably missing

[V] [Evaluating Chunking Strategies](https://www.trychroma.com/research/evaluating-chunking). Document-level IR metrics miss that retrieved chunks carry *"superfluous tokens … which may contain irrelevant distractors."* Token-level formulas (t_e = relevant excerpt tokens, t_r = retrieved tokens):
- `IoU = |t_e ∩ t_r| / |t_e ∪ t_r|` · `recall = |t_e ∩ t_r| / |t_e|` · `precision = |t_e ∩ t_r| / |t_r|` · `Precision_Ω` = precision at perfect recall

Results (n=5, text-embedding-3-large): ClusterSemanticChunker 200-token — recall 87.3%, **precision 8.0%, IoU 8.0%** (best); LLMSemanticChunker — **recall 91.9%** but precision 3.9%; the **OpenAI default (800/400 overlap)** had *"the lowest scores across all other metrics."* Smaller chunks improve precision 5× (7–8% vs 1.4–1.5%); removing overlap gains 2–3 IoU points.

Trick worth stealing: don't ask an LLM to emit modified text (hallucination). Split into 50-token pieces wrapped as `<start_chunk_0>…<end_chunk_0>` and ask for **split indices**.

### D.5 Context‑1 — the best eval taxonomy

[V] [Context-1](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-1) (Mar 2026). A 20B self-editing retrieval subagent returning **ranked documents, not answers**.

- **Output-level:** final answer found (binary), recall, precision, F1
- **Trajectory-level: trajectory recall** — fraction of targets *encountered during search* regardless of final inclusion. **The gap between trajectory recall and output recall separates exploration failure from selection failure.**
- **Edit quality: prune accuracy** (0.824 → 0.941 through training)
- **Reward design:** F1 with **16:1 recall:precision weighting**, annealed to 4:1. → **For memory retrieval, recall dominates precision by roughly an order of magnitude.**
- **Synthetic task verification:** the verifier extracts **document quotes** (verbatim source spans) and **clue quotes** and checks alignment — **>80% agreement with human judgments** across four domains.

### D.6 MemTrace — error attribution across the memory pipeline

[V] [arXiv:2605.28732](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.28732) (Zhejiang University + Alibaba). Transforms memory pipelines into **executable memory evolution graphs**; **MemTraceBench** has **160 human-annotated real failure cases** from Long-Context, RAG, Mem0 and EverMemOS across three datasets, each with QA pairs, execution logs, ground-truth error labels, faulty operations and human explanations.

Error classes: **extraction, retrieval, update, deletion, response**. Findings:
- RAG has no extraction errors (no extraction module); EverMemOS's extractor is notably robust across human-assistant *and* multi-party dialogues.
- *"For retrieval errors, Mem0, EverMemOS, and RAG all fail frequently"* under a top‑10 budget.
- *"we observe **no deletion errors**, likely because deletion is only supported by Mem0 and is **rarely tested in current benchmarks**"* — and **delete operations are only 1.02% of all add/update/delete operations in Mem0.**
- *"all systems exhibit **response errors**, showing even when related memories are retrieved successfully, effectively using them to give the final answer remains an open challenge."*

Attribution signals fed back into prompt optimization improved end-task performance **by up to 7.62%**.
