---
title: "Overview"
description: "Define repeatable scored checks for an eve agent with defineEval and run them with eve eval."
---

An eval is a scored check that runs your agent against real sessions and grades the result, catching regressions when you change a prompt or a tool. Drive the agent through one or more turns, assert on what it did (the run completed, the right tool ran, the reply contains the right text), and optionally ship the results to Braintrust.

Evals exercise the same HTTP surface your users hit. The runner boots (or targets) a real agent server, drives sessions through the [TypeScript client](../guides/client/overview) protocol, and grades what comes back, so a passing eval means the agent booted, accepted a request, and produced the result you asserted.

## `defineEval`

eve discovers evals under the app-root `evals/` directory, in `.eval.ts` files. Each file is one eval by default. A file can also default-export an array to fan out over a dataset (see [Cases](./cases)). The file path is the eval's identity, so you don't author an `id` or `name`. Directories group related evals (`evals/weather/brooklyn-forecast.eval.ts` becomes id `weather/brooklyn-forecast`).

```text
my-agent/
├── agent/
├── evals/
│   ├── evals.config.ts
│   ├── smoke.eval.ts
│   └── weather/
│       ├── brooklyn-forecast.eval.ts
│       └── no-tools-for-greetings.eval.ts
└── package.json
```

An eval is a single `async test(t)` function. You drive the agent with `t` and assert on the run with the same `t`:

```ts title="evals/weather/brooklyn-forecast.eval.ts"
import { defineEval } from "eve/evals";
import { includes } from "eve/evals/expect";

export default defineEval({
  description: "Basic message and tool-usage coverage for the weather agent.",
  async test(t) {
    await t.send("What is the weather in Brooklyn?");
    t.succeeded();
    t.calledTool("get_weather");
    t.check(t.reply, includes("Sunny"));
  },
});
```

`test` is the only required field. The rest are optional: `description`, `judge`, `tags`, `metadata`, `timeoutMs`, and `reporters`. The init template adds `evals/**/*.ts` to `tsconfig.json`, so your eval code type-checks alongside the app.

## `evals.config.ts`

Every `evals/` directory needs exactly one `evals.config.ts` at its root. It declares the defaults every eval shares:

```ts title="evals/evals.config.ts"
import { defineEvalConfig } from "eve/evals";
import { Braintrust } from "eve/evals/reporters";

export default defineEvalConfig({
  judge: { model: "openai/gpt-5.4-mini" },
  reporters: [Braintrust({ projectName: "my-agent" })],
});
```

Everything is optional. `judge` sets the default model for [LLM-as-judge](./judge) assertions (`t.judge.*`); a tree of fully deterministic evals can omit it. `reporters`, `maxConcurrency`, and `timeoutMs` round out the defaults. Config `reporters` observe every eval in the run, so set one `Braintrust()` here instead of adding it to each eval. CLI flags (`--max-concurrency`, `--timeout`) and per-eval values take precedence over the config defaults.

## Deterministic fixture models

Use `mockModel` when an eval fixture needs to exercise eve's runtime without calling a model provider. A static fixture can be one line:

```ts title="agent/agent.ts"
import { defineAgent } from "eve";
import { mockModel } from "eve/evals";

export default defineAgent({
  model: mockModel("A deterministic reply"),
});
```

Pass a callback when the reply depends on the conversation. The callback receives an eve-owned view of the prompt, including `lastUserMessage`, `userMessages`, `userMessageCount`, available `tools`, and prior `toolResults`:

```ts title="agent/agent.ts"
export default defineAgent({
  model: mockModel(
    ({ lastUserMessage, userMessageCount }) => `Turn ${userMessageCount}: ${lastUserMessage}`,
  ),
});
```

The callback may return `{ text, toolCalls, usage }` for deterministic tool loops or explicit token counts. Use the options form only when a fixture also needs a custom model identity:

```ts title="agent/agent.ts"
model: mockModel({
  modelId: "weather-script",
  provider: "my-fixtures",
  respond: ({ toolResults }) =>
    toolResults.length === 0
      ? { toolCalls: [{ name: "get_weather", input: { city: "Brooklyn" } }] }
      : `Weather: ${JSON.stringify(toolResults[0]?.output)}`,
});
```

`mockModel()` uses `"Mock response"` when no response is supplied. It handles both generated and streamed responses, derives deterministic response metadata, and estimates token usage. Because the model is part of the agent definition, use it for a dedicated fixture agent; it remains mocked whether that fixture runs locally or as a deployed eval target.

## The `t` context

`t` is both the driver and the assertion surface. There are no separate `input`, `run`, `checks`, or `scores` fields. You write ordinary control flow, sending turns and asserting inline.

- **Drive** the agent: `t.send(...)`, `t.start(...)`, `t.cancel()`, `t.respond(...)`, `t.respondAll(...)`, `t.sendFile(...)`, `t.requireInputRequest(...)`, `t.newSession()`. Live turns returned by `start()` can wait for typed mid-turn events before cancellation or settlement. Read what came back with `t.reply` (the last assistant message), `t.sessionId`, and `t.events`. See [Cases](./cases).
- **Assert** with three surfaces, covered next.

## Three assertion surfaces

Each surface matches a genuinely different kind of judgment:

- **Scoped methods** read the final whole run on `t`, snapshot one independent session when invoked there, or inspect one immutable `EveEvalTurn`. See [Assertions](./assertions).
- **`t.check(value, assertion)`** grades an explicit value with a deterministic builder from `eve/evals/expect`, such as `t.check(t.reply, includes("sunny"))`. Grade `t.reply`, an intermediate draft, parsed JSON, or anything else. See [Assertions](./assertions).
- **`t.judge.autoevals.*`** is the LLM-as-judge surface, like `t.judge.autoevals.closedQA("cites a source")`. It grades `t.reply` by default and uses the configured judge model, never the agent under test. See [Judge](./judge).

## Gate vs soft

Every assertion returns a chainable handle, so severity rides on the assertion itself. There is no separate thresholds map.

- **Gates** are hard. A failed gate marks the eval `failed` and `eve eval` exits non-zero. Run-level methods, `includes`, `equals`, and `matches` are gates by default.
- **Soft** assertions are tracked data. They land in reports and artifacts, and a below-threshold soft assertion marks the eval `scored` (visible but not fatal, unless you pass `--strict`). `similarity` and every `t.judge.*` assertion are soft by default. A soft assertion with no threshold is tracked-only and never fails.

Override per assertion: `.gate(threshold?)` promotes to a hard gate, `.soft(threshold?)` demotes to tracked, and `.atLeast(threshold)` is a soft assertion with a bar.

```ts
t.succeeded(); // gate
t.calledTool("get_weather").soft(); // record as a metric, don't gate
t.judge.autoevals.closedQA("cites a source"); // soft, tracked (no threshold)
t.judge.autoevals.factuality(reference).atLeast(0.7); // soft, gated under --strict at 0.7
```

Use `await t.require(value, assertion)` for a gate that must pass before the script can safely continue. Use `t.skip(reason)` as the first operation for an intentionally unsupported target capability.

## Run evals with eve eval

```bash
eve eval                       # run all discovered evals against a local dev server
eve eval weather               # run one eval, or every eval under evals/weather/
eve eval --url https://<app>   # target an existing server or deployment
```

Exit code `0` means every eval passed its gates. See [Running evals](./running) for the full flag list, exit codes, and CI guidance.

## A good baseline

Most apps do fine with a few small smoke evals. Assert behavior with `t.succeeded()` plus one or two content checks, keep dataset fixtures in `evals/data/`, and reach for a judge or Braintrust only when you need fuzzy grading or shared result review. In CI, run `eve eval --strict` so soft threshold misses fail the build too.

## What to read next

The rest of this section covers each piece:

- [Cases](./cases): single-turn evals, scripted multi-turn evals, and dataset fan-out
- [Assertions](./assertions): run-level methods and `t.check` value assertions, with matchers and severity
- [Judge](./judge): LLM-as-judge grading and the judge model
- [Targets](./targets): local vs remote targets for the same eval files
- [Reporters](./reporters): Braintrust experiments and JUnit XML
- [Running evals](./running): the `eve eval` CLI, exit codes, and artifacts
- [Tools](../tools): the surface most evals assert on

Eve has a dedicated chat SDK channel that connects to Vercel Chat SDK adapters for platforms like Slack, Discord, Telegram, and Resend email. The key advantage is being able to configure the exact webhook path for Resend inbound emails—like `/webhooks/inbound-email`—which integrates seamlessly with their existing API infrastructure.

For HITL workflows, Chat SDK Cards with buttons handle the review queue, letting button clicks resume parked sessions. The multi-tenant memory pattern mirrors their architecture exactly: tenant and user context lives on `ctx.session.auth`, a `requireTenantCaller` guard prevents accepting IDs from the model, dynamic instructions load memories on turn start, and tools handle writes and deletes. There's a critical trust boundary—memory values are treated as user-provided facts, never system instructions—and deletion requires HITL approval. For large memory corpora, they recommend semantic retrieval scoped by tenant and user at query time rather than as a post-filter, which aligns with the Google `scope` pattern and their tenantId-leading-index approach. They also note not to use `defineState` for long-term memory.

For evals, they're using `defineEval` with test files, assertion helpers like `t.send`, `t.succeeded`, `t.calledTool`, and `t.check`, plus auto-eval judges and a `mockModel` for deterministic fixtures. The Braintrust reporter and `eve eval --strict` in CI complete the setup. One particularly relevant assertion is `t.judge.autoevals.closedQA("cites a source")` — exactly what they need for citation validation.

2	title: "Schedules"
3	description: "Run an agent on a cron cadence, either a fire-and-forget prompt or a handler that hands work off to a channel."
4	---
5	
6	A schedule starts the agent on its own clock instead of waiting for an inbound message. Use one for daily digests, data syncs, cleanup sweeps, heartbeats, or anything that should fire on a cadence. 7	
8	The name comes from the path under `schedules/` (`agent/schedules/billing/sweep.ts` → `"billing/sweep"`), and nested directories are fine.
9	
10	## `defineSchedule`
11	
12	Every schedule provides a `cron` and exactly one of `markdown` or `run`:
13	
14	```ts
15	interface ScheduleDefinition {
16	  cron: string;
17	  markdown?: string; // fire-and-forget prompt (task mode)
18	  run?: (args: ScheduleHandlerArgs) => Promise<void> | void; // handler
19	}
20	
21	interface ScheduleHandlerArgs {
22	  receive: CrossChannelReceiveFn; // hand the work off to a channel
23	  waitUntil: (task: Promise<unknown>) => void; // keep the cron task alive past return
24	  appAuth: SessionAuthContext; // pre-built app principal
25	}
26	```
27	
28	`defineSchedule` is a type-level pass-through. The compiler is what enforces the one-of rule.
29	
30	`cron` is a standard 5-field string (`minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`) with minute granularity. On Vercel, each schedule becomes a Vercel Cron Job, and Vercel evaluates the expression in UTC, so `"0 9 * * 1-5"` fires at 09:00 UTC on weekdays. `eve dev` never fires schedules on their cron cadence. A built app served with `eve start` does run production scheduled tasks. To trigger one while iterating in dev, use the dispatch route below.
31	
32	## Markdown form (fire-and-forget)
33	
34	This is the minimal schedule. eve runs the agent on the prompt and throws away the output, though the agent can still call tools, write to backends, and log along the way. We call this task mode. A task-mode session runs to completion or fails, and cannot park to wait for a person or an OAuth sign-in.
35	
36	```ts title="agent/schedules/heartbeat.ts"
37	import { defineSchedule } from "eve/schedules";
38	
39	export default defineSchedule({
40	  cron: "*/5 * * * *",
41	  markdown: "Pull open Linear issues and POST a summary to the metrics endpoint.",
42	});
43	```
44	
45	You can write the same thing as a plain `.md` file: its frontmatter takes `cron` and nothing else, and the body is the prompt.
46	
47	`agent/schedules/cleanup.md`:
48	
49	```md
50	---
51	cron: "0 0 * * 0"
52	---
53	
54	Sweep stale workflow state.
55	```
56	
57	## Handler form (`run`)
58	
59	Use a handler when the schedule needs to deliver to a channel, branch on conditions, or compute its arguments at fire time. The handler is in full control. It has no channel of its own, so it passes the work to one with `receive`.
60	
61	```ts title="agent/schedules/critical-alerts.ts"
62	import { defineSchedule } from "eve/schedules";
63	
64	import slack from "../channels/slack";
65	
66	export default defineSchedule({
67	  cron: "* * * * *",
68	  async run({ receive, waitUntil, appAuth }) {
69	    waitUntil(
70	      receive(slack, {
71	        message: "Check for new critical alerts. Report only when there are any.",
72	        target: { channelId: "C0123ABC" },
73	        auth: appAuth,
74	      }),
75	    );
76	  },
77	});
78	```
79	
80	The agent does not have to deliver a message on every run. When a prompt makes delivery conditional, as in the alert check above, eve tells the agent how to finish successfully without sending anything to the channel. Frequent polling schedules do not need a separate filter or delivery setting.
81	
82	- `receive(channel, { message, target, auth })`: starts a session on another channel. Same contract as a route handler's `args.receive`.
83	- `waitUntil(promise)`: extends the cron task's lifetime so the parked session and any in-flight fetches settle before the task ends. Wrap the `receive` call in it.
84	- `appAuth`: the app principal (`{ authenticator: "app", principalId: "eve:app", principalType: "runtime" }`). Pass it as `receive(..., { auth: appAuth })` for work the agent does on its own behalf.
85	
86	A handler-form session runs on the same durable runtime engine as any other session, so it can park (durably suspend), for instance when the channel handoff is waiting for a Slack reply. Only markdown task mode is barred from waiting.
87	
88	## Trigger a schedule while iterating
89	
90	The dev server mounts a one-shot dispatch route that fires a schedule by name, out of band, exactly once. Since `eve dev` never runs schedules on their cron cadence, this is how you trigger one without waiting for the next production tick.
91	
92	```sh
93	curl -X POST http://localhost:2000/eve/v1/dev/schedules/heartbeat
94	# -> { "scheduleId": "heartbeat", "sessionIds": ["..."] }
95	```
96	
97	`:scheduleId` is the path-derived schedule name (`agent/schedules/heartbeat.ts` → `heartbeat`; URL-encode the `/` in nested names). It runs the exact dispatch path the production cron handler uses and returns the started session ids as JSON, so you can subscribe to each one's [stream](./concepts/sessions-runs-and-streaming) at `GET /eve/v1/session/:sessionId/stream`. An unknown id comes back `404` with `availableScheduleIds`, listing the schedules the app actually defines.
98	
99	The route is dev-only. Production builds never mount it, and it needs no auth since the dev server is local-only.
100	
101	## On Vercel
102	
103	Hosted Vercel builds turn every `defineSchedule(...)` into a Vercel Cron Job, with each `cron` written as an entry in `.vercel/output/config.json`. This also applies when [`withEve`](./guides/frontend/nextjs) embeds one or more agents in a Next.js deployment: Vercel assembles each generated eve service's schedules into the project Build Output config while preserving existing project cron entries. Named agents use their public `/eve/agents/<name>` route prefix automatically.
104	
105	When running `vercel build` locally, use Vercel CLI 56.4.0 or later so generated-service cron entries are included in the project output.
106	
107	Vercel evaluates cron expressions in UTC. Confirm discovery under **Settings → Cron Jobs** and watch execution history under **Observability → Cron Jobs**. Per-run logs land under **Observability → Logs**.
108	
109	## Self-deployed hosts
110	
111	Production builds register schedules as Nitro scheduled tasks. On Vercel, Nitro's Vercel preset wires those task registrations into Vercel Cron for you. Outside Vercel, the standard `eve build && eve start` path serves Nitro's Node output and starts Nitro's schedule runner, so the tasks fire on their cron cadence while that process is running.
112	
113	The gotcha is custom hosting. If you adapt the generated output to a process manager, container platform, or Nitro preset that only serves HTTP and does not start Nitro's scheduled task runner, the schedule definitions still compile, but they will not fire automatically. In that case, run eve through `eve start`, use a host that supports Nitro scheduled tasks, or trigger the same work from your own scheduler through an authenticated route, channel handoff, or application-specific job runner. The dev dispatch route above is only for `eve dev`; production builds do not mount it.
114

116	
117	- [Channels](./channels/overview): deliver schedule output to users.
118	- [Sessions, runs & streaming](./concepts/sessions-runs-and-streaming): inspect a schedule run.

Vercel evaluates cron expressions in UTC. Confirm discovery under **Settings → Cron Jobs** and watch execution history under **Observability → Cron Jobs**. Per-run logs land under **Observability → Logs**.

## Self-deployed hosts

Production builds register schedules as Nitro scheduled tasks. On Vercel, Nitro's Vercel preset wires those task registrations into Vercel Cron for you. Outside Vercel, the standard `eve build && eve start` path serves Nitro's Node output and starts Nitro's schedule runner, so the tasks fire on their cron cadence while that process is running.

The gotcha is custom hosting. If you adapt the generated output to a process manager, container platform, or Nitro preset that only serves HTTP and does not start Nitro's scheduled task runner, the schedule definitions still compile, but they will not fire automatically. In that case, run eve through `eve start`, use a host that supports Nitro scheduled tasks, or trigger the same work from your own scheduler through an authenticated route, channel handoff, or application-specific job runner. The dev dispatch route above is only for `eve dev`; production builds do not mount it.

## What to read next

- [Channels](./channels/overview): deliver schedule output to users.
- [Sessions, runs & streaming](./concepts/sessions-runs-and-streaming): inspect a schedule run.

1	---
2	title: "Human-in-the-loop"
3	description: "Pause a run for a person — gate a tool on approval or have the agent ask a question — and resume durably when they answer."
4	url: /human-in-the-loop
5	---
6	
7	Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is any point where the agent durably pauses and waits for a person. Two things trigger it, and both ride the same pause-and-resume protocol:
8	
9	- **Approvals** — a tool requires a person to sign off before (or instead of) running. The agent decides to call the tool; a human decides whether it does.
10	- **Questions** — the agent itself asks the user a clarifying question or a choice mid-turn, and parks until they answer.
11	
12	Either way the run parks at `session.waiting`, durably, for as long as it takes — seconds or days — and picks back up exactly where it left off once the answer arrives. Channels render the request for you.
13	
14	## Approvals
15	
16	Approval is a property of a [tool](/docs/tools) that pauses for a person before it runs. Gate a tool with `approval` and the helpers from `eve/tools/approval`:
17	
18	```ts title="agent/tools/refund_charge.ts"
19	import { defineTool } from "eve/tools";
20	import { always } from "eve/tools/approval";
21	import { z } from "zod";
22	
23	export default defineTool({
24	  description: "Refund a charge.",
25	  inputSchema: z.object({ tenantId: z.string(), chargeId: z.string(), amount: z.number() }),
26	  approval: always(), // or once() / never() / a policy
27	  async execute(input) {
28	    return refund(input);
29	  },
30	});
31	```
32	
33	| Helper     | Behavior                                                                           |
34	| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
35	| `never()`  | Never require approval (the default when omitted).                                 |
36	| `once()`   | Require approval only the first time the tool runs in a session; auto-allow after. |
37	| `always()` | Require approval before every call.                                                |
38	
39	By default, omitted `approval` behaves like `never()`, so tool calls may execute without human approval. Require human approval or other safeguards for sensitive, irreversible, regulated, financial, healthcare, employment, housing, legal, safety-impacting, user-impacting, or external side-effecting actions.
40	
41	When the decision depends on the input, pass your own policy instead of a helper. It receives the same session context as tool execution, plus `{ toolName, toolInput, approvedTools, callId }`, and returns an AI SDK 7 approval status synchronously or as a promise. Use `ctx.session.auth.current` to guard by the caller of the current turn and `ctx.session.auth.initiator` to guard by the caller that created the session. Return `"user-approval"` to pause for a person or `"not-applicable"` to continue without a prompt. `toolInput` can be undefined, so guard the access. This policy denies cross-tenant calls, then requires approval only when an amount crosses a threshold:
42	
43	```ts
44	approval: ({ session, toolInput }) => {
45	  const callerTenant = session.auth.current?.attributes.tenantId;
46	  if (callerTenant === undefined || callerTenant !== toolInput?.tenantId) {
47	    return { type: "denied", reason: "Caller cannot access this tenant." };
48	  }
49	  return (toolInput?.amount ?? 0) > 1000 ? "user-approval" : "not-applicable";
50	},
51	```
52	
53	For compatibility with the previous predicate shape, policies may return booleans: `true` is treated as `"user-approval"` and `false` as `"not-applicable"`. Boolean promises are supported too.
54	
55	Policies can also return `"approved"` or `"denied"` to decide automatically. Use `{ type: "approved" | "denied", reason }` when the model should receive a reason. The `Approval`, `ApprovalContext`, and `ApprovalStatus` types are exported from both `eve/tools` and `eve/tools/approval`.
56	
57	Gating a side effect on approval is also how you make non-idempotent work safe across replays: a charge or email that sits behind `always()` can't fire from a re-run step without a fresh human decision.
58	
59	### Skipping approval for schedule-dispatched turns
60	
61	`session.auth.current` identifies the caller of this turn. Markdown schedules use the app principal (`authenticator: "app"`, `principalId: "eve:app"`, `principalType: "runtime"`) automatically. A `run` schedule must pass its `appAuth` to `receive(...)` for the child session to use that principal. Match all three fields to skip approval for automated turns while still prompting when a person calls the same tool:
62	
63	```ts title="agent/tools/refund_charge.ts"
64	import { defineTool } from "eve/tools";
65	import { z } from "zod";
66	
67	export default defineTool({
68	  description: "Refund a charge.",
69	  inputSchema: z.object({ chargeId: z.string(), amount: z.number() }),
70	  approval: ({ session }) => {
71	    const auth = session.auth.current;
72	    return auth?.authenticator === "app" &&
73	      auth.principalId === "eve:app" &&
74	      auth.principalType === "runtime"
75	      ? "not-applicable"
76	      : "user-approval";
77	  },
78	  async execute(input) {
79	    return refund(input);
80	  },
81	});
82	```
83	
84	`session` in `approval` has the same shape as `ctx.session` in `execute`: `id`, `auth`, `turn`, and an optional `parent`. If a person later resumes a schedule-started session, `session.auth.current` becomes that person while `session.auth.initiator` remains the app principal. Inspect `initiator` only when the policy should apply to the whole session. Skipping approval on scheduled turns means any non-idempotent side effect will re-fire if a step replays, so pair this pattern with idempotency keys or `once()` where needed.
85	
86	## Questions
87	
88	The built-in `ask_question` tool lets the model pause and ask the user, rather than guessing. It has no `execute` — the model calls it with `{ prompt, options?, allowFreeform? }`:
89	
90	- `prompt`: the question to put to the user.
91	- `options`: an optional list of choices to offer. Channels render these as buttons or a select menu.
92	- `allowFreeform`: whether the user may answer with free text instead of picking an option.
93	
94	`ask_question` is part of the [default harness](/docs/concepts/default-harness), so it is available without you defining anything. It produces the same `input.requested` pause as an approval, and resumes the same way.
95	
96	## How pause and resume works
97	
98	Approvals and questions share one protocol:
99	
100	1. The model requests input (an approval, or an `ask_question`).
101	2. eve emits an `input.requested` stream event carrying the pending requests.
102	3. The turn parks at `session.waiting`, durably, for as long as it takes.
103	4. The client answers with `inputResponses` (structured, keyed by `requestId`) or a normal follow-up `message`. A follow-up whose text matches an option ID, option label, or numeric option index resolves automatically, including approval options such as `approve` and `deny`.
104	
105	Each request includes a `kind` discriminator: `tool-approval`, `question`, or
106	`session-limit`. Clients should use `kind` to choose behavior and presentation;
107	`toolName` and `requestId` identify the action and request but do not encode its
108	semantics.
109	
110	The run picks back up exactly where it parked. Because the pause is durable, nothing is held in memory while it waits — the process can restart and the parked turn survives.
111	
112	For approval requests, unrelated follow-up text does not deny the tool call. eve keeps the approval pending and holds that text until the approval is answered, then replays it as the next message in the session.
113	
114	See [Sessions, runs & streaming](/docs/concepts/sessions-runs-and-streaming) for the full event and resume contract that this builds on.
115	
116	## Answering from a client or channel
117	
118	Channels turn requests into native UI: the Slack adapter renders approvals as buttons and questions as select menus, and writes the user's choice back as the answer. You get this for free on every [channel](/docs/channels).
119	
120	From your own frontend, read the pending request off the latest message and answer through the same session — see [Building a frontend](/docs/guides/frontend/overview#human-in-the-loop-prompts) for the client-side reducer and `inputResponses` shape.
121	
122	## What to read next
123	
124	- [Tools](/docs/tools): define the typed actions an approval gates
125	- [Default harness](/docs/concepts/default-harness): the built-in tools, including `ask_question`
126	- [Sessions, runs & streaming](/docs/concepts/sessions-runs-and-streaming): the event and resume contract behind the pause
127	- [Building a frontend](/docs/guides/frontend/overview): render and answer requests from your own UI
128

2	title: "Security Model"
3	description: "eve's trust boundaries, where secrets live, how credentials reach hosts, and what fails closed by default."
4	---
5	
6	Your eve agent runs across two contexts, with a trust boundary between them and every secret kept on the trusted side. Use this mental model when deciding what an agent (and the model driving it) is allowed to reach.
7	
8	## Trust boundaries
9	
10	|                         | App runtime  | Sandbox               |
11	| ----------------------- | ------------ | --------------------- |
12	| `process.env` / secrets | Yes          | No                    |
13	| Your Node.js code       | Yes          | No                    |
14	| Network                 | Unrestricted | Controlled by policy  |
15	| Filesystem              | App's own    | Isolated `/workspace` |
16	
17	The app runtime is the trusted side. Your tool implementations, model calls, connections, state, and durable execution all run here, with `process.env` and full Node.js available. (On Vercel, this is a Vercel Function.)
18	
19	The sandbox is the isolated side. The model runs shell commands there through the built-in `bash`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `glob`, and `grep` tools. It gets its own `/workspace` filesystem, but no `process.env`, no secrets, and no path back into the app runtime. (On Vercel, each sandbox is a [Vercel Sandbox](https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox) microVM with hardware-level isolation.) Only shell commands execute in the sandbox. Even the built-in `bash`/`read_file`/`write_file` tools live in the app runtime and _proxy_ into the sandbox. The model sees tool definitions and results, never your secrets.
20	
21	A concrete trace makes the boundary clear. When the model calls a custom `charge_card` tool, its `execute` runs in the app runtime, reads `process.env.STRIPE_KEY`, calls Stripe, and returns `{ ok: true }`. The model sees only `{ ok: true }`: the key never leaves the app runtime, and nothing about the call touches the sandbox. The built-in `write_file` is the mirror image, running in the app runtime and proxying the write into the sandbox `/workspace`. Either way the model drives the work through tool calls and their results, never by holding a credential or reaching the runtime directly.
22	
23	See [Agent loop and sandbox](./execution-model-and-durability#agent-loop-and-sandbox) for how eve connects these contexts while keeping their state and lifetimes separate.
24	
25	## Data flow at a glance
26	
27	```mermaid
28	flowchart LR
29	  User["User or channel provider"] --> Channel["Channel route and route auth"]
30	  Channel --> Runtime["eve app runtime and durable session"]
31	  Runtime --> Model["Configured model provider or Vercel AI Gateway"]
32	  Runtime --> Tools["Authored tools and connections"]
33	  Tools --> Services["Customer-selected external services"]
34	  Runtime --> Sandbox["Per-session sandbox"]
35	  Sandbox --> Egress["Allowed sandbox network egress"]
36	  Runtime --> Telemetry["Configured telemetry or eval provider"]
37	```
38	
39	eve sends data where your agent configuration and runtime choices send it:
40	
41	- Inbound channel data flows through the channel provider you configure, then into the eve app runtime.
42	- Model inputs and outputs flow to the model or routing path selected in `agent.ts`, such as a Vercel AI Gateway model id or a provider-authored `LanguageModel`.
43	- Tool and connection calls flow to the external services, MCP servers, OpenAPI endpoints, and channels you configure.
44	- Sandbox commands can reach network destinations allowed by the sandbox network policy.
45	- Telemetry and eval data flows to the exporters and providers you configure in `instrumentation.ts` or eval settings.
46	
47	eve stores durable session and workflow state needed to resume conversations, stream events, replay completed steps, and show run observability. You are responsible for deciding whether the selected channels, model providers, connected services, sandbox egress destinations, telemetry exporters, retention settings, and deletion controls are appropriate for your data and use case.
48	
49	## Credential brokering
50	
51	Credential brokering gives the model _authenticated_ network access from inside the sandbox, like a `git clone` of a private repo or an authenticated `curl`, when there's no [tool](../tools) or [connection](../connections) to route it through. On the Vercel Sandbox backend, auth headers get injected at the sandbox's network firewall for matching domains. The secret stays in the app runtime; the sandbox process only ever sees the response. See [Vercel Sandbox Credential Brokering](https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox/concepts/firewall#credentials-brokering) for the platform mechanism, and [Sandbox](../sandbox) for the eve policy API.
52	
53	## Connection credentials
54	
55	[Connection](../connections) tokens (MCP and OpenAPI) come from either `getToken()` or an interactive OAuth flow, and eve injects the resolved token into every outbound request. The token is cached per step and never serialized to durable state.
56	
57	## Channel verification
58	
59	A [channel](../channels/overview) is your agent's front door, so authenticating inbound traffic is its job. The built-in platform channels follow two rules, and so must any channel you write yourself:
60	
61	- **Verify signatures in constant time.** Platform channels (Slack, GitHub,
62	  Telegram, Twilio) verify the platform's HMAC signature over the raw request body
63	  with a constant-time comparison, so timing the response can't reveal a forged
64	  signature. Use a constant-time compare for any secret you check, never `===` on
65	  a signature.
66	- **Don't trust body-supplied identity.** Derive the caller from a _verified_
67	  signature or token, never from a `principalId` (or similar) the request body
68	  claims. A body field is attacker-controlled; treating it as identity is
69	  cross-user impersonation.
70	
71	A custom channel that accepts dashboard-style webhooks should follow the same shape: authenticate the raw body with an HMAC, compare signatures in constant time, and trust any body-supplied principal only after the signature verifies.
72	
73	## Authored markdown is data
74	
75	[Skill](../skills) and [schedule](../schedules) files are markdown with YAML frontmatter, and eve treats that frontmatter strictly as data. The code-capable engines (`---js` / `---javascript`, which would `eval()` the frontmatter body the moment the file is parsed) are disabled, so such a fence throws rather than running. Frontmatter has to parse to a plain YAML object.
76	
77	## Auth fails closed
78	
79	Routes reject unauthenticated traffic by default. If no `AuthFn` in the walk accepts the request, it gets a `401`, and admitting anonymous callers takes an explicit `none()`. The scaffold's `placeholderAuth()` keeps a half-configured app closed in production until you replace it. See [Auth & route protection](../guides/auth-and-route-protection) for the full walk and verifiers.
80	
81	## Pre-production checklist
82	
83	Before exposing an agent to real traffic:
84	
85	- [ ] Replace `placeholderAuth()` in `agent/channels/eve.ts` with a real
86	      `AuthFn` (`vercelOidc()`, `httpBasic()`, `oidc()`, or your own). Verify an
87	      unauthenticated production request gets `401`.
88	- [ ] Verify channel signatures. Each platform channel needs its signing
89	      secret set; custom channels must verify signatures in constant time and never
90	      trust body-supplied identity.
91	- [ ] Keep secrets in `process.env`, never in compiled artifacts, never
92	      passed into the sandbox. Route privileged calls through tools or connections.
93	- [ ] Scope connection tokens to the least privilege the agent needs; they
94	      reach hosts but never the model.
95	- [ ] Set a sandbox network policy tighter than `allow-all` if the model
96	      shouldn't have open egress; use credential brokering for authenticated egress.
97	- [ ] Don't surface untrusted text as markup. Model- or user-controlled
98	      strings rendered into a channel UI should be escaped for that surface.
99	
100	## What to read next
101	
102	- [Auth & route protection](../guides/auth-and-route-protection): the full auth walk and verifier helpers
103	- [Sandbox](../sandbox): backends, network policy, and brokering config
104	- [Execution model and durability](./execution-model-and-durability): how durable sessions run
105	- [Connections](../connections): static-token and OAuth connections

---
title: "Security Model"
description: "eve's trust boundaries, where secrets live, how credentials reach hosts, and what fails closed by default."
---

Your eve agent runs across two contexts, with a trust boundary between them and every secret kept on the trusted side. Use this mental model when deciding what an agent (and the model driving it) is allowed to reach.

## Trust boundaries

|                         | App runtime  | Sandbox               |
| ----------------------- | ------------ | --------------------- |
| `process.env` / secrets | Yes          | No                    |
| Your Node.js code       | Yes          | No                    |
| Network                 | Unrestricted | Controlled by policy  |
| Filesystem              | App's own    | Isolated `/workspace` |

The app runtime is the trusted side. Your tool implementations, model calls, connections, state, and durable execution all run here, with `process.env` and full Node.js available. (On Vercel, this is a Vercel Function.)

The sandbox is the isolated side. The model runs shell commands there through the built-in `bash`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `glob`, and `grep` tools. It gets its own `/workspace` filesystem, but no `process.env`, no secrets, and no path back into the app runtime. (On Vercel, each sandbox is a [Vercel Sandbox](https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox) microVM with hardware-level isolation.) Only shell commands execute in the sandbox. Even the built-in `bash`/`read_file`/`write_file` tools live in the app runtime and _proxy_ into the sandbox. The model sees tool definitions and results, never your secrets.

A concrete trace makes the boundary clear. When the model calls a custom `charge_card` tool, its `execute` runs in the app runtime, reads `process.env.STRIPE_KEY`, calls Stripe, and returns `{ ok: true }`. The model sees only `{ ok: true }`: the key never leaves the app runtime, and nothing about the call touches the sandbox. The built-in `write_file` is the mirror image, running in the app runtime and proxying the write into the sandbox `/workspace`. Either way the model drives the work through tool calls and their results, never by holding a credential or reaching the runtime directly.

See [Agent loop and sandbox](./execution-model-and-durability#agent-loop-and-sandbox) for how eve connects these contexts while keeping their state and lifetimes separate.

## Data flow at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  User["User or channel provider"] --> Channel["Channel route and route auth"]
  Channel --> Runtime["eve app runtime and durable session"]
  Runtime --> Model["Configured model provider or Vercel AI Gateway"]
  Runtime --> Tools["Authored tools and connections"]
  Tools --> Services["Customer-selected external services"]
  Runtime --> Sandbox["Per-session sandbox"]
  Sandbox --> Egress["Allowed sandbox network egress"]
  Runtime --> Telemetry["Configured telemetry or eval provider"]
```

eve sends data where your agent configuration and runtime choices send it:

- Inbound channel data flows through the channel provider you configure, then into the eve app runtime.
- Model inputs and outputs flow to the model or routing path selected in `agent.ts`, such as a Vercel AI Gateway model id or a provider-authored `LanguageModel`.
- Tool and connection calls flow to the external services, MCP servers, OpenAPI endpoints, and channels you configure.
- Sandbox commands can reach network destinations allowed by the sandbox network policy.
- Telemetry and eval data flows to the exporters and providers you configure in `instrumentation.ts` or eval settings.

eve stores durable session and workflow state needed to resume conversations, stream events, replay completed steps, and show run observability. You are responsible for deciding whether the selected channels, model providers, connected services, sandbox egress destinations, telemetry exporters, retention settings, and deletion controls are appropriate for your data and use case.

## Credential brokering

Credential brokering gives the model _authenticated_ network access from inside the sandbox, like a `git clone` of a private repo or an authenticated `curl`, when there's no [tool](../tools) or [connection](../connections) to route it through. On the Vercel Sandbox backend, auth headers get injected at the sandbox's network firewall for matching domains. The secret stays in the app runtime; the sandbox process only ever sees the response. See [Vercel Sandbox Credential Brokering](https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox/concepts/firewall#credentials-brokering) for the platform mechanism, and [Sandbox](../sandbox) for the eve policy API.

## Connection credentials

[Connection](../connections) tokens (MCP and OpenAPI) come from either `getToken()` or an interactive OAuth flow, and eve injects the resolved token into every outbound request. The token is cached per step and never serialized to durable state.

## Channel verification

A [channel](../channels/overview) is your agent's front door, so authenticating inbound traffic is its job. The built-in platform channels follow two rules, and so must any channel you write yourself:

- **Verify signatures in constant time.** Platform channels (Slack, GitHub,
  Telegram, Twilio) verify the platform's HMAC signature over the raw request body
  with a constant-time comparison, so timing the response can't reveal a forged
  signature. Use a constant-time compare for any secret you check, never `===` on
  a signature.
- **Don't trust body-supplied identity.** Derive the caller from a _verified_
  signature or token, never from a `principalId` (or similar) the request body
  claims. A body field is attacker-controlled; treating it as identity is
  cross-user impersonation.

A custom channel that accepts dashboard-style webhooks should follow the same shape: authenticate the raw body with an HMAC, compare signatures in constant time, and trust any body-supplied principal only after the signature verifies.

## Authored markdown is data

[Skill](../skills) and [schedule](../schedules) files are markdown with YAML frontmatter, and eve treats that frontmatter strictly as data. The code-capable engines (`---js` / `---javascript`, which would `eval()` the frontmatter body the moment the file is parsed) are disabled, so such a fence throws rather than running. Frontmatter has to parse to a plain YAML object.

## Auth fails closed

Routes reject unauthenticated traffic by default. If no `AuthFn` in the walk accepts the request, it gets a `401`, and admitting anonymous callers takes an explicit `none()`. The scaffold's `placeholderAuth()` keeps a half-configured app closed in production until you replace it. See [Auth & route protection](../guides/auth-and-route-protection) for the full walk and verifiers.

## Pre-production checklist

Before exposing an agent to real traffic:

- [ ] Replace `placeholderAuth()` in `agent/channels/eve.ts` with a real
      `AuthFn` (`vercelOidc()`, `httpBasic()`, `oidc()`, or your own). Verify an
      unauthenticated production request gets `401`.
- [ ] Verify channel signatures. Each platform channel needs its signing
      secret set; custom channels must verify signatures in constant time and never
      trust body-supplied identity.
- [ ] Keep secrets in `process.env`, never in compiled artifacts, never
      passed into the sandbox. Route privileged calls through tools or connections.
- [ ] Scope connection tokens to the least privilege the agent needs; they
      reach hosts but never the model.
- [ ] Set a sandbox network policy tighter than `allow-all` if the model
      shouldn't have open egress; use credential brokering for authenticated egress.
- [ ] Don't surface untrusted text as markup. Model- or user-controlled
      strings rendered into a channel UI should be escaped for that surface.

## What to read next

- [Auth & route protection](../guides/auth-and-route-protection): the full auth walk and verifier helpers
- [Sandbox](../sandbox): backends, network policy, and brokering config
- [Execution model and durability](./execution-model-and-durability): how durable sessions run
- [Connections](../connections): static-token and OAuth connections

1	---
2	title: "Next.js"
3	description: "Run an eve agent and a Next.js app as one project with withEve."
4	---
5	
6	`eve/next` ships a Next.js frontend and an eve agent as a single project. Wrap your config with `withEve()` to run both from one dev server and one Vercel deploy. [`useEveAgent`](./overview) finds the mounted routes on its own, so there's no CORS to configure and no URL env vars to keep in sync.
7	
8	## Prerequisites
9	
10	- The `eve` package installed in your project (`npm install eve@latest`).
11	- An existing eve agent directory. If you don't have one, start from [Getting started](../../getting-started).
12	- A Next.js app to mount the agent in.
13	
14	## Wrap the Next.js config
15	
16	```ts title="next.config.ts"
17	import type { NextConfig } from "next";
18	import { withEve } from "eve/next";
19	
20	const nextConfig: NextConfig = {};
21	
22	export default withEve(nextConfig);
23	```
24	
25	By default `withEve()` looks for an `agent/` folder inside your Next.js project root. If the agent lives somewhere else, point at it with `eveRoot`:
26	
27	```ts
28	export default withEve(nextConfig, {
29	  eveRoot: "../my-agent",
30	});
31	```
32	
33	For multiple agents, use `agents`. String values are agent roots; object values can override the build command or private production service prefix for that agent:
34	
35	```ts
36	export default withEve(nextConfig, {
37	  agents: {
38	    support: "./agents/support",
39	    billing: {
40	      root: "./agents/billing",
41	      buildCommand: "pnpm build:billing-agent",
42	      servicePrefix: "/_eve_internal/billing",
43	    },
44	  },
45	});
46	```
47	
48	Named agents mount under `/eve/agents/<name>/eve/v1/*`. Call the matching agent from React with `agent`:
49	
50	```tsx
51	const support = useEveAgent({ agent: "support" });
52	const billing = useEveAgent({ agent: "billing" });
53	```
54	
55	Use either `eveRoot` or `agents`, not both. `eveRoot` remains the shorthand for a single unnamed agent mounted at `/eve/v1/*`.
56	
57	Generated agent services build with `EVE_PUBLIC_ROUTE_PREFIX` set to the agent's public mount (for example `/eve/agents/support`) so framework-minted callback URLs — OAuth connection callbacks and remote-subagent session callbacks — resolve to the public per-agent path. If you configure eve services manually in `vercel.json` instead, export that variable in each named agent's build command.
58	
59	### `withEve` options
60	
61	All fields are optional.
62	
63	| Option               | Type                  | Default                | Purpose                                                                                                                                                    |
64	| -------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
65	| `eveRoot`            | `string`              | Next.js app root       | Path to one unnamed eve app root, relative to `process.cwd()` unless absolute. Do not combine with `agents`.                                               |
66	| `agents`             | `Record<string, ...>` | unset                  | Named eve agents to mount under `/eve/agents/<name>/eve/v1/*`. Each value is a root string or `{ root, buildCommand?, servicePrefix? }`.                   |
67	| `eveBuildCommand`    | `string`              | generated              | Build command for generated eve Vercel services. In multi-agent mode this is the default for agents without their own `buildCommand`.                      |
68	| `servicePrefix`      | `string`              | `"/_eve_internal/eve"` | Private route namespace for legacy manual Vercel service configs and non-Vercel production proxying. Named agents derive unique defaults from this prefix. |
69	| `devServerTimeoutMs` | `number`              | `180000`               | Maximum time to wait for each eve development server to become available.                                                                                  |
70	
71	For slow cold starts, increase the development timeout:
72	
73	```ts
74	export default withEve(nextConfig, {
75	  devServerTimeoutMs: 300_000,
76	});
77	```
78	
79	## Call the hook
80	
81	With `withEve()` in `next.config.ts`, the eve routes are same-origin, so client code can call [`useEveAgent`](./overview) without naming a host. Cookie-based auth (Auth.js or any session cookie) needs no extra wiring, since the browser already sends those cookies on every eve request. For non-cookie schemes, attach the credentials yourself:
82	
83	```tsx
84	const agent = useEveAgent({
85	  headers: async () => ({
86	    authorization: `Bearer ${await getAccessToken()}`,
87	  }),
88	});
89	```
90	
91	The default eve channel is fail-closed. With no `agent/channels/eve.ts` authored, eve registers `eveChannel({ auth: [vercelOidc(), localDev()] })`: `vercelOidc()` gets the first chance to resolve a Vercel caller, `localDev()` opens the remaining localhost requests, and everything else gets a `401`. To run your app's own auth policy, add `agent/channels/eve.ts`:
92	
93	```ts title="agent/channels/eve.ts"
94	import { eveChannel } from "eve/channels/eve";
95	import { localDev, vercelOidc } from "eve/channels/auth";
96	
97	export default eveChannel({ auth: [vercelOidc(), localDev()] });
98	```
99	
100	For a public demo, use `none()` (also from `eve/channels/auth`) to skip authentication. See [Channels](../../channels/overview) and [Auth & route protection](../auth-and-route-protection).
101	
102	## Dev vs deploy topology
103	
104	- **Local dev.** `npm run dev` boots the eve dev server next to `next dev` and rewrites the eve routes over to it. The browser only ever talks to the Next.js origin.
105	- **Vercel.** The web app and the eve runtime deploy as a single project. `withEve()` writes Build Output `services` for eve and `routes` that send `/eve/v1/**` to that service before filesystem routing; the Next.js app itself remains the default app. Vercel assembles authored [schedules](../../schedules) into the project config as Vercel Cron Jobs, including correctly prefixed jobs for named agents, while cron entries owned by the Next.js app are preserved. By default, generated services run the installed eve binary from the agent root, so the agent directory does not need its own `package.json`. When the agent needs its own build step, set `eveBuildCommand`:
106	
107	  ```ts
108	  export default withEve(nextConfig, {
109	    eveBuildCommand: "npm run build:eve",
110	  });
111	  ```
112	
113	- **Local production build.** `next build && next start` serves the eve runtime from its built `.output/server/index.mjs` on a stable local port (`4274`) and proxies the eve routes to it. Run `eve build` first so that output exists. Change the port with `EVE_NEXT_PRODUCTION_PORT`:
114	
115	  ```bash
116	  EVE_NEXT_PRODUCTION_PORT=5000 npm run build && npm start
117	  ```
118	
119	- **Non-Vercel hosts.** When the eve service lives on a separate origin, tell Next.js where to find it with `EVE_NEXT_PRODUCTION_ORIGIN`:
120	
121	  ```bash
122	  EVE_NEXT_PRODUCTION_ORIGIN=https://agent.example.com npm run build
123	  ```
124	
125	## What to read next
126	
127	- [Frontend overview](./overview): the `useEveAgent` API
128	- [Auth & route protection](../auth-and-route-protection)
129	- [Deployment](../deployment/overview)

I'm seeing how Eve integrates into their existing Next.js setup—the `withEve` wrapper mounts it directly in their `apps/app` project on a single Vercel deployment. Their schedule definitions compile down to Vercel Cron Jobs, which would replace their current cron route handlers, and the session model runs on the same infrastructure.

The key insight is that handler-form sessions can durably suspend (park) across time, whereas markdown task-mode can't—so if their consolidation job needs human-in-the-loop approval, it has to use the handler form. Eve's HITL system with `approval: always()` and the built-in `ask_question` tool parks at `session.waiting` indefinitely, which becomes their review queue. The approval policy example shows cross-tenant access control—checking that the caller's tenant ID matches the tool input's tenant ID before allowing execution.

On the security side, the trust boundary separates the app runtime (where secrets and their tools live) from the sandbox (no secrets), auth fails closed by default, and there are specific rules for channel verification like constant-time signature checking and not trusting identity from the request body—both directly applicable to their Resend webhook handling. Authored markdown is treated as data, so frontmatter code engines are disabled.

For data flow, eve routes model calls through whatever they configure in agent.ts—whether that's a Vercel AI Gateway model ID or a custom LanguageModel—which means they can pin an EU provider to satisfy residency requirements. The skip-approval-for-scheduled-turns pattern is exactly what they need: their nightly consolidation runs as the `app` principal without prompting, but when a human calls the same tool, approval gets triggered.

One important caveat: eve is still in preview, so the framework, APIs, and behavior could change. There's also a warning that unless they configure stricter controls, eve agents default to permissive settings—tool execution without approval if approval isn't explicitly set, and sandbox network egress that isn't deny-all. The schedules documentation has a UTC gotcha around how Vercel evaluates cron expressions.

Strong structural fit emerging. Three things from the docs I've read directly:

**Your review queue is eve's HITL primitive.** A tool with `approval: always()` parks the run at `session.waiting` **durably — "seconds or days"** — and resumes exactly where it left off; the process can restart and the parked turn survives. Channels render approvals as buttons natively. And the docs' own example approval policy is a cross-tenant denial reading `session.auth.current?.attributes.tenantId`, which is precisely your `orgId`-as-`tenantId` model.

**Your cron jobs become `defineSchedule`.** Each one compiles to a Vercel Cron Job in the Build Output config. Note two gotchas: Vercel evaluates cron in **UTC** (your 03:00 consolidation is currently CEST), and **markdown task-mode schedules cannot park for HITL** — only the handler (`run`) form can. Your consolidation job proposes to humans, so it must use the handler form.

**The EU lever exists in `agent.ts`.** The security model says model I/O flows to "a Vercel AI Gateway model id **or a provider-authored `LanguageModel`**" — so you can pin an EU-resident provider rather than accept gateway defaults. That's where the residency decision gets made, and it's one config surface rather than scattered call sites.

Two caveats already visible: eve is **explicitly in preview** ("APIs, documentation, and behavior may change before general availability"), and it warns that agents "may operate with permissive settings, including tool execution without human approval where approval is omitted."

---

# 1. Project layout & agent config

**Directory shape** (`project-structure.mdx`, `reference/project-layout.md`):

```
my-agent/
├── package.json          # root agent name comes from `name`, else app-root dir name
├── tsconfig.json
├── agent/
│   ├── agent.ts          # runtime config (optional at root)
│   ├── instructions.md   # REQUIRED at root; optional on subagents
│   ├── instrumentation.ts# root-only, auto-discovered, runs before agent code
│   ├── channels/         # root-only
│   ├── connections/      # one per file
│   ├── hooks/            # module-backed only, recursive dirs OK
│   ├── skills/           # .md flat | <name>/SKILL.md packaged | .ts defineSkill
│   ├── lib/              # import-only, never mounted into sandbox
│   ├── sandbox/          # sandbox.ts + workspace/**
│   ├── tools/            # module-backed only
│   ├── schedules/        # root-only, <name>.ts or <name>.md (frontmatter cron:)
│   └── subagents/<id>/   # own agent root; nested OK
└── evals/                # SIBLING of agent/, not inside it
    └── evals.config.ts   # exactly one, required
```

**Naming rule**: identity is the path. `defineTool`/`defineSkill`/`defineAgent` never take `name` or `id` (`reference/project-layout.md`). `agent/tools/get_weather.ts` → tool `get_weather`; `agent/connections/linear.ts` → connection `linear`, tools called `linear__<tool>`; `agent/subagents/researcher/` → tool `researcher` (bare, no namespace prefix — collides with a tool named `researcher`, rejected at build time).

**What reaches the sandbox**: only `agent/sandbox/workspace/**` → `/workspace/...`. Skills → `$HOME/.agents/skills/...` (fallback `/workspace/skills/...`). `lib/` never reaches the sandbox.

**Flat layout** supported (`agent.ts` + `tools/` at app root) but discouraged.

**`defineAgent` fields** (`agent-config.md`, table at L223-231):

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | gateway id string \| AI SDK `LanguageModel` \| `defineDynamic({fallback, events})` | `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5` **only if `agent.ts` is absent**; required when present |
| `reasoning` | `"provider-default"\|"none"\|"minimal"\|"low"\|"medium"\|"high"\|"xhigh"` | provider default |
| `modelOptions` | `AgentModelOptionsDefinition` (incl. `providerOptions`) | none |
| `compaction` | `{ thresholdPercent }` | `0.9` |
| `limits` | `{ maxInputTokensPerSession, maxOutputTokensPerSession, sessionTimeoutMs }`, each settable to `false` | 40 000 000 in / unset out / 30 days |
| `experimental` | `{ workflow?: { world?: string } }` | unset — "can change or disappear in any release" |
| `outputSchema` | Standard Schema or JSON Schema | none; **task-mode only** (subagent/schedule/remote); interactive turns ignore it |
| `build` | `{ externalDependencies?: string[] }` | none |
| `description` | string | **required on subagents** |
| `modelContextWindowTokens` | number | (used in `reference/typescript-api.md` L111) |

**Model selection specifics** (`agent-config.md` L23-44):
- String id ⇒ **routes through Vercel AI Gateway**. Needs `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` or `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN`.
- Provider-authored `LanguageModel` ⇒ direct provider call, bypasses the gateway. `npm install @ai-sdk/anthropic`; `model: anthropic("claude-opus-4-8")`. Note the id-format difference: gateway `anthropic/claude-opus-4.8` (dot) vs native `claude-opus-4-8` (hyphens).
- `experimental_chatgpt()` from `eve/models/openai` bills a ChatGPT subscription via local `codex login`.

**Dynamic model** (`agent-config.md` L46-88):
```ts
model: defineDynamic({
  fallback: "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5",   // anchors build-time metadata; required for model only
  events: { "session.started": (_e, ctx) => /* id | LanguageModel | {model, modelContextWindowTokens?, modelOptions?} | null */ },
})
```
Scopes `session.started` / `turn.started` / `step.started`; precedence **step > turn > session > fallback**. Session/turn selections **must be strings**; live `LanguageModel` objects only from `step.started`. Resolver throw/invalid ⇒ logs + leaves scope unset (degrades, never fails the turn). Build-time validation covers **only** `fallback`. Runtime identity reports `dynamic:<fallback id>`.

**Per-tool model override: no such thing.** Model is per-agent. The only per-unit-of-work model control is (a) a declared subagent with its own `model`, or (b) the eval judge model (`t.judge` — separate resolution chain, never the agent under test). Compaction uses "the active turn model unless you override it" (`concepts/default-harness.md` L10) — but no doc shows the override option.

---

# 2. Execution model & durability

**Three levels** (`concepts/execution-model-and-durability.mdx`): session (durable conversation, days/weeks) → turn (one user message + all work it triggers) → step (durable checkpoint = one model call + its tool calls).

**Underneath: the open-source Workflow SDK** (`workflow-sdk.dev`). Vendored `@workflow/*` at the **`5.0.0-beta` line** (`@workflow/core 5.0.0-beta.38`, `world-vercel 5.0.0-beta.34`, `world-local 5.0.0-beta.32` per `package.json`). Nitro hosts HTTP routes + workflow entrypoints but is **not** the state store.

| Host | World | Storage |
|---|---|---|
| Vercel | Vercel Workflow | platform (adds latest-prod-deployment routing, dashboard run metadata) |
| local / `eve start` | SDK local world | `.eve/.workflow-data` on disk |
| custom | `experimental.workflow.world: "@workflow/world-postgres"` | that package's env vars |

Custom worlds "must implement the runtime protocol expected by eve's vendored `@workflow/*` packages… the Workflow SDK rejects incompatible protocol versions during initialization." npm `latest` for world packages "can lag behind that line" — pin explicitly.

**Crash / timeout / redeploy** (L57-63): run resumes from the last completed step. **Completed steps never re-run** — eve replays the recorded result from its journal and emits nothing to the stream. **A step interrupted mid-execution re-runs.** Consequence stated flatly: "make non-idempotent side effects like charges or emails idempotent, or gate them with approval." Whatever the interrupted attempt already wrote to the stream **stays**, and the retry re-emits under *new* `meta.id`s with the same `turnId`/`stepIndex`/`sequence`. **No field records which attempt finished** (`concepts/sessions-runs-and-streaming.md` L123).

**Retry budgets**:
- Durable steps: "eve runs each durable step up to four times" (`sessions-runs-and-streaming.md` L123).
- Subagent model calls: "at most three fresh model-call attempts" for classified transient provider failures incl. mid-stream overload; other recoverable errors fall back to Workflow's durable step retry from the last committed snapshot (`subagents.mdx` L141).

**Parked work** (L65-67): approvals, interactive OAuth, long-running subagents ⇒ the workflow suspends and **holds no compute**. `sleep()` tool (`eve/tools/sleep`, opt-in via `agent/tools/sleep.ts`) sleeps the durable turn workflow without holding an app runtime open.

**Serverless mapping / your nightly consolidation job**: the durable turn survives a function timeout because it checkpoints at step boundaries. Two caveats that matter for you:
1. **Markdown-form schedules run in "task mode": they cannot park.** "A task-mode session runs to completion or fails, and cannot park to wait for a person or an OAuth sign-in" (`schedules.mdx` L34). Task-mode sessions also **skip** the token-limit continuation prompt and instead fail the next model call with `SESSION_TOKEN_LIMIT_REACHED` (`agent-config.md` L161-165). A consolidation job that needs a human decision must use the handler form.
2. **Handler form (`run`) can park.** `run({ receive, waitUntil, appAuth })` — `waitUntil(promise)` extends the cron invocation's lifetime; `receive(channel, {message, target, auth})` starts a normal durable session that *can* park.

**Message queueing is not a queue** (L69-77): "eve does not maintain a durable FIFO queue of user messages for a session." One active session owns a continuation token; competing input is **not forwarded to the owner**. Concurrent sends to one session are best-effort folded. Guidance: send one turn, wait for `session.waiting`, keep your own per-session queue in the channel/app layer.

---

# 3. Context control (the heart of it)

**What goes into context each turn** (`concepts/context-control.md`, `concepts/default-harness.md`, `instructions.mdx`):
- `instructions.md`/`.ts` — always-on system prompt, prepended to **every** model call.
- Skills — **not** in the prompt; only their *descriptions* are advertised, plus a framework-owned `load_skill` tool. On call, eve "appends the skill's markdown to the active instructions for later turn work."
- Workspace — **not inlined**. Model gets "a shallow workspace hint, a separate skill-root hint," and inspects via `bash`/`read_file`/`glob`/`grep`.
- Conversation history — append-only, summarized by compaction.

**Instructions directory composition** (`instructions.mdx` L33-37): `agent/instructions/` read **non-recursively**, accepts `.md` and `.ts` (`defineInstructions` or `defineDynamic`). Entries combine **alphabetically by filename (`localeCompare`)**. A root flat file's content comes **first**, then sorted dir entries. Authoring both `instructions.md` and `instructions.ts` at root is a **build error**.

**Critical**: `defineInstructions` in a static `.ts` **runs once at build time** and is captured into the compiled manifest — "the runtime serves the same prompt every session and never re-runs the module." Only `defineDynamic` re-resolves per session/turn.

**Compaction** (`concepts/default-harness.md` L8-25):
- Trigger: conversation tokens **plus the estimated fixed checkpoint-prompt envelope** compared against `thresholdPercent` (default `0.9`) — so it fires sooner than a conversation-only estimate.
- Summarizes older turns; prompt asks the model to separate completed progress/decisions from remaining work and retain constraints, preferences, data, references.
- On re-compaction, the **previous checkpoint is passed separately and without per-message truncation**, then replaced.
- Automatically preserves framework tool state: **resets read-before-write tracking** (a later write re-reads the file) and **re-injects the active todo list**. "There is no per-tool hook to configure."
- Image/file content parts are **dropped** on compaction and replaced with a text stub. "The model cannot re-see a compacted image" (`tools/overview.mdx` L112).
- Events: `compaction.requested` (carries `modelId, sessionId, turnId, usageInputTokens`) → `compaction.completed`.
- Manual: `ClientSession.compact()`, custom-route `compact({continuationToken})`, `POST /eve/v1/session/compact`, TUI `/compact`. Queues behind an active turn; appends no user message. If summarization fails, previous history is preserved.
- Destructive alternative: `ClientSession.clear()` / `POST /eve/v1/session/clear` → discards model-message history, **preserves** session identity, system prompt, tools/skills, durable state, limits, sandbox. Stream boundary `context.cleared` → `session.waiting`.

**Pruning**: none beyond compaction and clear. No token-budget pruning knob, no per-message eviction policy exposed.

**Can you inject retrieved facts per-turn?** Two supported paths, and one explicitly forbidden one:

- ✅ **Dynamic instructions** — `agent/instructions/<file>.ts` exporting `defineDynamic({events})` returning `defineInstructions({markdown})`. Resolves on `session.started` and `turn.started`. This is the sanctioned per-turn injection point.
- ✅ **A retrieval tool** the model calls (`defineTool`), which is model-initiated rather than forced.
- ❌ **Hooks cannot do it.** `guides/hooks.md` L29: "Handlers are **observe-only. They cannot inject model context.** To contribute runtime model messages, use `defineDynamic` and `defineInstructions` in `agent/instructions/`."

**Exact firing order** — two docs state it identically (`concepts/sessions-runs-and-streaming.md` L213-222 "Dispatch order"; `guides/hooks.md` L122-129):

1. **Channel adapter handler** runs; can mutate adapter state.
2. **Metadata projection** — framework re-evaluates the channel's `metadata(state)` and stores the result.
3. **Event is stamped with its `meta` envelope and written to the durable stream.** (Hooks always run *after* durable recording, "so if a hook throws, the stream stays consistent.")
4. **Hooks** fire: **typed handlers first, then the `*` wildcard**. Return values ignored.
5. **Dynamic resolvers** (tool, skill, instruction, model, subagent) fire. By this point `ctx.channel.metadata` already holds the freshly projected metadata from step 2. "The order is structural, not incidental."

Resolvers across files run **concurrently**. The tool loop reads the current tool set **right before each model call**, so a mid-turn update is visible on the next call.

**Resolver event matrix** (`guides/dynamic-capabilities.md`):

| Surface | `session.started` | `turn.started` | `step.started` | `fallback` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| model | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | required |
| tools | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | build error |
| skills | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ reserved | build error |
| instructions | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | build error |
| subagents | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | build error |

Within one file, "the most recently fired one owns that file's tool set." Dynamic name overrides authored name; two dynamic resolvers emitting the same name **throws**.

**Hook failure semantics** (`guides/hooks.md` L131-133): a thrown handler "propagates through the emit composer and surfaces as `turn.failed`"; if a hook on a failure-cascade event throws, it escalates to `session.failed`. **eve treats a thrown hook as a real failure** — wrap bodies in try/catch. Hooks are **at-least-once**; "no key collapses a retry."

Subagent hooks fire **only** inside the subagent scope; parent hooks do not fire for subagent turns.

# 4. State vs memory

```ts
import { defineState } from "eve/context";
const budget = defineState<T>("my-agent.budget", () => ({ count: 0, cap: 25 }));
// StateHandle<T>: get(): T   |   update(fn: (cur: T) => T): void
```

Semantics (`guides/state.md`, `guides/session-context.md`):
- Declare **once at module scope**; import the handle everywhere.
- `get()` returns `initial()` on first access within a context.
- Values survive **workflow step boundaries** — crashes, redeploys, days-long sessions.
- `get()`/`update()` **require an active eve context**; they throw at module top level, in build scripts, and on discovery-time paths. Safe inside `defineTool().execute`, hook handlers, channel event handlers, connection `auth:`/`headers:` resolvers, and after async boundaries in the same authored chain.
- **Durable by default, does not reset between turns.** Reset explicitly from a `turn.started` hook.
- **Never shared with subagents** — every child (built-in `agent` copy *or* declared specialist) starts with fresh state. "`defineState` values never cross the parent/child boundary, even when the child is a copy of the same agent."

**Why the memory pattern says not to use it for long-term memory** (`guides/state.md` L71-72 + `patterns/multi-tenant-memory.md`): `defineState` is *conversation-scoped working memory that lives and dies with the session* — "the agent's short-term memory, persisted durably for the life of the session." Anything that must (a) outlive the session, (b) be shared across sessions or users, or (c) **be queried independently of a turn** belongs in an external store. Add three more reasons that matter to you specifically:
- It is only readable inside a managed runtime scope — you cannot query it from your Next.js app or a MongoDB aggregation.
- It has no tenant dimension; it's keyed by session, and sessions are one-per-conversation.
- **eve exposes no API to delete durable session state.** `agent-config.md` L144: session expiration "does not delete stored session data." Grepping all 79 doc files turns up **no** session-delete route, no purge/erase API. For GDPR Art. 17 that means anything you put in `defineState` (or in conversation history) is outside your erasure cascade unless you own the workflow world. This is the single strongest architectural argument for keeping facts in your Mongo layer and treating eve sessions as ephemeral compute.

# 5. Tools

```ts
import { defineTool } from "eve/tools";
export default defineTool({
  description: string,                       // written for the model
  inputSchema: ZodSchema | StandardSchema | JSONSchemaObject,   // REQUIRED; z.object({}) for none
  outputSchema?: ZodSchema | StandardSchema, // optional; types the execute return
  approval?: Approval,
  execute(input, ctx): unknown | Promise<unknown>,   // sync or async
  toModelOutput?(output): ToolOutput,
});
```
Plain JSON Schema types `input` as `Record<string, unknown>`.

**`ctx`** (`tools/overview.mdx` L37-45, `reference/typescript-api.md` L61-68):
- `ctx.session` — `{ id, turn: { id, sequence }, auth: { current, initiator }, parent?: { callId, sessionId, rootSessionId, turn } }` (read-only)
- `ctx.callId` — current tool call id, carried on stream events and approval context
- `ctx.toolName` — final runtime name incl. namespace qualification
- `ctx.abortSignal` — aborts on turn cancellation; `ctx.getSandbox()` sessions already bound to it
- `ctx.getSandbox()` — async, no args, one sandbox per agent
- `ctx.getSkill(id)` — sync handle, `{ name, file(relPath) }`, lazy read from sandbox
- `ctx.getToken(provider, options?)` / `ctx.requireAuth(provider, options?)` — inline auth providers; `requireAuth` evicts the cached token and re-challenges (use after a downstream 401)

Tools run **in the app runtime** with full `process.env` and `lib/` imports — not in the sandbox. "eve never runs authored tools during discovery."

**Approval** (`tools/overview.mdx`, `connections/mcp.mdx` L146-187, `patterns/multi-tenant-approvals.md`):
- Helpers from `eve/tools/approval`: `always()`, `once()` (first time per session), `never()`.
- **Conditional: yes.** `approval` accepts a policy function, sync or async, receiving `ApprovalContext = { session, toolName, toolInput, approvedTools }` and returning `ApprovalStatus`:
  - `"user-approval"` or `true` → pause for a human
  - `"not-applicable"` or `false` → run without prompt
  - `{ type: "approved", reason? }` / `{ type: "denied", reason? }` → decide automatically
- For connection tools, `toolName` arrives **qualified** (`social__delete_draft`) — match with `.includes()`/`.endsWith()`, not `===`. `toolInput` is `Record<string, unknown> | undefined` from a schema **you don't own** — read defensively.
- Types `ApprovalContext`, `ApprovalStatus` import from `eve/tools`.
- Ordering: **approval runs before `execute`**; with OAuth it's approve-then-sign-in, and "eve records the approval on session state the moment it's granted, and that record survives the sign-in park" — one approval, one sign-in, never a double prompt.
- Warnings the docs repeat: approval is a **gate, not authorization** — "the executor must still derive and enforce tenancy again"; and built-in approval "is not a four-eyes workflow that proves a different person or role approved it."

**Error handling**: throw from `execute` → surfaces as a failed tool result to the model. Malformed raw tool args now "preserve the original JSON syntax error and return it to the model as a failed tool result" (CHANGELOG 0.29.2). Tool outputs must be JSON-serializable — convert `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `NaN`, cyclic objects first.

**`toModelOutput`**: receives the full typed `execute` return, affects **only the model**. Channel handlers and hooks still see the full output on `action.result`. Shapes: `{type:"text", value}`, `{type:"json", value}`, or `toolOutput.content([toolOutputPart.text(...), toolOutputPart.file(base64, {mediaType})])`. **File payloads must be base64 strings** — raw `Uint8Array`/`Buffer` rejected (don't survive the durable JSON boundary). eve warns above 3 MiB; content-part images are persisted in session history and **re-sent on every subsequent model call**.

**Dynamic tools have a hard bundler constraint** (`guides/dynamic-capabilities.md` L96-98): `execute` **must be an inline function expression/arrow/method shorthand placed directly as the property value**. `execute: myFn` and `execute: makeFn()` "work on the first step but do not survive replay." Silent failure mode — worth a lint rule.

**Built-ins** (`concepts/default-harness.md`): `bash`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `glob`, `grep` (all → sandbox), `web_fetch`, `todo` (app runtime), `web_search` (provider-executed, no local executor), `ask_question`, `agent` (root only), `load_skill`, `connection_search`. Override by authoring the same slug (spread from `eve/tools/defaults` to keep description/schema/framework state — e.g. `todo`'s durable state key). Disable with `export default disableTool()`; an unknown slug **fails at build** rather than silently no-op'ing. Doc's own warning: "Review these built-in tools before production use. Disable, wrap, restrict, or require approval for any tool that can access the filesystem, network, shell, or sensitive data."
