# 7. Evals — full inventory

## 7.1 File shape and discovery

- Discovery: `evals/**/*.eval.ts` at the **app root**, sibling of `agent/`. Path = identity: `evals/weather/brooklyn-forecast.eval.ts` → id `weather/brooklyn-forecast`.
- **Exactly one `evals.config.ts`** at the root of `evals/` is **required**, even if empty: `export default defineEvalConfig({})`.
- Sibling non-`.eval.ts` files are helpers, not evals. Fixtures conventionally in `evals/data/`.

```ts
defineEval({
  test(t): void | Promise<void>,          // ONLY required field
  description?: string,
  judge?: { model: LanguageModel, modelOptions?: AgentModelOptionsDefinition },
  timeoutMs?: number,
  tags?: readonly string[],               // --tag / --exclude-tag
  metadata?: Record<string, unknown>,
  reporters?: readonly EvalReporter[],
})
```
```ts
defineEvalConfig({
  judge?: EveEvalJudgeConfig,
  reporters?: readonly EvalReporter[],
  maxConcurrency?: number,   // positive int; default 8
  timeoutMs?: number,
})
```
Precedence: CLI flag > per-eval > config default.

## 7.2 Dataset fan-out

Default-export an **array** of `defineEval(...)`. Eval modules are ESM ⇒ **top-level `await` works**. Ids = `<file-id>/<zero-padded index>` in array order: `sql/0000`, `sql/0001`. Loaders from `eve/evals/loaders`: `loadJson(path)`, `loadYaml(path)`, resolved **relative to the app root**. "The loaders are meant for fixtures, not runtime agent code."

```ts
const doc = await loadYaml("evals/data/cases.yaml");
export default (doc.evals as Row[]).map((row) =>
  defineEval({ description: row.task, async test(t) { await t.send(row.prompt); t.succeeded(); t.check(t.reply, equals(row.sql)); } }),
);
```
`eve eval sql` runs every entry of an array-exported `sql.eval.ts`.

## 7.3 The `t` object — drive surface

`EveEvalContext extends EveEvalSessionDriver, EveEvalAssertions` `[dist types.d.ts:324]`.

**Driver methods** (also on every `EveEvalSession` from `t.newSession()` / `t.target.attachSession()`):
| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| `t.send(input)` | `(SendTurnInput) => Promise<EveEvalTurn>` — waits for the turn to settle |
| `t.start(input)` | `=> Promise<EveEvalLiveTurn>` — returns once the server accepts |
| `t.cancel()` | `=> Promise<CancelSessionResult>` — `accepted` and `no_active_turn` both succeed |
| `t.sendFile(text, filePath, mediaType?)` | attaches a local file as a data URL |
| `t.requireInputRequest(filter?)` | **sync**, records a gate, requires **exactly one** matching pending request, returns `InputRequest` |
| `t.respond(...responses: InputResponse[])` | `=> Promise<EveEvalTurn>` |
| `t.respondAll(optionId: string)` | `=> Promise<EveEvalTurn>` |
| `t.events` | `readonly MessageStreamEvent[]` |
| `t.pendingInputRequests` | `readonly InputRequest[]` |
| `t.state` | `SessionState` — serializable resume cursor |
| `t.sessionId` | `string \| undefined` |

**Context-only members**:
`t.signal: AbortSignal` (fires on timeout) · `t.target: EveEvalTargetHandle` · `t.reply: string | null` (last assistant message) · `t.log(message)` · `t.sleep(ms?)` (defaults **1 s**, respects the timeout signal) · `t.newSession(): EveEvalSession` · `t.check(value, assertion): AssertionHandle` · `t.require<T>(value, assertion): Promise<T>` · `t.skip(reason): never` · `t.judge: JudgeContext`.

**`EveEvalTurn`** (returned by `send`/`respond`/`respondAll`/`live.result()`) — immutable, and carries the **full assertion vocabulary plus output assertions**: `.data`, `.events`, `.inputRequests`, `.message`, `.sessionId`, `.status: "completed"|"failed"|"waiting"`, `.toolCalls`, `.requireToolCall(name, opts?)` (gate + returns the call), `.expectOk()` (throws **only** when the turn ended failed; `waiting` is normal).

**`EveEvalLiveTurn`** (from `t.start()` / `t.target.watchTurn()`): `.events`, `.session`, `.sessionId`, `.cancel()`, `.result(): Promise<EveEvalTurn>`, `.waitForEvent(type, options?)`. The handle **owns one stream consumer**; `waitForEvent` **rejects** if the stream fails or hits the turn boundary first. Call `result()` after coordination to settle the stream into run-level assertions.

## 7.4 Complete assertion inventory (`EveEvalAssertions` `[dist types.d.ts:178-200]`)

Available on `t` (whole run, evaluated after `test` finishes), on any `EveEvalSession` (snapshot when called), and on any `EveEvalTurn` (that one response):

| Method | Signature | Asserts |
|---|---|---|
| `succeeded()` | `() => AssertionHandle` | run did not fail **and** did not park on unanswered HITL. Accepts a closed session *and* one left open for the next message |
| `parked()` | `()` | run cleanly parked on HITL input |
| `messageIncludes(token)` | `(string \| RegExp)` | joined assistant text contains token |
| `calledTool(name, opts?)` | `(string, EveEvalToolCallMatchOptions)` | a matching tool call |
| `loadedSkill(skill, opts?)` | `(string, Omit<ToolCallMatchOptions,"input">)` | sugar for `calledTool("load_skill", {input:{skill}})` |
| `notCalledTool(name)` | `(string)` | **no request for `name` in any lifecycle state** |
| `toolOrder(names)` | `(readonly string[])` | requests appear in order, unrelated requests allowed between |
| `usedNoTools()` | `()` | zero tool calls |
| `maxToolCalls(n)` | `(number)` | at most n |
| `noFailedActions()` | `()` | no tool/subagent/skill action reported failure |
| `calledSubagent(name, opts?)` | `(string, EveEvalSubagentCallMatchOptions)` | a delegation happened |
| `event(type, opts?)` | typed on `MessageStreamEvent["type"]`; opts = `{data?, count?}` | event presence + data + count |
| `notEvent(type, opts?)` | opts = `{data?}` (**no `count`**) | event absence |
| `eventOrder(matchers)` | `(readonly EveEvalEventMatch[])` | matching event **groups** occur in order |
| `eventsSatisfy(label, predicate)` | `(string, (events) => boolean)` | escape hatch over the typed stream |

**Output assertions** (`EveEvalOutputAssertions`) — on `EveEvalSession` and `EveEvalTurn` **only, not on `t`**:
- `outputEquals(value)` — **strict** structural equality (both sides must carry exactly the same keys; `deepEquals`, unlike matcher comparison)
- `outputMatches(schema: StandardSchemaV1)`

**Mutual exclusion**: "`t.calledTool` and `t.usedNoTools` are mutually exclusive; assert one or the other, never both in the same run."

## 7.5 `eve/evals/expect` — every matcher `[dist expect/index.d.ts]`

| Builder | Signature | Scores | Default severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| `includes(substring)` | `(string \| RegExp) => Assertion` | coerced string contains substring / matches RegExp | **gate** |
| `equals(expected)` | `(unknown) => Assertion` | deep structural equality | **gate** |
| `matches(schema)` | `(StandardSchemaV1) => Assertion` | validates against Standard Schema (e.g. Zod) | **gate** |
| `similarity(expected)` | `(string) => Assertion` | normalized **character-level Levenshtein** similarity, 1 = identical | **soft** |
| `satisfies(predicate, label)` | `<T>((value: T) => boolean, string) => Assertion` | custom boolean | **gate** |

That is the complete export list. `Assertion` itself exposes `score(value)`, optional `evaluate(value): AssertionEvaluation` (`{score, message?, metadata?}`), and chainable `gate(threshold?)` / `soft(threshold?)` / `atLeast(threshold)` returning a **new** Assertion. Types also re-exported from `eve/evals/expect`: `Assertion`, `AssertionEvaluation`, `AssertionHandle`, `AssertionSeverity`.

Failure output format: `✗ equals [status] (0% < 100%): expected {"status":"active"}; received {"status":"disabled"}`.

## 7.6 Matcher mini-language `[dist match.d.ts]`

A matcher value is one of:
- **literal** — objects **partial-deep-match** (every key in the matcher must match recursively; nested values are themselves matchers); arrays match **element-wise**; primitives compare with `Object.is`
- **RegExp** — tests string values directly, and the **JSON serialization** of anything else. eve resets `lastIndex` (`testRegExp`) so `g`/`y` flags don't produce order-dependent results
- **function** `(value) => boolean`

`EveEvalCountMatcher = number | ((count: number) => boolean)`. A number is an **exact** count of calls matching every supplied constraint; default is "at least one".

```ts
EveEvalToolCallMatchOptions      = { input?, output?, status?, count? }
EveEvalSkillLoadMatchOptions     = Omit<ToolCallMatchOptions, "input">
EveEvalSubagentCallMatchOptions  = { callId?, childSessionId?, remoteUrl?, output?, status?, count? }
EveEvalInputRequestMatchOptions  = { display?, input?, optionIds?, prompt?, toolName? }   // toolName is a plain string
EveEvalEventMatch<TType>         = { type: TType, data?: <partial-deep over that event's data>, count? }
EveEvalActionStatus              = "pending" | "completed" | "failed" | "rejected"        // default "completed"
```

`optionIds` receives ids **in request order**; a literal array must match the complete ordered list exactly.

```ts
t.calledTool("bash", { input: { command: /^pwd/ }, count: 1 });
t.calledTool("echo", { count: (c) => c >= 2 });
t.calledTool("echo", { output: (v) => String(v).includes(marker) });
parked.calledTool("guarded", { status: "pending", count: 1 });
t.calledSubagent("weather", { remoteUrl: (v) => v === process.env.WEATHER_AGENT_URL, output: /72F/ });
turn.eventOrder([
  { type: "subagent.called",    data: { name: "researcher" },          count: 2 },
  { type: "subagent.completed", data: { subagentName: "researcher" },  count: 2 },
]);
```

**Derived facts** the runner extracts (`EveEvalDerivedFacts`): `toolCalls[]` (`{name, input, output, status, turnIndex, sessionId?}`), `toolCallCount`, `subagentCalls[]` (`{callId?, childSessionId?, name, remoteUrl?, output?, status, turnIndex, sessionId?}`), `subagentCallCount`, `inputRequests[]`, `parked: boolean`, `messageCount`, `reasoningBlockCount`, `failureCode?`.

## 7.7 Severity & verdicts

`.gate(threshold?)` hard · `.soft(threshold?)` tracked (soft with **no threshold = tracked-only, never fails**) · `.atLeast(threshold)` ≡ `.soft(threshold)` · `.label(name)` stable name for repeated families.

Defaults: **all scoped/run-level methods are gates**; `includes`/`equals`/`matches`/`satisfies` are gates; `similarity` and **every `t.judge.*`** are soft.

`await t.require(value, assertion)` records a gate, **returns the original value** on pass, and **stops the test body** on fail without adding a duplicate execution error. `turn.requireToolCall(name, opts?)` and `session.requireInputRequest(filter?)` are the protocol-data equivalents. Recorded assertions never throw and are **not awaitable**.

Verdicts `[dist types.d.ts:460]`: `"passed"` (no execution error, every gate held, every soft threshold met) · `"failed"` (gate failed or execution errored) · `"scored"` (gates held, a soft assertion fell below threshold) · `"skipped"`.

## 7.8 Judge

`t.judge.autoevals.*` — eve-owned wrappers over **Braintrust autoevals** (dep `autoevals@0.0.132`). Complete list `[dist types.d.ts:303-308]`:

| Grader | Signature | Grades |
|---|---|---|
| `factuality(expected, opts?)` | `(string, JudgeOpts?)` | factual consistency of the reply against an expected answer, **A–E buckets** |
| `summarizes(expected, opts?)` | `(string, JudgeOpts?)` | how well the reply summarizes the expected text |
| `closedQA(criteria, opts?)` | `(string, JudgeOpts?)` | whether the reply satisfies a free-form **yes/no** criterion (no expected answer) |
| `sql(expected, opts?)` | `(string, JudgeOpts?)` | **semantic equivalence** of two SQL statements |

`JudgeOpts = { on?: unknown, model?: LanguageModel, modelOptions?: AgentModelOptionsDefinition }`. `on` defaults to `t.reply`.

Judge model resolution, **innermost wins**: per-call `opts.model` → per-eval `defineEval({judge})` → `defineEvalConfig({judge})`. Resolved **once when the runner builds `t`**; **never** the model under test.

- String id ⇒ Vercel AI Gateway, needs `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` or `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN`. `LanguageModel` instance ⇒ used directly.
- **Model configured but no credentials ⇒ the eval skips visibly**, not fails.
- **No judge model resolved at all + a `t.judge.*` call ⇒ recorded as a failed gate** (the runner scores after the test body, the missing model throws).
- Judge calls **start when recorded**; the runner awaits all of them during finalization.

Failure output includes prompt, criteria, response, rationale, choice.

## 7.9 `mockModel` `[dist mock-model.d.ts]`

```ts
import { mockModel } from "eve/evals";
mockModel(input?: MockModelOptions | MockModelResponder | string): LanguageModel
```
- `mockModel()` → `"Mock response"`. `mockModel("text")` → static.
- Callback `MockModelResponder = (req: MockModelRequest) => MockModelResponse | string | Promise<...>`
- `MockModelRequest = { messages: {role, text}[], userMessages: string[], lastUserMessage: string|null, userMessageCount: number, tools: {name, description?, inputSchema?}[], toolResults: {id, name, output, isError}[] }`
- `MockModelResponse = { text?, toolCalls?: {name, input?, id?}[], usage?: {inputTokens?, outputTokens?} }`
- Options form: `{ modelId?: string /* default "model" */, provider?: string /* default "eve-mock" */, respond? }`
- Handles both generated and streamed responses, derives deterministic response metadata, estimates token usage when `usage` omitted.
- **Caveat**: it goes in `agent/agent.ts` — it is part of the *agent definition*, so use it for a **dedicated fixture agent**. It stays mocked whether that fixture runs locally or as a deployed target. You cannot mock the model of your real agent from inside an eval file.

## 7.10 Targets

`EveEvalTarget = { kind: "local" | "remote", url: string, capabilities: { devRoutes: boolean } }`. Target is **always an HTTP URL**. Runner polls `/eve/v1/health`, verifies `/eve/v1/info`, exposes `t.target`.

`EveEvalTargetHandle` methods:
- `fetch(path, init?)` → authenticated fetch (channel/webhook ingress)
- `dispatchSchedule(id)` → `{ scheduleId, sessionIds }`. **Dev-routes only** — the local `eve eval` server or a deployment in development mode; **throws** otherwise
- `attachSession(sessionId, { startIndex? })` → `Promise<EveEvalSession>`; consumes **one turn** from an externally-created session so its events feed run-level assertions. On a `session.waiting` boundary it recovers the continuation token, so `.send()`/`.respond()` continue the same durable session
- `watchTurn(sessionId, { startIndex? })` → `EveEvalLiveTurn` (**sync**), starts consuming immediately

**Auth** (`evals/targets.mdx`): local sends none. For `--url`, eve reads `VERCEL_ORG_ID`+`VERCEL_PROJECT_ID` (or `.vercel/project.json`), asks Vercel to resolve the exact HTTPS origin, and sends ambient credentials **only when the project IDs match** — an arbitrary URL stays anonymous. Then sends the resolved OIDC token as bearer + Vercel trusted-IDP header, plus `VERCEL_AUTOMATION_BYPASS_SECRET` if set. `EVE_EVAL_AUTH_TOKEN` is the explicit bearer override for non-Vercel auth. Credential-bearing clients **do not follow redirects**.

## 7.11 Reporters

`eve/evals/reporters` exports `Braintrust`, `JUnit`, and the `EvalReporter` interface.

```ts
interface EvalReporter {
  onRunStart(evaluations: readonly EveEval[], target: EveEvalTarget): void | Promise<void>;
  onEvalComplete(result: EveEvalResult): void | Promise<void>;
  onRunComplete(summary: EveEvalRunSummary): void | Promise<void>;
}
```
- **`Braintrust({ projectName?, experimentName?, /* base experiment by name or id */ })`**. Requires `npm install braintrust` + `BRAINTRUST_API_KEY`. Gate assertions log as **binary scores under a `gate:` prefix** so experiments diff gate regressions like soft scores. Repeated names get `#2`, `#3` — use `.label()`. Failed assertion details land in metadata under **`eveFailedAssertions`**. A reporter **instance** observes the evals that reference it; share one instance to land in one experiment. Listing a config reporter on an eval too does **not** double-report.
- **`JUnit({ filePath })`** or `--junit <path>` (preferred: CI owns the path). One `<testcase>` per path-derived id; failed gates and execution errors → failures; `t.skip(reason)` → `<skipped>`.
- Config reporters observe **every** eval; per-eval `reporters` scope to that eval. `--skip-report` suppresses **both**.

`EveEvalResult = { id, result: EveEvalTaskResult, assertions: AssertionResult[] /* in record order */, verdict, error?, skipReason?, startedAt, completedAt }`. `EveEvalRunSummary = { target, results, startedAt, completedAt, passed, failed, scored, skipped, errored }` — `errored` is the execution-error **subset of** `failed`.

## 7.12 CLI & CI

```bash
eve eval [evalId...] [--url <url>] [--tag <t...>] [--exclude-tag <t...>] [--strict]
         [--timeout <ms>] [--max-concurrency <n>] [--junit <path>] [--list]
         [--verbose] [--json] [--skip-report]
```
Positional ids match **exactly or by directory prefix**. Tag filters compose: `--tag` keeps evals with ≥1 listed tag, then `--exclude-tag` drops. **A `--tag` that matches nothing is exit 2**; an `--exclude-tag` that removes everything is **exit 0** with nothing executed.

**Exit codes**: `0` all non-skipped passed gates (and soft thresholds under `--strict`) · `1` any failure (gate, execution error, strict threshold miss) · `2` configuration error. `t.skip()` never changes the exit code.

**Artifacts**: `.eve/evals/<timestamp>/` — `summary.json`, `results.jsonl` index, and per-eval assertion results, verdicts, **captured event streams**, and `t.log` lines under `evals/`.

**CI**: `eve eval --strict --junit .eve/junit.xml` (add `--url "$DEPLOY_URL"`). Upload `.eve/evals/` as a failure artifact. **Evals run against a live model** — CI must have provider credentials.

# 8. Multi-tenant auth & approvals

**How a tenant id gets onto `ctx.session.auth`** (`patterns/multi-tenant-auth.md`, `guides/auth-and-route-protection.md`): you write an `AuthFn` in `agent/channels/eve.ts` that verifies your app's credential and returns a `SessionAuthContext`:

```ts
{
  authenticator: "app",
  issuer?: "https://app.example.com",   // include when ids come from >1 identity system
  principalId: caller.userId,            // keep STABLE for the same user
  principalType: "user",
  subject?: caller.userId,
  attributes: { tenantId: caller.tenantId, roles: caller.roles },
}
```
"The tenant comes from verified route auth, never a prompt, tool argument, or remote API response." **There is no framework-native tenant object** — "the implementation is the composition of route auth, `ctx.session`, tool execution, and async connection auth/header resolvers."

**Direct mapping to your stack**: `appSession()` reads the better-auth session, sets `principalId = user.id`, `attributes.tenantId = activeOrganizationId`. "If one user can switch between orgs, authenticate the selected org on **every** session create or continue request and stamp that selected `tenantId` onto the current turn" — matches the better-auth active-org model exactly.

**Route protection**: an **ordered walk** on `eveChannel({ auth: [...] })` guarding `POST /eve/v1/session`, `POST /eve/v1/session/:sessionId`, `GET /eve/v1/session/:sessionId/stream`. `GET /eve/v1/health` is **always public**. Each entry: return `SessionAuthContext` (accept, stop) · return `null`/`undefined` (skip) · **throw** (`UnauthenticatedError` 401, `ForbiddenError` 403). All-skip ⇒ 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate` header derived from the configured entries' schemes. Fails closed: production browser traffic rejected unless configured; anonymous requires explicit `none()`.

Helpers from `eve/channels/auth`: `localDev()` (loopback-hostname only; **trusts the advertised Host header** — "never run on `localDev()` alone"), `vercelOidc({subjects})` + `vercelSubject({teamSlug, projectName, environment})`, `none()`, `httpBasic(creds, {realm})`, `jwtHmac()`, `jwtEcdsa()`, `oidc()`, `placeholderAuth()` (scaffolded, returns a structured 401 in production — **replace before launch**). Low-level verifiers: `verifyHttpBasic`, `verifyJwtHmac`, `verifyJwtEcdsa`, `verifyOidc`, `verifyVercelOidc`; helpers `extractBearerToken`, `withAuthChallenges(fn, challenges)`, `routeAuth(request, auth)`, `createUnauthorizedResponse({status, code, message, challenges})`, `createIpAllowList(...)`, `isIpAllowed(...)`.

**The load-bearing warning for you**, stated twice: **"Route auth does not enforce session ownership."** "There's no second per-session ownership ACL stacked on top of route auth." And in `patterns/multi-tenant-approvals.md`: you must protect `POST /eve/v1/session/:sessionId` (including `inputResponses`) and `GET /eve/v1/session/:sessionId/stream` yourself, persisting session→tenant ownership in your own DB and checking it before proxying. **`sessionId` is a bearer capability by default.**

`ctx.session.auth.current` = caller on the active inbound turn; `.initiator` = caller that started the session. A follow-up updates `current` but leaves `initiator` alone — so **a different caller can follow up on the same session** and `current` tracks them. Both are `null` only on internal runtime paths. Top-level schedule sessions get `principalId: "eve:app"`, `principalType: "runtime"`.

**Forwarded identity**: rejected with 403 by default. Requires `trustedForwarders: (forwarder) => boolean` on your authored `eveChannel` (the framework default channel never accepts one). The predicate authorizes **the forwarder, not the forwarded principal** — `() => true` lets any route-auth-passing caller assert any principal, "including preview deployments of your own project when `vercelOidc()` is in the walk."

**Multi-tenant approvals** (`patterns/multi-tenant-approvals.md`): one async adapter reused by tools + both connection protocols.

```ts
export async function decideTenantApproval(surface, ctx: ApprovalContext): Promise<ApprovalStatus> {
  const current = ctx.session.auth.current;
  const tenantId = tenantIdOf(current), initiatorTenantId = tenantIdOf(ctx.session.auth.initiator);
  if (current?.principalType !== "user" || !tenantId || tenantId !== initiatorTenantId)
    return { type: "denied", reason: "The session is not pinned to one tenant user." };
  const input = ctx.toolInput as Record<string, unknown> | undefined;
  if (typeof input?.tenantId === "string" && input.tenantId !== tenantId)
    return { type: "denied", reason: "Tool input cannot select another tenant." };
  // → your policy store
}
```
Notes: `ctx.toolName` is bare for authored tools (`transfer_funds`), qualified for connections (`billing__updateSubscription`). "The callback deliberately does not treat `approvedTools` as a session-wide grant. Every call is evaluated." Approval "is a gate, not authorization" — re-derive tenancy in the executor. Use an application idempotency key (`${ctx.session.id}:${ctx.session.turn.id}` in the doc's example). "Policy lookup failures should throw or deny, never silently allow. Recheck authorization inside side-effecting executors because membership or policy can change **while a run is parked**." And: built-in approval is not four-eyes.

Answering an approval by text works: a matching reply like `approve`/`deny` answers it; unrelated follow-up text is **held** so it does not implicitly deny. A **stale** approval never authorizes the earlier call — it's delivered to the model as a plain user message.

# 9. Deployment (and region pinning)

**Vercel** (`guides/deployment/vercel.mdx`): `eve link` → `eve deploy` (= install deps, `vercel deploy --prod`, pull env). Hosted builds set `VERCEL`, so `eve build` writes `.vercel/output`. Vercel configures: **Web runtime** (health/session/stream/channel/callback/schedule routes) · **Vercel Workflow** (durable runs, "optimistic replay preconditions enabled so stale event-log snapshots reload before they can commit") · **Vercel Cron** (schedules; cron evaluated in **UTC**) · **Vercel Sandbox**. During a Vercel build eve **automatically creates or reuses a sandbox template** when your sandbox has `bootstrap()` or seed files — "the build needs permission to create Vercel Sandbox templates, and a **prewarm failure stops the deployment**" (`--skip-sandbox-prewarm` opts out, "the output might not be deployable"). Agent Runs tab is **gated per team**.

**Self-hosting** (`guides/deployment/self-hosting.md`): `eve build` → `.output/` Nitro server → `PORT=3000 eve start --host 0.0.0.0`. You must forward **both** prefixes through your proxy, unrewritten: `/eve/` **and** `/.well-known/workflow/`. "A proxy restricted to `/eve/` lets a session start, but the run stalls when its callback can't reach eve." Workflow state defaults to `.eve/.workflow-data` — mount it on persistent storage. Or select a world package. Schedules: `eve build && eve start` starts Nitro's schedule runner; **a custom HTTP-only host or preset silently does not fire schedules** — "the schedule definitions still compile, but they will not fire automatically."

## Region pinning — the critical finding

**The eve docs never mention regions, data residency, or the EU.** I grepped all 79 doc files for `region|residenc|GDPR|frankfurt|fra1|iad1|data.transfer`. **Zero hits.** There is no `region` option on `defineAgent`, `defineSandbox`, any backend factory, `eveChannel`, or anything else in the documented surface.

**What eve pulls toward Vercel-managed components by default:**

| Component | Default | EU-residency escape hatch |
|---|---|---|
| Model routing | String model id ⇒ **Vercel AI Gateway**. Docs say only: "Model use is subject to the terms, data-processing commitments, **retention behavior**, and available controls of the selected provider and routing path" (`agent-config.md` L44) | Pass a provider-authored `LanguageModel` (`@ai-sdk/anthropic` etc.) — bypasses the gateway entirely, you own the provider contract and endpoint |
| Durable state (full conversation + tool I/O) | Vercel Workflow when `VERCEL` is set | `experimental.workflow.world: "@workflow/world-postgres"` on a self-hosted Node service — **but flagged as "opt-in settings that can change or disappear in any release. Treat them as unstable."** |
| Sandbox | `defaultBackend()` picks **Vercel Sandbox** whenever `process.env.VERCEL` is set — "since local container/VM runtimes can't run there" | `docker()`, `microsandbox()`, or a custom `SandboxBackend` — **only viable off-Vercel** |
| Cron | Vercel Cron | Nitro schedule runner via `eve start`, or your own scheduler hitting an authenticated route |
| Route auth | `vercelOidc()` in the framework default | Any custom `AuthFn`; "Vercel OIDC is optional" |
| Connection OAuth | Vercel Connect (optional) | `defineInteractiveAuthorization` — self-hosted OAuth, three methods, no Vercel Connect |
| Eval reporting | Braintrust (US SaaS) | `JUnit({filePath})` or a custom `EvalReporter` |
| Telemetry | zero-config local spool, or your OTel exporter | fully yours |

**Practical read**: on Vercel you get **no documented control over where durable session state, sandbox compute, or gateway inference physically run.** If EU residency is a hard requirement, the only shape the docs support is **self-hosted Nitro in an EU region + `@workflow/world-postgres` (unstable flag) on EU Postgres + `docker()`/`microsandbox()` sandbox + direct EU provider endpoints + no Braintrust.** That strips away most of what makes eve attractive on your existing Vercel stack, and puts you on an explicitly-unstable config surface. This is the single biggest architectural risk in your evaluation and it is a docs gap, not just a config gap — you would need to confirm with Vercel directly.

# 10. Instrumentation

`agent/instrumentation.ts`, **root-only**, auto-discovered, "runs at server startup before any agent code. Its presence implicitly enables telemetry, so there is no separate `isEnabled` toggle."

```ts
export default defineInstrumentation({
  setup: ({ agentName }) => registerOTel({ serviceName: agentName, traceExporter: /* ... */ }),
  recordInputs?: boolean,        // default TRUE — full message history on each step span
  recordOutputs?: boolean,       // default TRUE — model outputs on spans
  functionId?: string,
  traceChannelRequests?: boolean,// default false
  events?: { "step.started"(input): { runtimeContext } | undefined },
});
```

**Three surfaces**:
1. **Workflow run tags `$eve.*`** — automatic, framework-owned, **not configurable**, on the Vercel Workflow run (not on OTel spans). Structural: `$eve.type` (`"session"|"turn"|"subagent"`), `$eve.parent`, `$eve.root`, `$eve.subagent`, `$eve.trigger`, `$eve.title` (**truncated title derived from the first user message** — note that's user content leaving into run metadata). Usage: `$eve.model`, `$eve.input_tokens`, `$eve.output_tokens`, `$eve.cache_read_tokens`, `$eve.tool_count`. Authored code cannot set or override `$eve.`. Writes are best-effort.
2. **OpenTelemetry export** — any OTel backend (Braintrust, Raindrop, Arize, Honeycomb, Datadog, Jaeger). Trace hierarchy: `ai.eve.turn {eve.session.id}` → `ai.streamText` (step) → `ai.streamText.doStream` + `ai.toolCall`. **GDPR-relevant defaults** stated explicitly in the doc: "**By default, telemetry records full message history and model outputs.** You may need to disclose these data flows in your privacy materials." And: "For sensitive, regulated, or production data, set `recordInputs` and `recordOutputs` to `false` unless you have reviewed the exporter and its data-retention path." For your product these should be `false` from day one.

**Debugging**: `eve info [--json]`; artifacts under `.eve/discovery/agent-discovery-manifest.json`, `.eve/discovery/diagnostics.json`, `.eve/compile/compiled-agent-manifest.json`, `.eve/compile/compile-metadata.json`, `.eve/compile/module-map.mjs`. `eve logs` (JSONL), `eve logs --dump`, `eve logs --events` (interleaves session events resolved from `.eve/.workflow-data`).

# 11. Honest assessment

**The self-description.** `README.md` L15: "eve is in preview; the framework, APIs, documentation, and behavior may change before general availability." Version `0.29.5`, **88 releases** in the CHANGELOG, still `0.x`.

**What you'd be betting on — the dependency stack is pre-1.0 all the way down:**
- `@workflow/core@5.0.0-beta.38`, `@workflow/world-vercel@5.0.0-beta.34`, `world-local@5.0.0-beta.32` — the **durability substrate is a beta**, and eve *vendors* it. Custom worlds "must implement the runtime protocol expected by eve's vendored `@workflow/*` packages… the Workflow SDK rejects incompatible protocol versions during initialization." You are coupled to a beta protocol version.
- `next@16.3.0-preview.6`, `ai@^7.0.38`, `zod@4.4.3`, `vitest@4.1.10`.
- `engines: { node: ">=24" }`. Your monorepo is Bun 1.1.43 / Turborepo — eve's CLI adapts to the launching package manager, but the runtime floor is Node 24.

**Release velocity is high and minor bumps carry removals.** 0.29.0 removed `/channels`, `eve channels add`, and the programmatic onboarding API, and renamed `eve trace` → `eve traces`. 0.29.5 renamed the TUI `/new` → `/reset`. A prior release made `SandboxBackendHandle.shutdown()` required and removed `dispose()` — "Breaking change for custom sandbox backends." At ~5 releases per minor across 88 releases, expect churn on a quarterly cadence.

**Specific sharp edges:**

1. **No data-deletion API.** No documented route, helper, or config for deleting durable session state. `agent-config.md` L144: session expiration "does not delete stored session data." For GDPR Art. 17 you'd have to reach into the workflow world's storage yourself — which means self-hosting a world you control. On Vercel Workflow you have no documented deletion path at all.
2. **No region control.** Covered above. Zero doc coverage.
3. **At-least-once everywhere, with an explicit "no key collapses a retry."** Interrupted steps re-run; hooks re-fire; retried steps re-emit under new `meta.id`s with **identical** `turnId`/`stepIndex`/`sequence` and no field marking which attempt won. Consequence for you: **every fact write, every proposal insert, every erasure operation must be idempotent at the Mongo layer** — that's not optional, it's the framework's stated contract. And "durable history keeps only the attempt that completed, while the event stream keeps every attempt" — so if you persist events for audit, an interrupted turn leaves both attempts in your table by design.
4. **Sessions have no queue.** "eve does not maintain a durable FIFO queue of user messages." Bursty channel ingest (your inbound email/webhook path) needs your own per-session queue. The docs say so directly.
5. **`localDev()` trusts the `Host` header.** Documented as spoofable without a normalizing proxy in front. Never ship it as the only authenticator.
6. **Route auth ≠ session ownership.** Stated twice. `sessionId` is a bearer capability. For a multi-tenant German product this is the most likely security hole — you must own that ACL.
7. **Dynamic tools' `execute` must be a literal inline function.** `execute: myFn` compiles, runs once, then silently breaks on replay. No build-time check documented.
8. **Module-backed instructions bake at build time.** Anyone reaching for `instructions.ts` expecting per-session logic gets a frozen prompt. Only `defineDynamic` re-resolves.
9. **Hooks can't inject context** and **hooks that throw fail the turn** (escalating to `session.failed` on cascade events). Both are surprising given the "observe-only" framing.
10. **Subagents inherit nothing** — every declared child duplicates its skills/tools/sandbox, or you factor into `lib/`. This gets expensive fast with many specialists.
11. **`experimental` is explicitly disposable**: "Opt-in settings that can change or disappear in any release. Treat them as unstable." That flag covers the *one* mechanism (`workflow.world`) you'd need for EU residency.
12. **`Workflow` tool runs model-authored JavaScript.** QuickJS-sandboxed with a genuine allowlist (only `tools.<name>` + language built-ins, no `process`/`globalThis`/`import`), but it is still the model writing and executing code. Root-only, `maxSubagents` default 100.
13. **Schedules silently don't fire on custom hosts.** Definitions compile; nothing runs. Also: `eve dev` never fires schedules on cadence — only the dev dispatch route (`POST /eve/v1/dev/schedules/:id`, never mounted in production, **no auth** because it's local-only).
14. **Telemetry defaults capture everything.** `recordInputs`/`recordOutputs` default `true`; `$eve.title` puts a truncated first user message into run metadata regardless of instrumentation config; local traces capture prompts and tool I/O by default.
15. **Evals require a live model.** No documented way to mock the model of the agent under test from inside an eval — `mockModel` lives in `agent.ts`, so it's a fixture-agent tool. Every CI eval run costs real inference against real endpoints.
16. **Agent Runs observability is gated per Vercel team** — "Contact your Vercel representative."
17. **Docs hedge in a few places worth noting**: message-drain from a session's hook is "best-effort and depends on workflow and transport timing"; `meta.id` is "time-ordered, not a total order… do not use `where id > $cursor` as a lossless cursor"; sandbox `agent.session`/`agent.turn` spans "are recorded as zero-duration markers" so third-party OTel backends report zero.

**Where eve genuinely fits your product:** the eval framework is the standout — it is unusually complete for a 0.x framework (typed event matchers, deterministic + judge assertions, dataset fan-out, live-turn coordination, remote targets, JUnit/Braintrust, real exit codes). The multi-tenant auth/approval/credential patterns map cleanly onto better-auth + active-org-as-tenantId with no framework fighting. The human-review-queue shape is exactly what `approval` policies + `input.requested` are built for. Durable parked approvals that survive redeploys are hard to build yourself.

**Where it fights you:** EU residency and Art. 17 erasure are the two requirements the framework has no answer for, and they are the two you cannot compromise on. Both push you off managed Vercel onto a self-hosted Nitro service with an explicitly-unstable workflow world — at which point you've given up Vercel Workflow, Vercel Sandbox, Vercel Cron, and the Agent Runs dashboard, i.e. most of eve's operational value, while keeping all of its 0.x churn risk.

**A defensible middle path**, if you want the harness without the residency bet: use eve as the *orchestration and eval* layer with `defineState` unused, all facts/proposals/PII living exclusively in your EU MongoDB behind authored tools, sessions treated as short-lived and disposable (`limits.sessionTimeoutMs` short, `recordInputs/recordOutputs: false`, `EVE_TRACES_CONTENT=off`), and a direct EU provider endpoint instead of the gateway. That confines eve's durable state to conversation transcripts you can treat as transient — but you still need a written answer for "what's in Vercel Workflow's store, where does it live, and how do I delete it," and the docs do not give you one.</result>

# MongoDB Vector Search — limits & quantization (verified August 2026)

## 1. Max dimensions: **8192**, not 4096 — VERIFIED

- `numDimensions`: "**You must specify a value less than or equal to `8192`.**" — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/index/vector-search-type.md
- "MongoDB Vector Search supports embeddings that are **less than and equal to 8192 dimensions** in length." — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/index.md
- Changelog, **30 March 2025 release**: "**Increases the vector dimension limit to 8192.**" — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/search-changelog/ (this is the entry that superseded 4096; no later dimension-limit entry exists through the 06 July 2026 release)
- The old dedicated limitations page `https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-vector-search/limitations/` returns **HTTP 404** — VERIFIED. Limits are now spread across the index-type page, `feature-compatibility`, and `atlas-limits`.

## 2. Max dimension by quantization — same 8192 ceiling — VERIFIED

Requirements table at https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/about/vector-quantization.md:

| | `int1` ingest | `int8` ingest | Auto scalar | Auto binary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Requires index setting | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| Requires BSON `binData` | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Storage on `mongod` | `binData(int1)` | `binData(int8)` | `binData(float32)` / `array(double)` | `binData(float32)` / `array(double)` |
| Similarity | `euclidean` only | cosine/euclidean/dotProduct | all 3 | all 3 |
| **Max dimensionality** | **Multiple of 8** | **8192** | **8192** | **8192** |
| ANN + ENN | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Per-type constraints from the index page: `int8` → 1–8192; `int1` → multiple of 8; `binData(float32)`/`array(float32)` → 1–8192 for auto scalar, multiple of 8 for auto binary. Binary quantization **requires `numDimensions` to be a multiple of 8** — VERIFIED. The 8192 cap applies to int1 too (field-level rule) — INFERRED (table states the constraint as "multiple of 8" rather than a number).

## 3. Supported data types — VERIFIED

Index page: array of numbers of one of: BSON `double`; `BinData` vector subtype `float32`; `BinData` subtype `int1`; `BinData` subtype `int8`.

- **Atlas automatic quantization** accepts only `binData(float32)` and `array(double)` (Atlas stores all 32/64-bit embeddings as `double` internally).
- **Pre-quantized ingestion** requires BSON `binData` with subtype `float32`, `int8`, or `int1`. `int1` is euclidean-only.
- Timeline: `float32`+`int8` binData ingest → 18 Sep 2024; `int1` ingest + ENN on int8/int1 → 02 Dec 2024.
- Docs recommend converting to binData `float32`/`int1`/`int8` *before* indexing for storage efficiency; disk on `mongod` drops **66%** using binData vectors.

## 4. Quantization options & memory factors — VERIFIED

`"quantization": "none" | "scalar" | "binary"` (`none` is default) on `vector`-type fields.

- **Verbatim**: "Automatic quantization reduces the RAM for `mongot` by **3.75x for scalar** and by **24x for binary**; the vector values shrink by **4x and 32x** respectively, but [HNSW] graph itself does not shrink." — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/about/vector-quantization.md — **your 3.75x / 24x numbers are correct.**
- Changelog phrasing (02 Dec 2024): scalar "~75%" memory reduction, binary "~97%".
- **Rescoring**: only for binary (and for exact search against binary *or* scalar quantized vectors). Query float vector is binarized using the same midpoint, candidates identified in binary space, then re-evaluated against **original float values**. "The full fidelity vectors are stored in their own data structure **on disk**, and are only referenced during rescoring."
- Sizing: storage:RAM ratio ≈ **4:1 (scalar)**, **24:1 (binary)**; binary index disk ≈ `original size * (25/24)`; allocate free disk = **125%** of estimated index size. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/deployment/deployment-options.md
- Use automatic quantization when you have "typically over **100,000** vectors"; if index > **3 GB**, quantize (keeps only ~4% of the index in RAM).
- **Model guidance**: "For most embedding models, we recommend **binary quantization with rescoring**. If you want to use lower dimension models that are not QAT (Quantization-Aware-Trained), use scalar quantization."

**Your ">=1024 dims for binary" recall — partially right, but it's about quantization generally, not binary specifically** — VERIFIED at https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/benchmark/results.md:
- "**We recommend over 1024 dimensions when running larger workloads with quantization.**"
- "…when working with a large dataset, we recommend having dimensionality of **at least 1024d and applying quantization** to scale than having lower dimensionality and not using quantization."
- Evidence: at 5.5M docs, **256d never exceeds 70% recall** and **512d never exceeds 80% recall** at limit 10, under either quantization scheme.
- At 15.3M vectors / 2048d (voyage-3-large): 90–95% accuracy at <50 ms. Binary needs substantially higher `numCandidates` than scalar to hit 90–95%; scalar has higher QPS (no rescoring); binary costs ~1/4 to serve.
- 3%-selective filter made binary ~**4x** more expensive at low `limit` to reach 90–95% recall.

**Separate quantization enum for Automated Embedding** (`autoEmbed` index type, not `vector`): `"float" | "scalar" | "binary" | "binaryNoRescore"`, default **scalar**; float=4 bytes, scalar ≈1/4 of float, binary ≈1/24 with full-precision rescoring, `binaryNoRescore` = 1 bit, faster/cheaper/less accurate. Scalar recommended with `cosine`, binary/binaryNoRescore with `euclidean`.

## 5. Other limits — VERIFIED unless noted

**Index counts** (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/deployment/feature-compatibility.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/atlas-limits/):
- **3 indexes** (any type, `search` or `vector`) on **Free clusters**; **10 indexes** on **Flex clusters**.
- **Hard limit 2,500 search indexes per cluster.** "Smaller cluster tiers like `M10` might experience performance degradation or out-of-memory errors with far fewer indexes."
- **No documented per-collection index cap** — INFERRED (only per-cluster/per-tier limits are documented).
- Free/Flex only: index definition JSON ≤ **3 KB**; index builds with **>300 fields** fail; Lucene clause limit **1024**.
- Recommended max combined collections+indexes: M10 5,000 / M20–M30 10,000 / M40+ 100,000.

**`numCandidates`**: "**Value must be less than or equal to (`<=`) `10000`**"; must be ≥ `limit`; recommended **≥ 20x `limit`**. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/query/aggregation-stages/vector-search-stage.md

**ANN vs ENN**: `exact: false` (default) = HNSW ANN, requires `numCandidates`; optimal recall "around **90–95%** overlap with ENN". `exact: true` = exhaustive ENN — recommended for <10,000 documents, recall benchmarking, or when a pre-filter matches **<5%** of data. Versions: ANN needs MongoDB v6.0.11/v7.0.2+; ENN needs v6.0.16/v7.0.10/v7.3.2+.

**`indexingMethod`**: `"hnsw"` (default) or `"flat"` (exhaustive, 100% recall, lower CPU/memory, no graph). `flat` added in **preview 07 April 2026**. `hnswOptions.maxEdges` 16–64 (default 16); `hnswOptions.numEdgeCandidates` 100–3200 (default 100); exposed 10 June 2025.

**Filters**: boolean, date, objectId, numeric, string, UUID + arrays thereof. Operators: `$eq $ne $gt $lt $gte $lte $in $nin $exists $not $nor $and $or`. **No documented cap on number of filter fields** — INFERRED.

**Index-size / scale limits**: index stops replicating past **2.1 billion index objects** per replica-set member/shard (use `numPartitions` or shard); documents ≥16 MB fail to index and mark the index STALE (recommend no doc > 8 MB). **No documented maximum total number of vectors and no documented index build-time limit** — INFERRED; the practical ceiling is RAM (whole index held in memory) and the 2.1B object cap.

**Pipeline**: `$vectorSearch` must be the **first stage**; not allowed in view definitions, `$lookup` sub-pipelines, or `$facet`. Sharded clusters may return duplicates during chunk migration.

**Multi-vector fields**: "You can specify multiple `vector` type fields inside the `fields` array" — no documented max. Same embedding field can't be indexed twice in one definition; can't index embeddings inside arrays of documents/objects (though **30 April 2026** added *preview* support for `$vectorSearch` over arrays of embeddings / arrays of embedded documents).

## 6. EU residency & Search Nodes — VERIFIED

**AWS EU regions with dedicated Search Nodes** (verbatim Europe table, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/amazon-aws.md?tabs=europe): `eu-west-1` Ireland, **`eu-central-1` Frankfurt**, `eu-central-2` Zurich, `eu-north-1` Stockholm, `eu-west-2` London, `eu-south-2` Spain. **Not** `eu-west-3` (Paris) or `eu-south-1` (Milan). All 8 AWS EU regions support Free/Flex/M10+ clusters.

**Azure**: Search Nodes supported for M10+ in all Azure regions *except* an exclusion list. **`germanywestcentral` (Frankfurt) is NOT excluded → supported**; `germanynorth` (Berlin) is excluded. Also supported: `westeurope`, `northeurope`, `uksouth`, `francecentral`, `switzerlandnorth`, `polandcentral`, `swedencentral`, `norwayeast`; `italynorth` low-CPU only. Excluded: `francesouth`, `spaincentral`, `swedensouth`, `switzerlandwest`, `ukwest`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/microsoft-azure.md?tabs=europe

**Google Cloud**: Search Nodes available in **all** GCP regions. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/deployment/deployment-options.md

Search tiers in AWS Europe (Low-CPU S30 8 GiB / 53 GiB … S110 512 GiB; High-CPU S10 4 GiB … S80 128 GiB). Production requires **M10+ cluster and S30+ search tier** (or S10/S20 high-CPU). Search Node encryption with customer keys requires Search Nodes **on AWS**.

**EU sovereign offering: NO dedicated product** — VERIFIED by absence + INFERRED. MongoDB Atlas for Government exists only for **US** government (AWS GovCloud + AWS US East/West) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/government/overview/supported-regions/. For the EU, MongoDB offers **data residency**, not sovereignty: region pinning across 110+ regions, multi-region partitioning, and **Atlas Resource Policies** that can forbid cluster creation outside allowed providers/regions (e.g. `azure:westeurope`). No C5 / EU Cloud CoC / EU-sovereign Atlas variant is documented. MongoDB Inc. is US-incorporated and the Atlas control plane runs from US infrastructure, so Frankfurt residency ≠ CLOUD Act immunity — INFERRED from third-party analyses, not a MongoDB statement.

## 7. Hybrid search & native reranking — VERIFIED

- **`$rankFusion`** (Reciprocal Rank Fusion): "**`$rankFusion` is only available for deployments that use MongoDB 8.0 and later.**" Plus: "You must open a support case to use `$rankFusion` on 8.0.X versions." → so **8.0+, not 8.1+**; practical GA is 8.1+. RRF formula: `Σ w / (60 + r(d))`, 60 is MongoDB's sensitivity constant. Single-collection only; each input pipeline must be a Selection Pipeline (only `$match`/`$search`/`$vectorSearch`/`$sample`/`$geoNear`/`$sort`/`$skip`/`$limit`) *and* a Ranked Pipeline. `scoreDetails: true` for per-pipeline rank/weight breakdown. `$rankFusion` **on Views requires 8.2+**. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/rankFusion.md
- **`$scoreFusion`**: "**`$scoreFusion` is only available for deployments that use MongoDB 8.3+.**" `input.normalization: "none"|"sigmoid"|"minMaxScaler"`, `combination.method: "avg"|"expression"`, weights per pipeline; all normalizations map scores to 0–1. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/scoreFusion/
- **`$rerank`** (native reranking, **Preview**, added **30 June 2026**): reorders documents using Voyage AI rerankers `rerank-2.5`, `rerank-2.5-lite`, `rerank-2`, `rerank-2-lite`. Requires **MongoDB 8.3+** and enabling Native Reranking in Project Settings. `numDocsToRerank` **≤ 1000**. Cannot be used on self-managed/Atlas Local deployments, inside `$rankFusion`/`$scoreFusion` input pipelines, or on Views. Replaces `$meta: "score"`. Runs off-cluster (not on your Atlas resources); billed separately. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/query/aggregation-stages/rerank.md
- Hybrid-search tutorial prerequisite: Atlas cluster on **MongoDB v8.0+**. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/tutorial/hybrid-search.md

---

## Corrections to your priors

1. **4096 is stale** — it is 8192 since 30 March 2025.
2. **3.75x / 24x are exactly right**, and the vector values themselves shrink 4x/32x (the gap is the uncompressed HNSW graph).
3. **">=1024 dims for binary quantization"** — the doc recommendation is >1024 dims for **any** quantization at large scale, not binary-specific; binary's hard requirement is only that `numDimensions` be a **multiple of 8**.
4. **`$rankFusion` is 8.0+ (support case on 8.0.X), not 8.1+**; `$scoreFusion` is 8.3+; there is also now a true native reranker (`$rerank`, 8.3+, Preview).
5. **Frankfurt is fine** for Search Nodes on both AWS (`eu-central-1`) and Azure (`germanywestcentral`).</result>

Index page: array of numbers of one of: BSON `double`; `BinData` vector subtype `float32`; `BinData` subtype `int1`; `BinData` subtype `int8`.

- Changelog phrasing (02 Dec 2024): scalar "~75%" memory reduction, binary "~97%".
- **Rescoring**: only for binary (and for exact search against binary *or* scalar quantized vectors). Query float vector is binarized using the same midpoint, candidates identified in binary space, then re-evaluated against **original float values**. "The full fidelity vectors are stored in their own data structure **on disk**, and are only referenced during rescoring."
- Sizing: storage:RAM ratio ≈ **4:1 (scalar)**, **24:1 (binary)**; binary index disk ≈ `original size * (25/24)`; allocate free disk = **125%** of estimated index size. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/deployment/deployment-options.md

**Your ">=1024 dims for binary" recall — partially right, but it's about quantization generally, not binary specifically** — VERIFIED at https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/benchmark/results.md:
- "**We recommend over 1024 dimensions when running larger workloads with quantization.**"

- Evidence: at 5.5M docs, **256d never exceeds 70% recall** and **512d never exceeds 80% recall** at limit 10, under either quantization scheme.

**`numCandidates`**: "**Value must be less than or equal to (`<=`) `10000`**"; must be ≥ `limit`; recommended **≥ 20x `limit`**. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/query/aggregation-stages/vector-search-stage.md

**Multi-vector fields**: "You can specify multiple `vector` type fields inside the `fields` array" — no documented max. All 8 AWS EU regions support Free/Flex/M10+ clusters.

Also supported: `westeurope`, `northeurope`, `uksouth`, `francecentral`, `switzerlandnorth`, `polandcentral`, `swedencentral`, `norwayeast`; `italynorth` low-CPU only. Excluded: `francesouth`, `spaincentral`, `swedensouth`, `switzerlandwest`, `ukwest`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/microsoft-azure.md?tabs=europe

**Google Cloud**: Search Nodes available in **all** GCP regions. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/deployment/deployment-options.md

Search tiers in AWS Europe (Low-CPU S30 8 GiB / 53 GiB … S110 512 GiB; High-CPU S10 4 GiB … S80 128 GiB). Production requires **M10+ cluster and S30+ search tier** (or S10/S20 high-CPU). Search Node encryption with customer keys requires Search Nodes **on AWS**.

**EU sovereign offering: NO dedicated product** — VERIFIED by absence + INFERRED. MongoDB Atlas for Government exists only for **US** government (AWS GovCloud + AWS US East/West) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/government/overview/supported-regions/. For the EU, MongoDB offers **data residency**, not sovereignty: region pinning across 110+ regions, multi-region partitioning, and **Atlas Resource Policies** that can forbid cluster creation outside allowed providers/regions (e.g. `azure:westeurope`). No C5 / EU Cloud CoC / EU-sovereign Atlas variant is documented. Single-collection only; each input pipeline must be a Selection Pipeline (only `$match`/`$search`/`$vectorSearch`/`$sample`/`$geoNear`/`$sort`/`$skip`/`$limit`) *and* a Ranked Pipeline. `scoreDetails: true` for per-pipeline rank/weight breakdown. `$rankFusion` **on Views requires 8.2+**. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/rankFusion.md

The eve docs digest is back, and it surfaces a blocker I need to put in front of you before the rest of the plan, because it may change what you want to build.

## eve has no documented answer for your two hard requirements

The agent grepped all 79 doc files for `region|residenc|GDPR|frankfurt|fra1|iad1|data.transfer`. **Zero hits.** There is no `region` option on `defineAgent`, `defineSandbox`, `eveChannel`, or anywhere else in the documented surface.

And separately: **there is no data-deletion API.** No session-delete route, no purge, no erase helper. `agent-config.md` states that session expiration "does not delete stored session data."

That matters because of what eve stores. Durable session state on Vercel is held in **Vercel Workflow**, and it contains the full conversation plus tool inputs and outputs. For your product a session transcript *is* personal data — a voice memo about a named person, a forwarded client email. So Art. 17 erasure would have a reachable copy in MongoDB and an unreachable copy in Vercel Workflow.

Three further defaults compound it:
- **Telemetry records everything by default.** `recordInputs` and `recordOutputs` both default to `true` — full message history and model outputs on every step span. The docs say plainly: "For sensitive, regulated, or production data, set `recordInputs` and `recordOutputs` to `false`."
- **`$eve.title` is framework-owned and not configurable** — it puts a truncated version of the first user message into Vercel Workflow run metadata regardless of your instrumentation config.
- **Local traces capture system prompt, messages, and tool I/O** (32 KB cap) unless `EVE_TRACES_CONTENT=off`.

The documented escape hatch is `experimental.workflow.world: "@workflow/world-postgres"` on a self-hosted Nitro service — but `experimental` is explicitly labelled "opt-in settings that can change or disappear in any release. Treat them as unstable." Taking it means giving up Vercel Workflow, Vercel Sandbox, Vercel Cron and the Agent Runs dashboard — most of eve's operational value — while keeping its 0.x churn risk (v0.29.5, 88 releases, `@workflow/core` vendored at `5.0.0-beta.38`).

**This is a docs gap, not necessarily a product gap.** Vercel Workflow may well support EU region pinning; eve's documentation simply doesn't say. That's a question worth putting to your Vercel contact directly, and I'd treat the answer as a gate on the whole approach.

## What eve is genuinely excellent at, and it's the part you asked for

Setting residency aside, the fit is strong and specific:

- **The eval framework is unusually complete for a 0.x project** — typed event matchers, deterministic assertions plus LLM judges, dataset fan-out, live-turn coordination, remote targets, JUnit and Braintrust reporters, real exit codes. `t.judge.autoevals.closedQA("cites a source")` is a one-liner for the citation check you need.
- **The review queue maps exactly onto `approval` policies.** Parked approvals survive redeploys, and the docs' own worked example is a cross-tenant denial reading `session.auth.current?.attributes.tenantId`.
- **Multi-tenant auth maps onto better-auth with no fighting** — the docs describe stamping `attributes.tenantId` from the verified session on every create/continue, which is precisely your active-org model.

Two sharp edges you'd need to design around regardless:
- **Route auth does not enforce session ownership.** Stated twice in the docs. `sessionId` is a bearer capability; you must persist session→tenant ownership yourself and check it before proxying `POST /eve/v1/session/:id` and the stream route. For a multi-tenant German product this is the most likely security hole.
- **Everything is at-least-once, with "no key collapses a retry."** Interrupted steps re-run and hooks re-fire. Your idempotent `deterministicId` + `insertIgnoringDuplicate` discipline stops being a nicety and becomes a framework requirement.

I'm still waiting on the AI Elements and EU-retrieval research — that determines the UI layer and what replaces `$rerank`. I'll fold everything into one implementation plan when it lands, structured around whichever residency answer you get.

# A) Hugging Face Inference Endpoints

## A1. Regions — only ONE EU region exists

**VERIFIED** via the live public catalog API `https://api.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v2/provider` (queried 2026-08-03):

## A2. Is region pinning a hard guarantee?

- **VERIFIED**: The container (inference engine + model weights) runs on the instance in the selected region. ## A4. HF Inference Providers — NOT EU-safe

**VERIFIED, and worse than "undocumented":**
- Provider list (https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/en/index): Cerebras, Cohere, DeepInfra, Fal AI, Featherless, Fireworks, Groq, HF Inference, Novita, Nscale, **OVHcloud AI Endpoints**, Public AI, Replicate, **Scaleway**, Together, WaveSpeedAI, Z.ai.
- **No provider geography is documented anywhere.** The only sovereignty language is marketing prose on two provider pages: Scaleway *"is a European cloud provider"* (https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/en/providers/scaleway) and OVHcloud *"enables developers to easily integrate AI capabilities … with data sovereignty, privacy, and GDPR compliance"* (https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/en/providers/ovhcloud). **Neither is a contractual residency commitment from HF.**
- **Default routing is `auto` = fastest provider**, i.e. non-deterministic and can land on US infra. You *can* pin: `provider="scaleway"` in the SDK, or `model-id:provider` suffix in the OpenAI-compatible route. There is also a per-account **preference order** setting, but it only sets order — it is **not an allowlist/restriction** and only applies to widgets/snippets + the `:preferred` policy.
- **Embeddings via Providers:** only **HF Inference** and **Scaleway** support Feature Extraction. Scaleway's embedding model is `Qwen3-Embedding-8B`. **No provider supports reranking at all** — there is no rerank task in the Providers task matrix.
- **HF's own data handling is actually good** (https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/en/security): *"We do not store the request body or response when routing requests through Hugging Face. Logs are kept for debugging purposes for up to 30 days, but no user data or tokens are stored."* But: *"External providers are responsible for their own security measures"* and *"please refer to the Data Security Policies of each provider."*

**Conclusion: treat Inference Providers as NOT EU-safe.** Even pinning `provider="scaleway"` leaves you with (a) a US-incorporated router in the path, (b) no reranking, (c) no contractual residency guarantee from either HF or your sub-processor chain. Rejected.

## 1. Hugging Face Text Embeddings Inference (TEI)

**Version & license**

## 4. ONNX / CPU serving

**sentence-transformers backends** — **[V]** https://sbert.net/docs/sentence_transformer/usage/efficiency.html
Three backends: `torch`, `onnx` (optimum + ONNX Runtime), `openvino`. Benchmarked on `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (22.7M), `bge-base-en-v1.5` (109M), `mxbai-embed-large-v1` (335M), `bge-m3` (567M).
- CPU (i7): ONNX **1.39x**, OpenVINO **1.29x**, **ONNX + int8 dynamic quantization 3.08x** (shortest-text dataset).
- GPU (RTX 3090): ONNX 1.46x, ONNX-O4 **1.83x**, fp16 1.54x, bf16 1.53x.
- The docs explicitly warn the aggregate numbers hide per-model/per-batch variation.

**Intel/Optimum CPU numbers (the most credible CPU anchor)** — **[V]** https://huggingface.co/blog/intel-fast-embedding
Hardware: 4th-gen Intel Xeon 8480+ (Sapphire Rapids), 1 socket, 22–56 cores.
- Latency at **batch size 1**: BGE-small (45M) **<10 ms**, BGE-base (110M) **<10 ms**, **BGE-large (355M) <20 ms**. Up to **4.5x latency speedup** vs fp32 baseline.
- Throughput: **up to 4x** vs bf16 baseline; peak at batch size 128.
- **Accuracy retention (int8 vs fp32): reranking <1% error-rate delta; retrieval <1.55%. BGE-large retrieval 0.5429 → 0.5346 (−1.53%).**

**int8 dynamic quantization, ONNX Runtime specifics** — **[V]** https://medium.com/nixiesearch/how-to-compute-llm-embeddings-3x-faster-with-model-quantization-25523d9b4ce5
- Hardware AWS `m7i.2xlarge` (8 vCPU, **AVX-VNNI**) vs AMD Zen2 (no VNNI).
- With VNNI: e5-base/large **>3x faster** than fp32. **e5-base-v2: 50 ms fp32-optimized → 15 ms QInt8 opt-level-2 (3.5x)**. e5-small only 1.38x (too small to amortize).
- Without VNNI (Zen2): only **1.2–1.6x**; QInt8 ~15% faster than QUInt8.
- **fp16 on CPU is 2x–7x SLOWER than fp32** — do not ship fp16 CPU.
- ONNX graph optimization alone: level 1 **+33%**, level 2 **+4%** more.

**Realistic CPU throughput, ~300M-param XLM-R-class encoder (multilingual-e5-large 560M / bge-m3 568M)** — **[I]**
Derived from the two anchors above plus FLOP scaling (forward ≈ 2·P·T):
- At **short inputs (~64–128 tok)**, int8 ONNX on a VNNI-capable 8-vCPU box: roughly **30–80 docs/s** for a 300M model, **15–40 docs/s** for a 560M model.
- At **512 tokens**, the same box: roughly **3–10 docs/s** for 560M, **6–20 docs/s** for 300M. So a 100k-chunk German corpus at 512 tokens is on the order of **3–9 CPU-hours on 8 vCPUs** — feasible for batch indexing, painful for interactive.
- On a **56-core Sapphire Rapids socket** these scale roughly linearly with cores until memory bandwidth binds; expect ~5–8x the 8-vCPU numbers.
- **Non-VNNI CPUs (older Xeon, Zen2, ARM without i8mm) lose most of the int8 win** — check the target instance's flags before budgeting.

**Ultra-cheap options**
- **model2vec / static embeddings [V]**: https://huggingface.co/blog/static-embeddings — `static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1` is **397x faster on CPU / 24x on GPU** than `all-mpnet-base-v2` while retaining **87.4%** of its quality; measured **107,419.51 sentences/s on CPU** vs **270.40 sentences/s** for all-mpnet-base-v2. Multilingual variant `static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1` (Apache-2.0) is **~125x faster on CPU / ~10x on GPU** than `multilingual-e5-small`, retaining **92.3% average on STS**. model2vec itself (MIT, MinishLab): ~30 MB on disk, up to 500x CPU speedup, 50–100k docs/s on a MacBook CPU.
  - **[I]** Caveat for German RAG: static embeddings are bag-of-token-vectors — no word order, no negation handling. Fine as a **first-stage recall net or a cheap dedup/clustering signal**, not as your only retriever, and definitely not as the reranker.
- **fastembed (Qdrant)**: ONNX-only, quantized, no torch dependency. Search hits quoting "2,500 qps vs 120" and "12x" are from SEO-farm blogs (`markaicode.com`, `johal.in`) — **not verified, do not quote those numbers.** The library itself is real and is the pragmatic "pip install and go" CPU path.

**FP16/BF16 weight VRAM (2 bytes/param) — [I], arithmetic:**

| Size | Weights | + runtime slack (TEI, 16k batch tokens) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3B | ~0.61 GB | ~1.5–2.5 GB |
| 0.6B | ~1.19 GB | ~2.5–4 GB |
| 4B | ~8.0 GB | ~10–13 GB |
| 8B | ~15.1–16.4 GB | ~18–22 GB |

**What fits — [I]:**
- **L4 (24 GB, Ada sm89, 72 W)** and **A10G (24 GB, Ampere sm86)**: 0.3B/0.6B trivially; you can co-host an embedder **and** a reranker in two TEI containers on one card. 4B comfortable. **8B fp16 fits (~16 GB) but leaves only ~6–8 GB** — fine at 512-token passages, tight at 8k context or large batches. L4 is the cheapest sane production card for TEI; A10G is ~15–25% faster on fp16 GEMM.
- **RTX 4090 (24 GB, sm89)**: ~1.5–2x an L4 on fp16 for the same models, but no ECC, no NVLink, and NVIDIA's datacenter EULA restricts GeForce in rented DCs — check your German host's terms.
- **L40S (48 GB, Ada)**: 8B embedder + 0.6B–4B reranker co-resident with room to spare. **[I]** This is the sweet spot if you want a single card doing both stages.
- **H100 (80 GB)**: everything, including 8B embed + 8B rerank + long context. Overkill unless you're batch-indexing millions of chunks.

**Batch-size and long-context effects — [I], arithmetic:**
- TEI's `--max-batch-tokens` (default **16384**) is the real VRAM dial, not "batch size". Activation memory scales ~linearly with total batch tokens when FlashAttention is on.
- **The 8k blowup is an attention-materialization problem.** Without FlashAttention, one attention score matrix costs `batch × heads × L² × 2 bytes`. For **L=8192, 16 heads: 16 × 8192² × 2 B = 2.15 GB for a single sequence, per layer step.** With FlashAttention it's O(L) and effectively free. Practical consequences:
  - **Turing/T4 images ship with FA off by default** (precision bug) → do not run 8k context on T4.
  - **ONNX Runtime / CPU paths generally do not use FlashAttention** → 8k-token CPU embedding is memory-hostile. Chunk to ≤1024 tokens on CPU.
- **Decoder-based embedders (Qwen3) additionally pay KV cache during prefill — [I]:** Qwen3-0.6B (28 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128) = `2×28×8×128×2 B` = **112 KiB/token** → **0.88 GiB for one 8k sequence**. Qwen3-8B (36 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128) = **144 KiB/token** → **1.13 GiB per 8k sequence**. Batch 8 of those on an L4 running an 8B model will OOM.
- **vLLM specific [V/I]**: `--gpu-memory-utilization` defaults to 0.9, so vLLM claims 90% of the card regardless of model size — you cannot naively co-host a vLLM reranker and a vLLM embedder on one GPU without lowering it on both.

**Third-party ballparks (secondary source, treat as order-of-magnitude only)** — Spheron blog https://www.spheron.network/blog/self-host-embedding-reranker-tei-gpu-cloud/ **[I, low authority]**: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B ~2 GB, 4B ~8 GB, 8B ~16 GB, BGE-M3 ~2.5 GB, BGE-large ~1.5 GB — consistent with the arithmetic above, which is the main reason to trust it at all.

**Embedding, GPU** — **[I, low authority]** (Spheron, same caveat): tokens/s at batch 512 — BGE-M3 on A100 ~60,000; on H100 ~90,000; Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B on A100 ~55,000, on RTX 4090 ~20,000. Single-query p50 embed **5–15 ms**.
**[V]** TEI's own README benchmark banner is `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5` on an **NVIDIA A10 at 512 tokens**, charted at batch 1 and batch 32 (charts only, no tabulated figures).

**Embedding, CPU** — **[V]** BGE-large (355M) int8 on Sapphire Rapids: **<20 ms at batch 1**; e5-base-v2: **15 ms** int8 vs 50 ms fp32 on 8 vCPU.
**[V]** EmbeddingGemma-300M: **<15 ms for 256 input tokens on EdgeTPU**, sub-200 MB RAM with QAT. https://developers.googleblog.com/en/introducing-embeddinggemma/
**[V]** `gte-multilingual-base` (305M) claims **10x inference speedup vs decoder-only embedders** like gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct. https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-multilingual-base

**Cross-encoder reranking — this is your critical path. Best numbers found:**

**[V]** https://bigdataboutique.com/blog/rag-reranking-improving-retrieval-quality-with-cross-encoders (explicitly labelled "ballparks", A10/L4-class GPU):
| Model | Latency |
|---|---|
| MiniLM-class (22M) | **50–80 ms for 100 docs @ 256 tokens** |
| **BGE-reranker-v2-m3 (568M)** | **80–200 ms for 100 docs @ 512 tokens** |
| bge-reranker-v2-gemma (2B) | **200–400 ms** |

> "A single A10 typically handles **50–100 QPS at top-100 rerank depth at 512-token passages.**"
> Production systems see "**under 200 ms of added latency**" reranking 50–100 candidates.

**[V]** https://aimultiple.com/rerankers — measured, **NVIDIA H100 PCIe 80GB (Runpod), transformers 5.2.0 / torch 2.8.0 / CUDA 12.8.1, 100 candidates/query, 300 queries**, retriever `multilingual-e5-base`, corpus = English Amazon reviews (short docs, not 512 tokens):
| Model | Rerank time (100 docs) | Hit@1 |
|---|---|---|
| `gte-reranker-modernbert-base` (149M) | **~170 ms** | 83.00% |
| `jina-reranker-v3` (560M) | **~188 ms** | 81.33% |
| `nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-1b-v2` (1.2B) | **~243 ms** | 83.00% |
| `Qwen3-Reranker-4B` (4B) | **>1,000 ms** | 77.67% |
| no reranker baseline | — | 62.67% |

**Practical read for your 20–50 candidates @ ~512 tokens — [I]:**
- **20–50 docs is ~0.2–0.5x the 100-doc cost** (compute is close to linear in doc count at these batch sizes).
- **`bge-reranker-v2-m3` (568M XLM-R, Apache-2.0) on an L4/A10G: ~40–100 ms for 20–50 passages @ 512 tokens.** This is the number to plan around for a German product.
- **`gte-multilingual-reranker-base` (306M, Apache-2.0, 8k ctx) on the same card: ~25–60 ms** — roughly half the FLOPs of bge-v2-m3, and it runs in TEI today.
- **Anything ≥4B (Qwen3-Reranker-4B/8B) pushes you past 500 ms–1 s** for 20–50 docs even on strong hardware. Not viable in an interactive path.
- **CPU reranking of 50 × 512-token passages is ~5–20 s** for a 300–568M cross-encoder even with int8. **Do not put a CPU cross-encoder on the request path.** If you must be CPU-only, use `cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2` (22.7M, Apache-2.0) — but it is English-only, so for German you'd need a distilled multilingual MiniLM.
- **Two-stage RAG budget [I]**: bi-encoder query embed (5–15 ms GPU) + vector search (5–30 ms) + rerank 30 candidates (40–100 ms) ≈ **60–150 ms** before the LLM. Matches the "<200 ms added" figure above.

1. **[V] IONOS is the only EU-native managed provider with a genuine reranking endpoint** — `POST https://openai.inference.de-txl.ionos.com/v1/rerank` with `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Reranker-8B`, hosted in Berlin, at **$0.045/M tokens**. ## 8. Licensing landmines for a commercial German product — [V]

- **Every current Jina text model is CC-BY-NC-4.0**: `jina-embeddings-v3` (572M), `jina-embeddings-v5-text-small` (596M, released 2026-02-18, 32K ctx, MRL 32–1024, MTEB-multilingual 67.0 / English 71.7), `jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual` (278M), `jina-reranker-v3` (597M), `jina-reranker-v3.5` (0.6B, 131K ctx, released 2026-07-27). **Non-commercial. You cannot self-host these in a paid product** without a commercial licence from Jina. The one exception: **`jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-de` is Apache-2.0** (161M, German+English bilingual) — and T-Systems hosts exactly that one in Germany.
- **`google/embeddinggemma-300m`** is under the **Gemma licence** (not OSI, gated on HF, use restrictions apply) — usually fine commercially but requires accepting terms and passing `HF_TOKEN` to TEI.

## 9. Bottom line for your stack

**[I]** Recommendation, given a German-language RAG product that must self-host or use an EU host:

- **Engine: TEI v1.9.3 (Apache-2.0)** for both stages. Two containers on one GPU: `ghcr.io/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference:89-1.9` (L4/L40S/4090) or `:86-1.9` (A10G). It has `/embed` + `/rerank` + `dimensions` (MRL) + Prometheus + OTLP + `--api-key`, boots in seconds, and is the lowest-latency option at batch 1. Local dev on your Mac via `brew install text-embeddings-inference` (Metal).
- **Embedder**: `intfloat/multilingual-e5-large-instruct` (560M, MIT) or `Alibaba-NLP/gte-multilingual-base` (305M, Apache-2.0, 8192 ctx, 768 dims — ~1.8x cheaper to run, and 768 dims halves your Atlas Search vector index size vs 1024). Set `--default-prompt-name query` for e5.
- **Reranker**: `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3` (568M, Apache-2.0, XLM-R — strong German) or `Alibaba-NLP/gte-multilingual-reranker-base` (306M, Apache-2.0) if you need the extra ~2x speed. Both run in TEI today. Budget **40–100 ms for 20–50 passages @ 512 tokens on an L4**.
- **Avoid**: Qwen3-Reranker (unsupported in TEI, >500 ms in vLLM), any Jina model (CC-BY-NC), Scaleway's rerank endpoint (it's just cosine similarity), OVH for reranking (doesn't exist).
- **Reach for vLLM only** if you specifically need Qwen3-Reranker / mxbai-rerank-v2 / bge-reranker-v2-gemma, or a Cohere-compatible `/v2/rerank` wire format — and read its own warning that pooling models aren't optimized there.
- **EU managed fallback**: IONOS (Berlin, real rerank endpoint, $0.02/M for bge-m3 embeddings) is the only one that covers both stages today. Scaleway dedicated + custom HF model import is the escape hatch if you need a specific cross-encoder on French soil.
- **CPU is viable for indexing, not for the request path**: int8 ONNX via TEI's `ort` backend on VNNI-capable hardware gets you ~3–10 docs/s at 512 tokens for a 560M model. Cross-encoder reranking on CPU is 5–20 s for 50 passages — don't.

## 4. ONNX / CPU serving

**sentence-transformers backends** — **[V]** https://sbert.net/docs/sentence_transformer/usage/efficiency.html
Three backends: `torch`, `onnx` (optimum + ONNX Runtime), `openvino`. Benchmarked on `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (22.7M), `bge-base-en-v1.5` (109M), `mxbai-embed-large-v1` (335M), `bge-m3` (567M).
- CPU (i7): ONNX **1.39x**, OpenVINO **1.29x**, **ONNX + int8 dynamic quantization 3.08x** (shortest-text dataset).
- GPU (RTX 3090): ONNX 1.46x, ONNX-O4 **1.83x**, fp16 1.54x, bf16 1.53x.
- The docs explicitly warn the aggregate numbers hide per-model/per-batch variation.

**Intel/Optimum CPU numbers (the most credible CPU anchor)** — **[V]** https://huggingface.co/blog/intel-fast-embedding
Hardware: 4th-gen Intel Xeon 8480+ (Sapphire Rapids), 1 socket, 22–56 cores.
- Latency at **batch size 1**: BGE-small (45M) **<10 ms**, BGE-base (110M) **<10 ms**, **BGE-large (355M) <20 ms**. Up to **4.5x latency speedup** vs fp32 baseline.
- Throughput: **up to 4x** vs bf16 baseline; peak at batch size 128.
- **Accuracy retention (int8 vs fp32): reranking <1% error-rate delta; retrieval <1.55%. BGE-large retrieval 0.5429 → 0.5346 (−1.53%).**

**int8 dynamic quantization, ONNX Runtime specifics** — **[V]** https://medium.com/nixiesearch/how-to-compute-llm-embeddings-3x-faster-with-model-quantization-25523d9b4ce5
- Hardware AWS `m7i.2xlarge` (8 vCPU, **AVX-VNNI**) vs AMD Zen2 (no VNNI).
- With VNNI: e5-base/large **>3x faster** than fp32. **e5-base-v2: 50 ms fp32-optimized → 15 ms QInt8 opt-level-2 (3.5x)**. e5-small only 1.38x (too small to amortize).
- Without VNNI (Zen2): only **1.2–1.6x**; QInt8 ~15% faster than QUInt8.
- **fp16 on CPU is 2x–7x SLOWER than fp32** — do not ship fp16 CPU.
- ONNX graph optimization alone: level 1 **+33%**, level 2 **+4%** more.

**Realistic CPU throughput, ~300M-param XLM-R-class encoder (multilingual-e5-large 560M / bge-m3 568M)** — **[I]**
Derived from the two anchors above plus FLOP scaling (forward ≈ 2·P·T):
- At **short inputs (~64–128 tok)**, int8 ONNX on a VNNI-capable 8-vCPU box: roughly **30–80 docs/s** for a 300M model, **15–40 docs/s** for a 560M model.
- At **512 tokens**, the same box: roughly **3–10 docs/s** for 560M, **6–20 docs/s** for 300M. So a 100k-chunk German corpus at 512 tokens is on the order of **3–9 CPU-hours on 8 vCPUs** — feasible for batch indexing, painful for interactive.
- On a **56-core Sapphire Rapids socket** these scale roughly linearly with cores until memory bandwidth binds; expect ~5–8x the 8-vCPU numbers.
- **Non-VNNI CPUs (older Xeon, Zen2, ARM without i8mm) lose most of the int8 win** — check the target instance's flags before budgeting.

**Ultra-cheap options**
- **model2vec / static embeddings [V]**: https://huggingface.co/blog/static-embeddings — `static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1` is **397x faster on CPU / 24x on GPU** than `all-mpnet-base-v2` while retaining **87.4%** of its quality; measured **107,419.51 sentences/s on CPU** vs **270.40 sentences/s** for all-mpnet-base-v2. Multilingual variant `static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1` (Apache-2.0) is **~125x faster on CPU / ~10x on GPU** than `multilingual-e5-small`, retaining **92.3% average on STS**. model2vec itself (MIT, MinishLab): ~30 MB on disk, up to 500x CPU speedup, 50–100k docs/s on a MacBook CPU.
  - **[I]** Caveat for German RAG: static embeddings are bag-of-token-vectors — no word order, no negation handling. Fine as a **first-stage recall net or a cheap dedup/clustering signal**, not as your only retriever, and definitely not as the reranker.
- **fastembed (Qdrant)**: ONNX-only, quantized, no torch dependency. Search hits quoting "2,500 qps vs 120" and "12x" are from SEO-farm blogs (`markaicode.com`, `johal.in`) — **not verified, do not quote those numbers.** The library itself is real and is the pragmatic "pip install and go" CPU path.

**FP16/BF16 weight VRAM (2 bytes/param) — [I], arithmetic:**

| Size | Weights | + runtime slack (TEI, 16k batch tokens) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3B | ~0.61 GB | ~1.5–2.5 GB |
